Applejack (drink):
{{Short description|Alcoholic drink produced from apples}}
{{ntbcw|text=the American [[breakfast cereal]] known as [[Apple Jacks]]}}
[[file:ApplejohnV1.jpg|thumb|250px|Bottles of applejack demonstrating the [[apple cider]]-like coloration of the [[alcoholic spirit|spirit]] with an [[apple]] to the bottles' right]]
'''Applejack''' is type of [[apple brandy]] traditionally associated with the [[Colonial history of the United States|American colonial era]]<ref>{{cite news|last=Morganstern|first=Adam|title=Applejack: America's Original Distilled Spirit Returns To Its Roots|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/adammorganstern/2018/04/30/applejack-americas-original-distilled-spirit-returns-to-its-roots/|work=[[Forbes]]|publisher=Forbes Media|date=30 April 2018|language=en|quote=It’s an apple brandy, historically called Applejack in America|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190920222442/https://www.forbes.com/sites/adammorganstern/2018/04/30/applejack-americas-original-distilled-spirit-returns-to-its-roots/|archive-date=20 September 2019}}</ref> and is generally considered to be one of the United States' "original" [[alcoholic spirits|spirits]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Morganstern|first=Adam|title=Applejack: America's Original Distilled Spirit Returns To Its Roots|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/adammorganstern/2018/04/30/applejack-americas-original-distilled-spirit-returns-to-its-roots/|work=[[Forbes]]|publisher=Forbes Media|date=30 April 2018|language=en|quote=Long before there was such a thing as American whiskey, the Laird family started producing Applejack in New Jersey in 1698.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190920222442/https://www.forbes.com/sites/adammorganstern/2018/04/30/applejack-americas-original-distilled-spirit-returns-to-its-roots/|archive-date=20 September 2019}}</ref> Applejack was traditionally created via [[freeze distillation]] (or "jacking") of [[apple wine]] or [[apple cider]] and while [[homebrewing]] methods may still involve freeze distillation, modern professional [[brewing|brewers]] use standard [[alcohol distillation|distillation]] processes.

Very popular in the early- to mid-[[Colonial History of the United States|colonial era]], the drink's prevalence declined in the [[17th century|17th-]] and [[18th century|18th-centuries]] amid competition from other [[alcoholic spirits]] as they became easier to manufacture.<ref name="pop">{{cite encyclopedia|title=Applejack|encyclopedia=Alcohol in Popular Culture: An Encyclopedia |editor=Rachel Black|author=Ken Albala|year=2010|publisher=ABC-CLIO|location=Santa Barbara, CA|isbn=978-0-313-38048-8 |page=10| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mb0SZIYCXREC&pg=PA10}}</ref><ref name="Foley">Michael Foley, ''Drinking with the Saints: The Sinner's Guide to a Holy Happy Hour'' (2015, {{ISBN|1-62157-383-4}}): Perhaps the most interesting option is applejack, the first distilled liquor native to North America and a great favorite among the colonists. [Now] usually a blend of apple brandy and neutral spirits that retains the flavor of the apples[.]</ref><ref name="SBC"/> Applejack experienced a revival during the [[Prohibition era]], primarily due to the drink's ease-of-manufacture, but again declined in prevalence after the [[Repeal of Prohibition in the United States|repeal of Prohibition]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Moskin|first=Julia|title=America’s First Moonshine, Applejack, Returns in Sleeker Style|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/02/dining/drinks/applejack.html|work=The New York Times|publisher=The New York Times Company|date=2 February 2021|location=United States|language=en|quote=Up to and through the Prohibition era, there were countless producers making and (illegally) selling applejack in the Blue Ridge Mountains, where roads were limited and trees provided thick cover from government agents.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202162952/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/02/dining/drinks/applejack.html|archive-date=2 February 2021}}</ref> It experienced another resurgence in popularity in the mid-[[2010s]]<ref name="ModernPopularity"></ref> and early-[[2020s]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Moskin|first=Julia|title=America’s First Moonshine, Applejack, Returns in Sleeker Style|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/02/dining/drinks/applejack.html|work=The New York Times|publisher=The New York Times Company|date=2 February 2021|location=United States|language=en|quote=The Blue Ridge Mountains aren’t the only region with a crush of new applejack makers in the last decade.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202162952/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/02/02/dining/drinks/applejack.html|archive-date=2 February 2021}}</ref>

Applejack is generally considered to be a type of [[brandy]]<ref>{{cite news|last=Saladino|first=Emily|title=Applejack vs. Apple Brandy: The Main Differences|url=https://www.liquor.com/applejack-apple-brandy-guide-8347204|work=Liquor.com|publisher=[[People Inc.]]|date=10 October 2023|language=en|quote=All applejack is apple brandy, but not all apple brandy is applejack.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241001110953/https://www.liquor.com/applejack-apple-brandy-guide-8347204|archive-date=1 October 2024}}</ref> and is, in the United States, legally classified as such.<ref>{{cite web|title=Applejack vs. Brandy vs. Whiskey: What Sets Laird’s Applejack Apart|url=https://www.lairdandcompany.com/post/applejack-vs-brandy-vs-whiskey-what-sets-laird-s-applejack-apart|website=Laird & Company|date=16 December 2025|language=en|quote=According to U.S. regulations, applejack is classified as apple brandy—a spirit distilled from fermented apple juice and aged in oak.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251216201436/https://www.lairdandcompany.com/post/applejack-vs-brandy-vs-whiskey-what-sets-laird-s-applejack-apart|archive-date=16 December 2025}}</ref> Applejack is used in several [[cocktails]], including the [[Jack Rose (cocktail)|Jack Rose]].<ref name="pop" />

== History ==
[[File:Home of Laird's Apple Jack sign, Laird & Company, Scobeyville, NJ.jpg|thumb|Laird's Apple Jack sign in Scobeyville]]
Applejack was first produced in [[colonial New Jersey]] in 1698 by William Laird, a [[Scots Americans|Scots American]] who settled in [[Monmouth County, New Jersey|Monmouth County]].<ref name="New Jersey Monthly">Karen Tina Harrison, [http://njmonthly.com/articles/restaurants/jersey-lightning.html Jersey Lightning], ''New Jersey Monthly'', July 13, 2009.</ref> The drink was once known as '''Jersey Lightning'''.<ref name="New Jersey Monthly"/> Laird's great-grandson, Robert Laird, who served in the [[Continental Army]], incorporated Laird's Distillery in 1780,<ref name="New Jersey Monthly"/> after previously operating a [[tavern]].<ref name="Ginzburg"/> The oldest licensed applejack distillery in the United States, [[Laird & Company]] of [[Scobeyville, New Jersey]], was until the 2000s the country's only remaining producer of applejack, and continues to dominate applejack production.<ref name="New Jersey Monthly" /><ref>Joseph D'Agnese, [https://www.nytimes.com/2000/06/11/nyregion/in-search-of-not-your-toddler-s-apple-cider.html In Search Of ...; Not Your Toddler's Apple Cider], ''The New York Times'' (June 11, 2000).</ref> 

Once popular in early America, applejack declined in popularity due to the rise of other spirits that were easier to manufacture on a commercial basis, including rum and whiskey (especially bourbon) in the 19th century and gin, vodka, and tequila in the 20th century.<ref name="pop"/> In 1920, with the beginning of the [[Prohibition era]], Laird's ended the production of liquor and began producing [[apple juice]]. In 1931, John Evans Laird received permission to produce apple brandy for "medicinal purposes" and stockpiled its product until the repeal of Prohibition in 1933.<ref name="Ginzburg">Ralph Ginzburg, [https://www.nytimes.com/1986/10/26/nyregion/harvest-is-in-at-centuries-old-distillery.html Harvest Is In at Centuries-Old Distillery], ''The New York Times'' (October 26, 1986).</ref>

Applejack has been associated with four [[presidents of the United States]]: After the American Revolution, [[George Washington]] requested from Robert Laird his family's recipe for applejack; [[Abraham Lincoln]] served it during a [[Early life and career of Abraham Lincoln|brief stint as a tavern keeper]] in [[Springfield, Illinois]]; [[Franklin D. Roosevelt]] included applejack in the [[Manhattan (cocktail)|Manhattans]] he regularly consumed; and [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] gave a case of applejack to Soviet leader [[Alexei Kosygin]] in the 1967 [[Glassboro Summit Conference]].<ref name="Ginzburg"/>
 
In the 2010s, a number of smaller craft distilleries began to produce applejack in places such as New Hampshire,<ref>[http://tamworthdistilling.com/spirits/old-hampshire-applejack/ Tamworth Distilling]{{better source|date=May 2021}}</ref> Pennsylvania's [[Lehigh Valley]],<ref>Kurt Bresswein, [https://www.lehighvalleylive.com/entertainment/2016/11/how_its_made_apples_to_appleja.html How it's made: Apples to applejack in the Lehigh Valley], ''lehighvalleylive.com'' (November 2016).</ref> New York's [[Hudson Valley]],<ref name="ModernPopularity">{{cite news|last=Newman|first=Kara|title=Are People Taking Applejack Seriously Now? Johnny Appleseed goes craft|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-02-04/applejack-and-american-apple-brandy-best-bottles-cocktail-recipes|work=Bloomberg News|date=4 February 2016|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160205093546/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-02-04/applejack-and-american-apple-brandy-best-bottles-cocktail-recipes|archive-date=5 February 2016}}</ref> [[Holland, Michigan]],<ref>Garret Ellison, [https://www.mlive.com/business/west-michigan/2014/09/applejack_coppercraft_distille.html Applejack is back: Coppercraft Distillery goes to market with historic American spirit], MLive.com (September 30, 2014) </ref> and in [[Toronto]].<ref>[https://www.nickel9distillery.com/shop/jacky-apple-jack/ Jacky Apple Jack]</ref>

== Production ==

=== Home-made ===
The name ''applejack'' derives from the traditional method of producing the drink, ''[[wikt:jack#Verb|jacking]]'', which is the process of [[Freeze distillation#Freeze distillation|freezing fermented cider]] and then removing the ice, increasing the alcohol content.<ref name=pop/> [[Cider]] produced after the fall harvest was left outside during the winter. Periodically the frozen chunks of ice that had formed were removed, thus concentrating the unfrozen alcohol in the remaining liquid.<ref name=SBC/> An alternative method involved placing a cask of hard cider in snow, allowing ice to form on the inside of the cask as the contents began to freeze, and then tapping the cask and pouring off the still-liquid portion of the contents. Starting with the fermented juice, with an alcohol content of less than ten percent, the concentrated result can contain 25–40% alcohol.<ref name=SBC/> Because freeze distillation is a low-infrastructure method of production compared to evaporative [[distillation]], and does not require the burning of firewood to create heat, hard cider and applejack were historically easier to produce,<ref name=SBC/> though more expensive than grain alcohol.<ref name="NicholsProulx">Lew Nichols, Annie Proulx, ''Cider: Making, Using & Enjoying Sweet & Hard Cider'', 3rd Edition (2015, {{ISBN|1-60342-839-9}})</ref> 

The disadvantage of freeze distillation, also called [[Fractional freezing|fractional crystallization]], is that the substances remaining after the removal of the water include not only ethanol, but also harmful [[methanol]], [[ester]]s, [[aldehyde]]s, and [[fusel alcohol]]s.<ref>Matthew B. Rowley, ''Moonshine!'' (Lark Books, 2007), p. 141.</ref> In modern times, reducing methanol with the absorption of a [[molecular sieve]] is a practical method for production.<ref>{{cite journal|url=http://www.spkx.net.cn/EN/abstract/abstract15544.shtml|title=Study on Method of Decreasing Methanol in Apple Pomace Spirit|journal=Food Science |author=Hui-Ling Ma |author2=Xiu-Ping Yang |author3=Ying Zuo |date=15 April 2006 |volume=27|issue=4|pages=138–142}}</ref>

=== Commercial ===
When commercial production began, applejack was also starting to be produced through evaporative distillation.<ref>Scott C. Martin, ''The SAGE Encyclopedia of Alcohol'' (2015, {{ISBN|1-4833-3108-3}}): The evaporative technique was used when commercial applejack production began.</ref>
Modern commercially produced applejack is often no longer produced by jacking but rather by blending apple [[brandy]] and neutral grain spirits.<ref name=Ginzburg/><ref name=Foley/><ref name=SBC>Sanborn Conner Brown, ''Wines & Beers of Old New England: A How-to-do-it History'' (1978, {{ISBN|0-87451-148-8}})</ref>

==Comparison to calvados==
Applejack is somewhat similar to [[Calvados (brandy)|calvados]], an apple brandy from [[Normandy]], France,<ref name="pop"/> to which it is often compared.<ref>Eric Asimov, [https://www.nytimes.com/2004/12/08/dining/an-apple-orchard-in-a-glass.html An Apple Orchard in a Glass], ''The New York Times'' (December 8, 2004).</ref> However, calvados is made from [[cider apple]]s, while applejack is made from apples such as [[Winesap]].<ref name="pop"/>

The '''Blue Hawaii''' is a tropical [[cocktail]] made of [[rum]], [[pineapple]] juice, [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Blue Curaçao]], sweet and sour mix, and sometimes vodka.

==History and popularity==
The Blue Hawaii was invented in 1957 by [[Harry Yee]], head [[bartender]] of the [[Hilton Hawaiian Village]] (formerly the Kaiser Hawaiian Village) in [[Waikiki, Hawaii]]<ref>{{cite web|title=Harry Yee, King of Tropical Cocktails|author=Rick Carroll|url=http://www.kevdo.com/maitai/harryyee.html|access-date=2007-07-03|publisher=kevdo.com}}</ref> when a sales representative of [[Netherlands|Dutch]] [[distiller]] [[Lucas Bols|Bols]] asked him to design a drink that featured their blue color of [[Curaçao liqueur]]. After experimenting with several variations, Yee settled on a version somewhat different from the most popular version today, but with the signature blue color, pineapple wedge, and [[cocktail umbrella]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Tropical drinks, part of the Hawaiian experience | url=http://www.aloha-hawaii.com/hawaii/tropical+drinks/|author=Lance Tominaga|access-date=2007-07-03|publisher=alohahawaii.com}}</ref>

The name "Blue Hawaii" is related only indirectly to the 1961 [[Elvis Presley]] [[Blue Hawaii|film of the same name]], and apparently derives instead from the film's [[Blue Hawaii (song)|title song]], a hit composed by [[Leo Robin]] for the 1937 [[Bing Crosby]] film ''[[Waikiki Wedding]]''. Yee named the drink which, along with the films and songs, the many other tropical drinks he invented, and [[tiki bar]]s such as [[Trader Vic]], did much to popularize a faux Hawaiian [[tiki culture]], both in Hawaii and on the mainland. The era was immediately pre-statehood, a time when Hawaii was thought of by Americans as a playground for the rich.

==Preparation and variations==
A Blue Hawaii is typically served [[ice cube|on the rocks]]. There are many variations in preparation, presentation, and ingredients. Hence, it is often blended with ice, [[margarita]]-like, to be served as a frozen cocktail. Many variations of glassware are used, the more whimsical the better: [[tiki mug]]s, [[cocktail glass]]es, [[parfait]] glasses, or carved-out coconuts or pineapples.

The base liquor is usually light [[rum]] but [[vodka]] may be partially or completely substituted as a matter of taste. The Blue Hawaii is often confused with the Blue Hawaiian. Yee's Blue Hawaii does not use cream of coconut like the Blue Hawaiian. In the case of the Blue Hawaiian, a flavored rum or vodka such as [[Malibu Rum]] may eliminate the need for crème of coconut, or the coconut flavor may be omitted entirely (coconut milk, a very different product, should ''not'' be used). The Blue Hawaii and the Blue Hawaiian are different drinks; the Blue Hawaii does not use any coconut. Some venues will attempt to pass off their “version” without the pineapple in favor of [[sour mix]]. Any respectable moderately stocked bar should be able to recreate the authentic Blue Hawaii. Seemingly the only constant is the name and the blue Curaçao.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.sundaypaper.com/CurrentArticles/tabid/98/articleType/ArticleView/articleId/159/060307-FOOD-My-blue-heaven.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071010110302/http://www.sundaypaper.com/CurrentArticles/tabid/98/articleType/ArticleView/articleId/159/060307-FOOD-My-blue-heaven.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-date=2007-10-10|title=My blue heaven|author=Jason Tesauro and Phineas Mollod|date=2007-06-03|access-date=2007-07-03|publisher=the Sunday Paper}}</ref>

Because it is easy and inexpensive to make, it is often served as a [[Punch (drink)|punch]]. At its simplest, it is a bottle or two of plain or coconut-flavored [[light rum]], a bottle of blue curacao, a can of pineapple juice, and a bag of ice, mixed together in a [[punch bowl|punchbowl]]. The Blue Hawaii is seasonal, often considered a warm weather drink. Occasionally, because it contains yellow pineapple juice, the Blue Hawaii will have a green coloration instead.<!--How about calling it a Green Hawaii instead?-->

Meeting local notables at the [[Schuylkill River]] in Philadelphia, he described being served "a Bowl of fine Lemon Punch big enough to have Swimmed half a dozen of young Geese." Another version states that it was created in 1848 by Shippen Willing of Philadelphia, to celebrate the momentous occasion of women being allowed into the premises of the "fish house" for the first time in order to enliven the annual Christmas party.[http://www.greatpartyrecipes.com/history-of-fish-house-punch.html The "Shocking" History of Fish House Punch] It was supposed to be just "something to please the ladies' palate but get them livelier than is their usual wont." '''Gosling Brothers Limited''' is a [[Bermuda|Bermudian]] company primarily concerned with blending and distributing [[rum]], importing and distributing spirits on the island, and maintaining a retail presence.

==History==
In early 1806 James Gosling set out from England with £10,000 in merchandise bound for America. The ship's charter had expired on the ninety-first day of the voyage, so they set in at the nearest port, Bermuda. However, instead of going on to America, Gosling set up shop on the island later that year.<ref name="ourhistory">{{Cite web |url=http://www.goslingsrum.com/discover_ourhistory.asp |title=Our History |access-date=2009-10-05 |archive-date=2009-12-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091212074644/http://www.goslingsrum.com/discover_ourhistory.asp |url-status=dead |publisher=Goslings Brothers}}{{primary source inline|date=February 2024}}</ref>

In 1824, the company rented their iconic store on Front Street.<ref name="ourhistory"/>

The Goslings started formulating [[rum]] blends in 1860, and in three years, they had developed '''Old Rum''', a dark, full-bodied rum. Originally distributed only in barrels and sold to those bringing their own bottles, the rum became more widely available with the introduction of bottling in [[Champagne bottles]], the most widely available at the time. The bottles were salvaged from the [[Bermuda Garrison]] Officers' Messes and were sealed with black sealing [[wax]]. Soon, people were asking for more of the 'black seal' rum, prompting the change to the name Black Seal Rum.<ref name="ourhistory"/>

Gosling Brothers holds the trademark for the [[Dark 'N' Stormy|Dark 'N Stormy]] cocktail.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/07/05/fashion/05shaken.html|title = The Right Stuff (By Law)|newspaper = The New York Times|date = 3 July 2009|last1 = Miles|first1 = Jonathan}}</ref>

==Products==
[[File:16-09-17-WikiLovesCocktails-Flaschen-Img0081.jpg|thumb|upright|A bottle of Black Seal Rum]]
* Black Seal Rum – Gosling's flagship 80 proof Bermuda Black Rum. This is the rum that is mixed with Bermuda [[ginger beer]] to create the signature Dark 'N' Stormy drink.  The company also bottles 140 proof and 151 proof renditions of this product.
* Gold Rum – Gosling's amber rum offering, with lighter color and flavor profile than Black Seal.
* Old Rum – Also called "Gosling's Family Reserve", this is a Bermuda black rum made of the same blend used for Black Seal rum.  However, it is aged longer and specially packaged. This rum is designed to be enjoyed on its own.
* Stormy Ginger Beer – A [[ginger beer]] taking inspiration from locally made brews and meant to be the second ingredient in a [[Dark 'N' Stormy]] (displacing [[John Barritt & Son Ltd.]]'s ''Bermuda Stone Gingerbear'').

'''Araqi''' ({{Langx|ar|عرقي|ʿaraqī}}; also ''araki'', ''aragy'')<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.wrmea.org/002-november/after-decades-of-civil-war-can-sudan-survive-peace.html|title=After Decades of Civil War, Can Sudan Survive Peace?|website=WRMEA}}</ref> is a [[Phoenix dactylifera|date]]-[[liquor]] distilled in [[Sudan]]. The [[September 1983 Laws|1983 introduction of sharia]] in Sudan prevented licit sales of alcohol, but a black market exists to meet local demand. The drink is made by mixing dates with water and yeast, fermenting the mix, and then distilling it. It is usually drunk neat.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/8638670.stm|title=Sudan's date-gin brewers thrive despite Sharia | work=BBC News | date=2010-04-29}}</ref> 

During the [[war in Darfur]], a number of southern Sudanese women came to the north as refugees, and found that some of the only professions available to them were prostitution or brewing araqi, the latter being a skill some already had, with a reliable market demand. A 2000 UN report noted that 80% of the women in Khartoum's women's prison were there on charges of prostitution or brewing araqi.<ref name="Abusharaf2009">{{cite book|author=Rogaia Mustafa Abusharaf|title=Transforming Displaced Women in Sudan: Politics and the Body in a Squatter Settlement|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xGTGmi_sYqgC&pg=PA73|date=1 August 2009|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-00201-9|pages=73–}}</ref>

Araqi is also popular in [[South Sudan]], which split from Sudan in 2011 and where alcohol is legal.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://theinquisitivevintner.wordpress.com/2018/03/28/wine-gin-making-in-the-sudan/|title="Wine/Gin" Making in the Sudan|date=March 28, 2018}}</ref>

Home distilling can lead to [[methanol poisoning]]; 10 died and several others were blinded by a batch of incorrectly distilled araqi in [[East Darfur]] in 2017.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dabangasudan.org/en/all-news/article/deadly-drink-kills-at-least-ten-blinds-two-in-east-darfur|title=Deadly drink kills at least ten, blinds two in East Darfur|website=Radio Dabanga|date=15 December 2017 }}</ref>

In 2020, a new law permitted alcohol sales to non-Muslims in Sudan.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/world/africa/sudan-legalises-alcohol-for-non-muslims-for-first-time-in-40-years-1.4303524|title=Sudan legalises alcohol for non-Muslims for first time in 40 years|newspaper=The Irish Times}}</ref>

Death in the Afternoon (cocktail):
{{short description|Cocktail made up of absinthe and Champagne}} {{Infobox drink | name = Death in the Afternoon | image = Death In The Afternoon.jpg | caption = Death in the Afternoon | type = [[Wine cocktail]] | base = [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]], [[Absinthe]] | drinkware = [[Champagne flute]] }} '''Death in the Afternoon''', also called the '''Hemingway''' or the '''Hemingway Champagne''',{{cite book|title = Ultimate Bar Book: The Comprehensive Guide to over 1,000 Cocktails|last = Hellmich|first = Mittie|publisher = [[Chronicle Books]]|year = 2006|isbn = 978-0-8118-4351-5|page = 154}}{{cite book |title= Knack Bartending Basics: More Than 400 Classic and Contemporary Cocktails|last= Bourgoin|first= Susan|year= 2009|publisher= Globe Pequot|isbn= 978-1-59921-504-4|page= 132}} is a [[cocktail]] made up of [[absinthe]] and [[Champagne (wine)|Champagne]], invented by [[Ernest Hemingway]]. The cocktail shares a name with Hemingway's 1932 book ''[[Death in the Afternoon]]'', and the recipe was published in ''So Red the Nose, or Breath in the Afternoon'', a 1935 cocktail book with contributions from famous authors.{{cite news |title= Trying to Clear Absinthe's Reputation|author= McGee, Harold|url= https://www.nytimes.com/2007/01/03/dining/03curi.html|newspaper= [[The New York Times]]|date= 3 January 2007|access-date=15 July 2011}}{{cite book |title= Diffordsguide Cocktails 7|last= Difford|first= Simon|year= 2008|publisher= Diffordsguide|isbn= 978-0-9556276-0-6|page= 122}} Hemingway's original instructions were:
"Pour one jigger absinthe into a Champagne glass. Add iced Champagne until it attains the proper opalescent milkiness. Drink three to five of these slowly."
It is claimed that the cocktail was invented by Hemingway after he spent time in the [[Rive Gauche|Left Bank]], Paris, and enjoyed the absinthe there. The original printed recipe for the drink claimed that it was invented "by the author and three officers of H.M.S. Danae after having spent seven hours overboard trying to get Capt. Bra Saunders’ fishing boat off a bank where she had gone with us in a N.W. gale."{{Cite web|url=http://belikehemingway.com/2016/02/29/drink-like-hemingway-how-to-make-a-death-in-the-afternoon/|title=Drink Like Hemingway: How to Make a Death in the Afternoon|last=Duffy|website=Be Like Hemingway.|access-date=2016-03-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160405210536/http://belikehemingway.com/2016/02/29/drink-like-hemingway-how-to-make-a-death-in-the-afternoon/|archive-date=2016-04-05|url-status=dead}} Death in the Afternoon is known for both its [[decadence]] and its high [[Alcohol proof|strength]].{{cite news|title= Top 5 Absinthe Cocktails|author= English, Camper|url= http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/drinking/cocktails/top5_absinthecocktails|publisher= [[Epicurious]]|access-date= 15 July 2011|archive-date= 21 July 2011|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110721142043/http://www.epicurious.com/articlesguides/drinking/cocktails/top5_absinthecocktails|url-status= dead}}{{cite news |title= Ernest Hemingway's Death in the Afternoon|url= http://www.esquire.com/drinks/ernest-hemingway-drink-recipe|newspaper= [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]]|access-date=15 July 2011}} There are a number of alternative ways to produce Death in the Afternoon. The absinthe can be added to the glass after the Champagne, as some brands of absinthe will float on the Champagne for a short time. Other alternatives have arisen because of the difficulty of acquiring absinthe; the absinthe can be replaced with [[Absente]], an alternative to absinthe available where it is illegal, or a strong [[pastis]], such as [[Pernod]]. Variants which use an alternative to absinthe are sometimes given a different name, but are also sometimes still referred to as Death in the Afternoon.{{cite book|title= Night+Day San Francisco|author1= Balmain, Julianne|author2= Chynoweth, Kate|year= 2006|publisher= ASDavis Media Group|isbn= 978-0-9759022-9-5|page= [https://archive.org/details/nightdaysanfranc00balm/page/132 132]|url-access= registration|url= https://archive.org/details/nightdaysanfranc00balm/page/132}} Some recipes direct the person making the cocktail to use ingredients in addition to the Champagne and absinthe; Valerie Mellema recommends that a [[sugar|sugar cube]] and several dashes of [[bitters]] be added to the glass prior to the main ingredients.{{cite book |title= The Professional Bartender's Handbook: A Recipe for Every Drink Known|last= Mellema|first= Valerie|year= 2007|publisher= Atlantic Publishing Company|isbn= 978-0-910627-95-5|page= 154}} The cocktail is milky in appearance on account of the [[Ouzo effect|spontaneous emulsification]] of the absinthe (or substitute), and bubbly, which it takes from the Champagne. After the first sip, however, it becomes significantly less bubbly. Harold McGee, dining and wine writer for ''[[The New York Times]]'', said that it "seemed a waste of effervescence" (though substituting Pernod for the absinthe). ==See also== {{Portal|Drink}} *[[List of cocktails]] ==References== {{reflist}} {{Wine cocktails}} [[Category:Cocktails with absinthe]] [[Category:Cocktails with Champagne]] [[Category:Ernest Hemingway]]

'''Ara''', or '''Arag''', ([[Tibetic languages|Tibetan]] and [[Dzongkha]]: ཨ་རག་; [[Wylie transliteration|Wylie]]: ''a-rag''; "alcohol, liquor") is a traditional [[alcoholic beverage]] consumed in [[Bhutan]] and Indian state of [[Arunachal Pradesh]]. Ara is made from native high-altitude tolerant [[barley]], [[rice]], [[maize]], [[millet]], or [[wheat]], and may be either [[Fermentation (food)|fermented]] or [[distillation|distilled]]. The beverage is usually a clear, creamy, or white color.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.windhorsetours.com/countrypages/meraksakteng.php |title=Merak and Sakteng - The Land of Brokpas |publisher=Wind Horse Tours online |access-date=2011-07-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927045148/http://www.windhorsetours.com/countrypages/meraksakteng.php |archive-date=2011-09-27 }}</ref>

==Production==
Ara is most commonly made from [[rice]] or [[maize]] at private homes or farms. Ara may be either fermented or distilled,<ref name=Tri>{{cite web|url=https://tricycle.org/magazine/making-moonshine/ |title=Making Moonshine: How to Make Bhutanese Rice Wine |first=Noa |last=Jones |publisher=Tricycle online |date=2011-06-02 |access-date=2019-11-24}}</ref> and in Bhutan is only legally produced and consumed privately. Ara production is unregulated in both method and quality, and its sale is prohibited in Bhutan. Previously, private individuals sold ara through shopkeepers despite the prohibition and faced a harsh government crackdown. However, because Ara returns far more profit than other forms of maize, many Bhutanese farmers have pressed for legal reform.<ref name=BO1>{{cite web|url=http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/ara-production-and-sale-should-be-legalized-farmers-say/ |title=Ara Production and Sale Should Be Legalized, Farmers Say |publisher=[[Bhutan Observer]] online |first=Tempa |last=Wangdi |date=2011-01-27 |access-date=2011-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110725153236/http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/ara-production-and-sale-should-be-legalized-farmers-say/ |archive-date=25 July 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The Bhutanese government, meanwhile, is intent on discouraging excessive alcohol consumption, abuse, and associated diseases through taxation and regulation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/reduce-alcohol-abuse-lyonchhen-urges-local-leaders/ |title=Reduce Alcohol Abuse, Lyonchhen Urges Local Leaders |date=2011-03-15 |publisher=Bhutan Observer online |first=Gyembo |last=Namgyal |access-date=2011-07-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120403030739/http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/reduce-alcohol-abuse-lyonchhen-urges-local-leaders/ |archive-date=2012-04-03 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/alcohol-price-hike-doesn%E2%80%99t-discourage-drinking/ |title=Alcohol Price Hike Doesn't Quite Discourage Drinking |first=Gyembo |last=Namgyal |publisher=Bhutan Observer online |date=2011-07-18 |access-date=2011-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110726233312/http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/alcohol-price-hike-doesn%E2%80%99t-discourage-drinking/ |archive-date=26 July 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Ara is also produced for religious purposes, especially in eastern Bhutan, where it serves as a Lhasoel offering on certain auspicious days.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/it-is-lhasoel-time-in-the-east/ |publisher=Bhutan Observer online |title=It is Lhasoel Time in the East |first=Gyembo |last=Namgyal |date=2010-01-19 |access-date=2011-07-27 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110120121521/http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/it-is-lhasoel-time-in-the-east/ |archive-date=2011-01-20 }}</ref><ref name=WoK>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q_snDwAAQBAJ&q=Lhasoel&pg=PA113 |title=Bhutan: Ways of Knowing |editor1-first=Frank |editor1-last=Rennie |editor2-first=Robin |editor2-last=Mason |publisher=IAP |year=2008 |isbn=978-16-07528-24-1 |page=113 |access-date=24 November 2019 }}</ref> Ara is also believed to chemically ward off snakes, and is sometimes carried by children for protection.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kuenselonline.com/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=8546 |title=Trongsa: Slithering with Snakes |first=Tashi |last=Dema |publisher=[[Kuensel]] online |date=2007-06-04 |access-date=2011-07-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402032834/http://www.kuenselonline.com/modules.php?name=News&file=article&sid=8546 |archive-date=2012-04-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Through government efforts to reduce ara production and consumption in [[Lhuntse District]], eastern Bhutan, locals conceded something should be done to curb the distinctly eastern Bhutanese tradition of heavy drinking. The government's strategy is to reduce ara production and consumption gradually until it is eliminated. Alcoholism and ara production have been notable topics of political discussion Bhutan, especially at the local level.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/ara-faces-banishment-lhuentse/ |first=Jigme |last=Wangchuck |title=Ara Faces Banishment in Lhuentse |date=2011-09-05 |publisher=Bhutan Observer online |access-date=2011-09-08 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110907072804/http://www.bhutanobserver.bt/ara-faces-banishment-lhuentse/ |archive-date=2011-09-07 }}</ref>

==Consumption==
Ara is usually consumed hot. It may be served neat, with smooth additives like [[butter]] and [[poached egg]], or with chunky additives like [[scrambled egg]] and rice.<ref name=Tri/>

'''Apo''', '''apong''' is an [[alcohol drink]] prepared by fermentation of rice, commonly found among the [[Tani people|Tani]] tribes in the [[Northeast India]] states of [[Arunachal Pradesh]] and [[Assam]]. Traditionally, there are two types of apo; Nogin apong and Poro apong. It is known by various names across different tribes in Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. It is commonly produced in households of northeastern states of Arunachal Pradesh and Assam in India. Although distinctive methods for brewing exist, the process of fermentation remains the same across these regions, inidicating common origins of brewing.

Many tribal communities of Arunachal Pradesh use apo during their respective festivals, such as [[nyokum]]. The tribal people offer the drink, every time they drink it, to the spirits (''wiyu'') by letting a few drops of it fall on the ground.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8vxtAAAAMAAJ&q=apung | title=Women in a tribal community: a study of Arunachal Pradesh | publisher=Vikas Pub. House | author=Kiran Mishra | year=1991 | pages=76| isbn=9780706958362 }}</ref> Other occasions when Apo is served include annually organized ancestor worship ceremonies, the festivals of [[Ali Ai Ligang|Ali aye ligang]], [[Nyokum]], [[Dree Festival|Dree]], and others, and annual agricultural programs.<ref>{{cite web |date=5 September 2019 |title=All About Assam |url=https://allaboutassam.in/2019/09/apong-or-apung/ |url-status=dead |access-date=November 14, 2020 |website=What Is Apong or Apung or Haaz? |archive-date=14 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201014213125/https://allaboutassam.in/2019/09/apong-or-apung/ }}</ref>

Apo is known in different names across different tribes in North-Eastern India, such as haaz ([[Ahom language|Ahom]]), apong ([[Mising language|Mising]]), zou (zu mai) ([[Bodo language|Bodo]]) and Sujen ([[Deori people|Deori]]). Apo is not distributed in shops, as apo forms part of a tradition and culture, the apo is shared through generations like a piece of cultural knowledge. Apos are commonly brewed in households and often served along with rice and chutney as well, irrespective of gender or age differences.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chakravorty |first1=Jharna |last2=Ghosh |first2=Sampat |last3=Meyer-Rochow |first3=Victor Benno |title=Practices of entomophagy and entomotherapy by members of the Nyishi and Galo tribes, two ethnic groups of the state of Arunachal Pradesh (North-East India) |journal=Journal of Ethnobiology and Ethnomedicine |date=14 January 2011 |volume=7 |issue=1 |page=5 |doi=10.1186/1746-4269-7-5|pmid=21235790 |pmc=3031207 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== History ==
The origins of the apo tradition in the North-Eastern regions are not recorded, However, the tradition may date back to [[Neolithic]] period.<ref name="auto">{{cite journal |last1=Tanti |first1=Bhaben |last2=Gurung |first2=Lisha |last3=Sarma |first3=Hridip Kumar |last4=Buragohain |first4=Alak K |title=Ethnobotany of starter cultures used in alcohol fermentation by a few ethnic tribes of Northeast India |journal=Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge |date=1 July 2010 |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=463–466}}</ref> Similarly, the word Apo is not a general term for a rice-based drink, as each tribe identifies the drink with different names. However, it is believed that the traditional rice beer was first developed by the '[[Mising people]] in Assam.<ref name="auto3">{{cite web |last1=Barman |first1=Rini |title=Assam: How tribal communities brew apong, their drink, reveals a lot about gender and tradition |url=https://scroll.in/article/857160/assam-how-tribal-communities-brew-apong-their-drink-reveals-a-lot-about-gender-and-tradition |website=Scroll |date=11 November 2017 |access-date=14 November 2020}}</ref> Thus the etymology of the word refers to its [[Mising language]] origins. Across the different tribes, the brewing method has certain differences, but the substrates used for fermentation are the same. This indicates a common ancestor to the brewing culture in North-Eastern India. Traditionally, two kinds of Apo are being brewed in these regions known as Po:ro Apong and Nogin Apong.

The starter cakes called épob are made out of crushed rice and medicinal plants are used to make the health quotient.<ref name="auto3" />  These starter cakes are one of the most important elements of the rice beers made in the North-Eastern region, including Apo. This also refers to the idea of sacredness associated with the Apo making across different tribes as it is not made on an everyday basis, but only for ceremonies, festivals, marriage, and group gatherings.<ref name="auto1">{{cite journal |last1=Das |first1=Arup |last2=Deka|first2=Sankar Chandra |last3=Miyaji |first3=T |title=Methodology of rice beer preparation and various plant materials used in starter culture preparation by some tribal communities of North-East India: A survey |journal=International Food Research Journal |date=1 January 2012 |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=101–107|url=http://www.ifrj.upm.edu.my/19%20(01)%202011/(14)IFRJ-2011-137%20Deka.pdf}}</ref> In this regard, historically and culturally, the Apo remains as an element of identity in these regions.

=== Apo and the Mising people ===

Apo is known in different traditional names based on the respective tribes. Apo is believed to be first developed by the Mising people in Assam. The term Apo is derived from the traditional name "Apong" in the Mising language.<ref name="auto4">{{cite journal |last1=Gogoi |first1=Barnali |last2=Dutta |first2=M. |last3=Mondal |first3=Prodyut |title=Various ethno medicinal plants used in the preparation of Apong, a traditional beverage use by mising tribe of upper Assam |journal=Journal of Applied Pharmaceutical Science |date=1 May 2013 |volume=3 |issue=4 |page=S85-S85 |doi=10.7324/JAPS.2013.34.S16|doi-broken-date=11 July 2025 |url=https://japsonline.com/abstract.php?article_id=886}}</ref> The Mising community is generally known for its passion for traditional cooking methods and food items. The cooking method of the Apo is also believed to be shared by the ancestors of Mising community and later spread throughout the tribes in North East India.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baruah |first1=Madhumita |last2=Kalita |first2=Dilip |title=Ethnomedicine used by Mishings tribes of Dibrugarh district, Assam |journal=Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge |date=1 October 2007 |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=595–598}}</ref>

== Production ==
[[File:Filtration of apong.jpg|thumb|The fermentated epop mix is being filtered to make apong.]]
Apo is commonly produced in households of northeastern states of [[Arunachal Pradesh]] and [[Assam]] in India. Although distinctive methods for brewing exist across the North-Eastern region of India, the process of fermentation remains the same across these regions, inidicating common origins of brewing.

As a first step, the rice collected for making beverage is cooked and then mixed with ash from burnt paddy sticks, which makes the mixture black in color. Once the rice is cooked, it is mixed with the fermenting ingredient E-Pob made out of rice and medicinal plants. Time is taken for the formation of ration changes along with the climate and temperature.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Sandor Ellix |first1=Katz |title=The art of fermentation : an in-depth exploration of essential concepts and processes from around the world |date=2012 |publisher=White River Junction, Vt. : Chelsea Green Publishing}}</ref> During the summer season, the fermentation took 5–6 days. The fermented mixture is filtered and finally poured into bamboo shoots. During these processes, around 30 medicinal plants use to the beverage along with rice.  This includes leaves, creepers, and grass. The total period taken for the production of Apo beer is more than 3 months. Although the alcohol content on the Apo is 18-25% it is more intoxicating in nature.

Recent studies indicate the Apo Beer can be economically benefiting the community as the beer provides the entrepreneurial potential to the community as the rice beer produced in Northeast regions, including Apo are high quality in nature.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Das |first1=Arup |last2=Seth |first2=Dibyakanta |last3=Miyaji |first3=Tatsuro |last4=Deka |first4=Sankar Chandra |title=Fermentation optimization for a probiotic local northeastern Indian rice beer and application to local cassava and plantain beer production |journal=Journal of the Institute of Brewing |year=2015 |volume=121 |issue=1(2) |pages=273–282 |doi=10.1002/jib.211}}</ref>
[[File:Saccharum officinarum 01.JPG|thumb|Plants such as Saccharum Officinarum are used in the production of Apo beer.]]

=== The Épob  (starter cake) ===
The starter cake is one of the most indispensable elements of the Apo beer production process. The Apo beer produced by the Mising community is identified to have various medicinal and therapeutic properties as a result often used during the preparation of starter cake known as 'épob'.  The beer-making process in each tribe varies according to the environmental factors and other socio-cultural practices associated with the individual tribes.<ref name="auto4"/> These factors are essential in determining the colour, flavour, and sweetness of the flower.  One major process during the production of Apong is the use of starter cake, i.e. 'épob' which has significant medicinal qualities. This quality is of starter cake is determined by the medicinal plants used during the production along with the sanitary conditions used while making the beer.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Deka |first1=Dipali |last2=Sarma |first2=Gajen chandra |title=Traditionally used herbs in the preparation of rice-beer by the Rabha tribe of Goalpara district |journal=Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge |date=1 July 2010 |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=459–462}}</ref>  The making of 'épob in this regard include the process of collecting a variety of medicinal plant leaves. The leaves collected are dried placing it on a bamboo mat known as 'époh' after cleaning it.<ref name="auto1"/>  Fresh leaves can also be used for making the starter cake for making the beer.  The leaves are later ground separately using a wooden tools hand mixer together to make an 'épob' in the shape of oval-shaped balls from the dough made from the mixture.<ref name="auto1"/>  Kuhiar ([[Saccharum officinarum]]), senikuthi ([[Scoparia dulcis]]), bhilongoni (Cyclosorus exlensa), anaras ([[pineapple]], also known as Ananas comosus), bam kolmou ([[Ipomoea]] species), kopou dhekia, lexuosum Lygodium flexuosum,  lai jabori (Drymaria cordata), horumanimuni ([[Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides]] jalokia ([[Capsicum annuum]]), dhapat tita (Clerodendrum viscosum), bormanimuni ([[Centella asiatica]]) etc. are some of the most basic medicinal plants and herbs used for the making of 'épob'.<ref name="auto1"/>

=== Folk medicine ===
The [[traditional medicine|folk medicine]] beliefs of the starter cake derive from the use of local herbs.<ref name="auto4"/>  Tribes believe that the combination of herbs makes Apo beer an effective agent against various minor diseases.<ref name="auto1"/>  Most of the plants used for the preparation of the beer are indigenous. The varieties of Apo beer in the northeast region of India include methods of infusion and decoction used by the local peoples.<ref name="auto4"/>

== Cultural significance ==
Apo is an important element in the socio-cultural aspect of the Mising people. The Apo beer is served during religious festivals and ceremonies in Assam such as Marriages, death ceremonies, [[Ali A:yé lígang]],  [[Porag]], and other major community gatherings and celebration.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Awesome Assam |url=https://assamtourism.gov.in/festival-month.php |access-date=2025-07-28 |website=assamtourism.gov.in}}</ref> Apong is usually served along with pork and [[Purang apin]] in festivals like Ali A:yé lígang.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sultana |first1=Mehzabin |title=Ali aye ligang: spring festival of song, dance & feasting in Assam |url=http://www.eastmojo.com/assam/2020/02/19/ali-aye-ligang-spring-festival-of-song-dance-feasting-in-assam |website=EastMojo |date=19 February 2020 |access-date=17 November 2020}}</ref>

== Local economy ==
In local markets, Apo beer is a source of income and livelihood for many families, and contributes to community development.<ref name="auto1"/>

In Assam, it has been reportedly found to be sold by local brewers in small bottles.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Purwar |first=Krari |date=22 November 2025 |title=What Is Apong, The Traditional Rice-Based Alcohol Of The Northeast, Showcased In The Family Man 3 |url=https://www.ndtv.com/lifestyle/what-is-apong-the-traditional-rice-based-alcohol-of-the-northeast-showcased-in-the-family-man-3-9681955 |access-date=16 December 2025 |work=[[NDTV]]}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
Apo was featured in the Indian Amazon Prime Video web series ''[[The Family Man (Indian TV series)|The Family Man]]'' (season 3), where it is depicted as a traditional rice-based alcoholic beverage consumed in Northeast India.<ref name=":0" />

'''Artos''' is a regional [[soft drink]] and the first [[aerated]] soft drink in the state of [[Andhra Pradesh]].<ref name="bs1">{{cite web|last1=Kanth|first1=K. Rajani|title=Artos simply fizzles despite all odds|url=http://www.business-standard.com/article/companies/artos-simply-fizzles-despite-all-odds-104032301027_1.html|publisher=Business Standard India|accessdate=5 November 2017|date=23 March 2004}}</ref> It was first named as "Ramachandra Raju soft drinks" and later renamed as "A.R Raju Tonics" and later converted into Artos. It was originated in Ramachandrapuram in East Godavari district, Andhra Pradesh. At first, Ramachandra Raju bought a soda machine from British collectorate but he did not know how to use it. Later, he came to Visakhapatnam with the machine and meet a person in [[Visakhapatnam|Vizag Port]] and he helped the machine with new parts and also told how to use it and he returned to Ramachandrapuram and started marketing it as a soda drink in 1912. At first, local people scared to drink due to gaseous content or some myths but after observing British soldiers consuming it they started. In 1919, it was officially made as a drink and the required sugars, gas and flavours are imported from Europe. But during the 2nd World War, the imports had stopped and many industries in India halted. But Artos continued its production using the flavours taken from fruits. Many international companies offers franchises but Artos never stopped. In 2019, it has completed 100 years and Artos was growing furthermore in Andhra Pradesh.

==History==
Artos was established in 1919 by Adduri Ramachandra Raju and Adduri Jagannadha Raju in [[Ramachandrapuram, East Godavari]] with a soda machine procured from the British. In the beginning, people avoided the drink as it was seen as a devil's bottle and its consumption by the [[British soldiers]] made it popular during World War-II.<ref name="hind1"/>

==Flavours==
It is available in Grape, Lemon, Orange, Gingeera, Lemon Salt Soda, Zibb Gluco and soda flavours.<ref name="hind1">{{cite web|last1=Reddem|first1=Appaji|title=100-year-old Artos in expansion mode|url=http://www.thehindu.com/todays-paper/tp-national/tp-andhrapradesh/100-year-old-artos-in-expansion-mode/article19788892.ece|website=The Hindu|accessdate=5 November 2017|language=en-IN|date=3 October 2017}}</ref>

== Ingredients ==
Bangla is made from grains such as [[Sorghum bicolor|sorghum]], [[Pearl millet|bajra]] and [[wheat]].<ref name=an/>

==Production and consumption==

A major proportion of excise revenue in the state of [[West Bengal]] comes from cheap Bengali liquor. In the 2014-15 fiscal year, the figure reached 3,600 [[crore]].<ref name=an/>

Doctor (cocktail):
[[File:Cocktail recipe for Doctor Cocktail(1922).png|thumb]]
The '''doctor cocktail''' is a pre-prohibition era cocktail that traces in drink guides to as far back as 1917, when it appeared in Hugo R. Ensslin's ''Recipes for Mixed Drinks''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Ensslin |first1=Hugo |title=Recipes for Mixed Drinks |date=1917 |publisher=Unknown |location=New York |page=15}}</ref>  As originally described the cocktail called simply for [[punsch|Swedish Punsch]] mixed with lime juice.

Like many older cocktails, many variations with the same name have been created over time, and drink guides sometimes listed multiple variations in the same book. The core of the cocktail consists of Swedish punsch and some variation of citrus (lime, lemon, or orange), with later variations skewing away from lime and also adding Jamaican [[rum]].

==Historical variations==
After Ensslin's recipe, the doctor cocktail was also listed in Robert Vermiere's 1922 drink book where it dropped the use of lime, calling for 2 parts Swedish punsch, 1 part orange juice, and 1 part lemon juice (2:1:1 ratio).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vermiere |first1=Robert |title=Cocktails How to Mix Them |date=1922 |publisher=Mayflower Printing |location=Plymouth, England |page=28}}</ref>

[[Harry MacElhone|Harry MacElhone's]] guide ''Harry Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails'' listed the ingredients as equal parts Swedish punsch, orange juice, and lemon juice (1:1:1 ratio),<ref>{{cite book |last=MacElhone |first=Harry |authorlink=Harry MacElhone |title=Harry of Ciro's ABC of Mixing Cocktails |date=1923 |publisher=Dean & Sons Ltd |location=London |page=28}}</ref> as did a 1927 Italian version (1:1:1 ratio).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Grande |first1=Piero |title=Cocktails |date=1927 |publisher=unknown |location=Roma |page=33 |edition=3rd}}</ref> MacElhone's guide however also carried an illustration for "The Recipe of the famous Dr. Cocktail" which called for 2/3 punsch and 1/3 lime juice, while suggesting that lemons could be substituted if one did not have limes on hand.

In 1936 fellow drink book author Frank Meier listed the cocktail as equal parts punsch and white rum, with a teaspoon each of orange and lemon juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Punch and Rum - The Doctor Cocktail |url=https://cold-glass.com/2012/08/15/punch-and-rum-the-doctor-cocktail/ |website=cold-glass.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref>

[[Trader Vic's]] listed the ingredients as 1.5 oz. Swedish punsch, 3/4 oz. Jamaican rum, 1 tsp. orange juice, and 1 tsp. lemon juice. The guide also noted that equal parts Swedish punsch and rum could also be used, and that the juice of 1/2 a lime could take the place of the orange and lemon juice.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bergeron |first1=Trader Vic |title=Bartender's Guide |date=1947 |publisher=Garden City Books |location=Garden City, NY |page=216 |edition=1948 reprint}}</ref>

In 1948 Dave Embury noted that there were "several" versions of the cocktail and was going to list four in his book.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Embury |first1=Dave |title=Fineart of Mixing Drinks |date=1948 |publisher=Doubleday Company |location=Garden City, NY |page=227}}</ref> The Doctor Cocktail No.1 listed Ensslin's original punsch and lime recipe. No.2 called for equal parts punsch, gin, and lemon juice. No.3 called for the more now common 2:1:1 ratio of punsch, orange juice, and lemon juice.  No.4 called for 3 parts punsch, 2 parts Jamaican rum, and 1 part lime.

Difford's guide likewise lists four different versions, although not all the same as Embury's.<ref>{{cite web |title=Search results for "doctor" |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/search?force_limit=20&q=doctor |website=diffordsguide.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref>

==Similar cocktails==
In his 1941 bartender's book, ''"Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies Companion"'', Gaige listed a drink that he called the ''Greta Garbo Bows'', that called for one jigger of Swedish Punsch, 1/2 jigger of orange juice, and a 1/2 jigger of lemon juice. This was essentially Vermier's Doctor cocktail version from 1922. Despite the same ingredients, Gaige makes no mention of the doctor cocktail in his notes but says "shake well, strain into cocktail glass, and God bless Miss Garbo".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gaige |first1=Crosby |title=Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies Companion |date=1941 |publisher=M. Barrows & Company |location=New York |page=171 |edition=First}}</ref> [[Greta Garbo]] was a Swedish-American actress, a potential reason for the renaming of a drink that contained Swedish Punsch.

Another cocktail simply called the ''[[Greta Garbo]]'' calls for equal parts Swedish Punsch, gin, and lemon juice.<ref>{{cite web |title=Greta Garbo Cocktail |url=https://www.absolutdrinks.com/en/drinks/greta-garbo-cocktail/ |website=absolutdrinks.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref> This is the same drink as the Doctor No.2 from Emburry's 1948 cocktail guide.

== Later "doctor" cocktails ==
Early alcoholic concoctions were often thought of as "medicinal", and even in 1948 cocktail books were pondering such questions as "Why are rye and bourbon whiskies frequently prescribed by doctors and Scotch practically never?"<ref>{{cite book |last1=Embury |first1=David |title=The Fine Art of Mixing Drinks |date=1948 |publisher=Doubleday |location=Garden City, NY |page=31}}</ref>

Other "doctor" cocktails include the '''Doctor Johnson''', which was a tropical cocktail by design that called for<ref>{{cite book |last1=Tarling |first1=W. J. |title=Cafe Royal Cocktail Book |date=1937 |publisher=Pall Mall |location=London |page=DO |edition=Coronation}}</ref> 1/4 gin, 1/2 pineapple syrup, 1/8 passion fruit juice, and 1/8 lemon juice shaken with a dash of grenadine and egg white, making it a potential precursor for later [[Tiki bar|Tiki drinks]]. The author of the particular cocktail guide, W.J. Tarling, did not provide notes as to whom the drink was named after, other than saying it was "invented by Tim Hollings".  However, it is potentially telling that the book also included a recipe for the ''Doctor Johnson Jr'', which contained no liquor. Dr. [[Samuel Johnson]] was a prolific English writer who is attributed with many quotes on the character of man and drinking.<ref>{{cite web |title=Quotes on Drinking |url=https://www.samueljohnson.com/drinking.html |website=www.samueljohnson.com |accessdate=10 February 2019}}</ref> His alcohol problem and ultimate need for abstinence was well documented<ref>{{cite journal|title=SAMUEL JOHNSON'S ALCOHOL PROBLEM|last=Madden|first=J.S|date=1967|citeseerx = 10.1.1.284.4792}}</ref> and he was quoted as saying "I can't drink a little, child, therefore I never touch it".

The '''Doctor Funk''' cocktail has more certainty as to its name and has been described as a Tiki drink precursor. Jeff Berry in ''Beachbum Berry Remixed'' states that, unlike most Tiki drinks that were called Polynesian but "made up" in California that "the ''Doctor Funk'', alone among "Polynesian" drinks, does, in fact, have Polynesian roots".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=Jeff |title=Beachbum Berry Remixed |date=2010 |publisher=Club Tiki Press |location=San Jose|page=109 }}</ref> The drink was named after Dr. Bernard Funk, a German physician who was a doctor for [[Robert Louis Stevenson]] in Samoa.<ref>{{cite web |title=The late Dr. Fong has a funky and famous history |url=http://www.slammie.com/atomicgrog/blog/2013/02/03/lost-cocktails-of-the-mai-kai-the-late-dr-fong-has-a-funky-and-famous-history/ |website=slammie.com |accessdate=27 February 2019}}</ref> Berry provides evidence that the doctor was also a bartender in his own right and lists the drink as being a mixture of light Puerto Rican rum, lime juice, and pomegranate syrup stirred with a teaspoon of Pernod and club soda.

[[Trader Vic's]] attempt to "improve" the Dr. Funk was called '''Dr. Funk's Son'''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vic |first1=Trader |title=Bartender's Guide, Revised |url=https://archive.org/details/tradervicsbarten00trad |url-access=registration |date=1972 |publisher=[[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]] |location=Garden City, NY |page=[https://archive.org/details/tradervicsbarten00trad/page/152 152] |edition=revised}}</ref>

[[Joseph Stephen Crane|Stephen Crane]] called his version of the Dr. Funk the '''Dr. Fong''' at ''The Luau'' and his ''Kon-Tiki'' chain of restaurants.<ref>{{cite web |title=From the Los Angeles Public Library Menu Collection: The Luau, a 1950s Tiki Bar in Beverly Hills |url=https://www.laweekly.com/restaurants/from-the-los-angeles-public-library-menu-collection-the-luau-a-1950s-tiki-bar-in-beverly-hills-2376567 |website=laweekly.com |accessdate=17 February 2019}}</ref> Crane, who tongue in cheek referred to himself as high chief "Stefooma", claimed that a "Dr. Fong Foo" was also the overseer of the food and drinks at his ''The Luau'' restaurant.<ref>{{cite web |title=LA public library data base |url=https://dbase1.lapl.org/images/menus/fullsize/c/rb01454-02.jpg |website=dbase1.lapl.org |accessdate=26 February 2019}}</ref> He additionally listed a ''Doc's Grog'' on his 1956 ''The Luau'' menu, which may have been a reference to Dr. Fong Foo, and was likely a rebranded [[Navy Grog]] (Crane called the [[Test Pilot (cocktail)|Test Pilot]] the ''Jet Pilot'', ''Don's Pearl'' became ''Steve's Pearl'', etc.).

== Relationship to 21st century cocktail enthusiasts==
Although similar in name, there is no formal connection between the Doctor cocktail and the author of the book ''Vintage Spirits & Forgotten Cocktails'', written by Ted Haigh (aka, "Doctor Cocktail").<ref>{{cite web |title=Doctor Cocktail |url=https://forgottencocktails.com/?p=621 |website=forgottencocktails.com |accessdate=28 January 2019}}</ref>

There is also no formal connection between the cocktail and [[Jeff Macpherson]] (aka, "Dr. Tiki", former host of [[Tiki Bar TV]]).<ref>{{cite web |title=Tiki Bar TV |url=http://www.canada.com/nationalpost/artslife/story.html?id=aadbdfb5-4d90-424e-b638-4c9232c69cdf&k=56529 |website=canada.com |accessdate=26 February 2019|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120805125939/http://www.canada.com/nationalpost/artslife/story.html?id=aadbdfb5-4d90-424e-b638-4c9232c69cdf&k=56529|archive-date = 2012-08-05}}</ref>

Chatham Artillery punch:
{{Short description|Alcoholic beverage}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=May 2021}}
{{Infobox drink
| name        = Chatham Artillery punch
| image       = File:Chatham Artillery Punch.jpg   
| type        = [[Mixed drink]]
| ingredients ={{plainlist|Lemons, sugar, whiskey, brandy, rum, Champagne<ref name="Stern 2014">{{cite web|last=Stern|first=Steven|date=29 April 2014|title=Original Chatham Artillery Punch Recipe|url=https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1013708-original-chatham-artillery-punch|access-date=27 February 2021|website=NYT Cooking}}</ref>}}
| served      = Chilled
| garnish     = Grated nutmeg, cherries
}}

'''Chatham Artillery punch''' is a potent [[Punch (drink)|punch]] containing [[rum]], [[whisky]], [[brandy]], and Champagne.<ref name="McKibben 2016">{{cite web|last=McKibben|first=Beth|date=8 July 2016|title=Chatham Artillery Punch: Maybe the Strongest Drink in American History|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/drink/chatham-artillery-punch-maybe-the-strongest-drink/|access-date=27 February 2021|website=pastemagazine.com}}</ref> It also contains [[lemon]]s and sugar.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> Named after the [[Chatham Artillery|Savannah regiment]], it is well-known in the city of [[Savannah, Georgia]],<ref name="McKibben 2016" /> which is located in [[Chatham County, Georgia|Chatham County]].

== History ==
The original recipe and creator are unknown.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> One legend has it that [[George Washington]] was presented the punch when he arrived at [[Chatham Artillery]] in 1792, and he gave the regiment two [[cannon]]s.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016">{{cite web|date=8 June 2016|title=Drink This: Chatham Artillery Punch|url=https://www.atlantamagazine.com/dining-news/drink-chatham-artillery-punch/|access-date=27 February 2021|website=Atlanta Magazine}}</ref> 

A more plausible story was reported in an 1885 article for the [[The Augusta Chronicle|''Augusta Chronicle'']].<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> It stated that the punch was created in the 1850s, when the [[Republican Blues]] returned from a drill in [[Macon, Georgia|Macon]] and were welcomed back by Sergeant A. B. Luce and the Chatham Artillery.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> The punch was said to have been created by adding a quart of brandy, whiskey, and rum along with Champagne, lemon, and sugar to a horse bucket containing crushed ice.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> According to this story, every man who drank it was [[Alcohol intoxication|inebriated]].<ref name="McKibben 2016"/>

In 1870, a group of [[Southern United States|Southern]] journalists held a convention in Savannah and were served the punch on a [[riverboat]] cruise.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> They became inebriated and reported their encounter with the drink, proposing guesses of the actual content.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> The punch subsequently received national attention.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> President [[Chester A. Arthur|Chester Arthur]] was said to have been bested by the drink.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/>

In 1900, Admiral [[George Dewey]], a war hero from the [[Battle of Manila Bay|1898 Battle of Manila Bay]], also became inebriated when he imbibed the punch.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> One recipe was later named after him.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/>

The drink was later revised to become less potent.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/><ref name="Miller 2011">{{cite web|last=Miller|first=Marleigh Riggins|date=11 April 2011|title=Chatham Artillery Punch Recipe|url=https://www.seriouseats.com/recipes/2011/04/drink-the-book-chatham-artillery-punch-original-recipe-wondrich.html|access-date=27 February 2021|website=Serious Eats}}</ref> In a recipe from 1907, it was written: "Experience has taught the rising generation to modify the receipt of their forefathers to conform to the weaker constitutions of their progeny."<ref name="Miller 2011"/><ref name="Wondrich 2010">{{cite book|last=Wondrich|first=D.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=t6LabYdVTZ8C|title=Punch: The Delights (and Dangers) of the Flowing Bowl|publisher=Penguin Publishing Group|year=2010|isbn=978-1-101-44512-9|page=|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref>

After the end of [[Prohibition in the United States|Prohibition]] in the late 1930s, the cocktail grew in popularity again.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> One of the last variations was published after Prohibition by the ''[[The New York Sun|New York Sun]]'' in 1939.<ref name="McKibben 2016"/> The new recipes were substantially different, and sometimes included [[liquor]]s like [[Scotch whisky|scotch]] and [[gin]] and even excluded Champagne.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/>

Another legend is that during [[Sherman's March to the Sea|Sherman's March]] in the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], the residents of Savannah provided Sherman with so much of the punch that he decided to spare the city.<ref name="Pariseau">{{cite web|last=Pariseau|first=Leslie|title=The Great American Bar Crawl: Nine Bartenders Pick Their Favorite Cocktails|url=https://www.gq.com/story/bar-crawl-bartenders-favorite-cocktails-in-america|access-date=27 February 2021|website=GQ|date=21 June 2012 }}</ref>

== Ingredients ==
Many punch recipes call for Santa Cruz rum, which became more popular after Prohibition.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193">{{cite book|last=Moss|first=R.F.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vELTCwAAQBAJ|title=Southern Spirits: Four Hundred Years of Drinking in the American South, with Recipes|publisher=Ten Speed Press|year=2016|isbn=978-1-60774-867-0|page=193|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> It is more likely that heavy, dark rum is more similar to one used in the original recipe.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193"/> [[Catawba (grape)|Catawba wine]] is difficult to find in modern times, and is substituted with a white wine or Champagne.<ref name="Moss 2016 p. 193"/> In the [[Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil (film)|1997 film adaptation]] of the [[John Berendt]] novel ''[[Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil]]'', the punch is referenced as "three parts fruit, seven parts liquor{{snd}} whatever's available on both counts".<ref>{{cite AV media|url=|title=Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil|date=November 21, 1997|people=Eastwood, Clint (director); Hancock, John Lee (screenwriter)|language=English|publisher=Warner Bros. Pictures|trans-title=|location=|time=|access-date=|archive-url=|archive-date=|format=|id=|isbn=|oclc=|quote=|medium=motion picture}}</ref>

== Preparation ==
The drink can be prepared by taking lemon [[Zest (ingredient)|peels]] and [[Muddler|muddling]] them with sugar which will extract oils from the lemon peels.<ref name="Stern 2014"/><ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> This mixture is added to lemon juice and is strained.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> The lemon-sugar mixture is then added to a large bowl with crushed ice along with brandy, rum, whiskey, and Champagne.<ref name="Atlanta Magazine 2016"/> Although not likely traditional, [[Candied fruit|candied cherries]] (and sometimes the juice from the jar) are often added as well.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46">{{cite book|last1=Fowler|first1=D.L.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Y-rCfsqL5cC|title=The Savannah Cookbook|last2=Carrington|first2=J.R.|publisher=Gibbs Smith, publisher|year=2008|isbn=978-1-4236-0224-8|page=46|access-date=27 February 2021}}</ref> Similarly, gin is sometimes added in modern recipes.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

== Variations ==
One variation is called Champagne punch.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> This is less potent version of the drink, and uses [[Curaçao (liqueur)|Curaçao]] or [[Cointreau]], a few shot of [[bitters]], fresh [[Strawberry|strawberries]], lemon, [[Syrup|simple syrup]], brandy, and Champagne.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> It is popular at [[wedding reception]]s and Christmas parties.<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

There are similar drinks that exist. One is regent's punch, which is popular along the [[East Coast of the United States]].<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/> Another is the [[Fish house punch]], which is found in the [[Northeastern United States|Northeast United States]].<ref name="Fowler Carrington 2008 p. 46"/>

Airmail (cocktail):
{{Short description|Rum-based cocktail}}
[[File:Air Mail Cocktail.png|thumb|Airmail Cocktail,<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=In the mix|url=https://augustine-bar.de/in-the-mix/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=augustine-bar.de|language=English|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140504212541/http://augustine-bar.de:80/in-the-mix/ |archive-date=2014-05-04 }}</ref> garnished with a postal stamp]]
The '''''Airmail'' or ''Air Mail''''' (also ''Airmail cocktail'') is a classic cocktail based on [[rum]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] or [[lemon]] juice, [[honey]], and [[sparkling wine]]. It was probably created during or shortly after the period of [[prohibition]] in the [[United States|United States of America]] or on [[Cuba]], i.e. in the 1920s or 1930s.

Airmail Cocktail is also a brand of [https://www.airmailcocktail.com/ ready-to-drink cocktails] created and produced in Cognac (France) since 2020.

== History ==
As with the slightly older [[Aviation (cocktail)|Aviation cocktail]], to whose recipe there is no similarity, the name is reminiscent of [[aviation]] which developed rapidly at that time. In those years when international telephone connections were still a rarity, [[airmail]] was the fastest means of communication across national borders. Because of [[Prohibition in the United States|prohibition]], Americans were only able to legally drink alcohol abroad until 1933. Cuba, among other countries, benefited from this as a pronounced bar and cocktail culture began developing on the island in the 1920s. Since 1925, flights were available from [[Key West]] to [[Havana]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Pioneering Years: Commercial Aviation 1920 – 1930|url=https://www.centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/1920s/Tran1.htm|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=centennialofflight.net - U.S. Centennial of Flight Commission|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626001311/http://www.centennialofflight.net/essay/Commercial_Aviation/1920s/Tran1.htm|archive-date=2015-06-26}}</ref> and in 1930, a regular [[Airmail|airmail service]] was established to and from the island.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|last=Ford|first=Doug|date=31 December 2014|title=A return to Havana: the Airmail Cocktail|url=https://cold-glass.com/2014/12/31/a-return-to-havana-the-airmail-cocktail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=cold-glass.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150111001408/http://cold-glass.com/2014/12/31/a-return-to-havana-the-airmail-cocktail/|archive-date=11 January 2015}}</ref> Shortly after, the ''Airmail Cocktail'' appeared for the first time in an advertising brochure of the then still Cuba-based rum manufacturer [[Bacardi|Bacardí]].<ref name=":8" />

In 1941, the recipe was published in a mixology book.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Campbell Whitfield|first=William|title=Here's How. Mixed Drinks.|publisher=Three Mountaineers Inc.|year=1941|editor-last=Shell|editor-first=Ted (Illustrator)|edition=1|pages=36}}</ref> In his recipe collections, ''Just Cocktails'' (1939) and ''Here's How'' (1941), the author W.C. Whitfield had collected numerous drinks from the years of prohibition and provided them with comments partly in laconic style. As far as the ''Airmail Cocktail'' is concerned, Whitfield commented on it  ‘It ought to make you fly high’.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book|last=Meehan|first=Jim|title=The PDT Cocktail Book|last2=Gall|first2=Chris|publisher=Sterling Epicur|year=2011|isbn=978-1-4027-7923-7|location=New York|pages=48; 30}}</ref> The cocktail gained further popularity when the recipe was mentioned in the ''Handbook for Hosts'' in [[Esquire (magazine)|Esquire]] magazine in 1949.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Esquire's Handbook for Hosts.|publisher=Grosset & Dunlap Publishers|year=1949|location=New York}}</ref>

In the following decades, the cocktail wasn't very popular, having been published rarely. In the 2010s, however, the cocktail experienced another boom by being mentioned in the ‘[https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/11420025-the-pdt-cocktail-book PDT Cocktail Book]’ (2011) and by the promotion of alcoholic drinks by the brand [[Bacardi|Bacardí]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|date=26 July 2019|title=Rum trifft Champagner: Das völlig verdiente Revival des Air Mail Cocktails|url=https://mixology.eu/air-mail-cocktail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=mixology.eu|language=German|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210614140819/https://mixology.eu/air-mail-cocktail/ |archive-date=2021-06-14 }}</ref>

== Ingredients and similar cocktails ==
The basis for the ''Airmail Cocktail'' is a sour mixture of [[rum]], [[Lime (fruit)|lime]] juice and [[honey]] (or honey syrup), which are first shaken on ice in a [[cocktail shaker]] and then strained into a pre-cooled [[Cocktail glass]]. The mixture is then topped up with sparkling wine. The drink is similar to the [[Canchanchara|Canchánchara]],<ref name=":5" /> which consists of the same ingredients except for the [[sparkling wine]]. ‘Esquire’ magazine calls the ''Airmail Cocktail''  a "combination of the cocktails ''French 75'' and ''Honey Bee''".<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|last=Rense|first=Sarah|date=27 September 2019|title=How to make an Air Mail|url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3760/air-mail-drink-recipe/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=esquire.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150216154029/http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3760/air-mail-drink-recipe/|archive-date=16 February 2015}}</ref> The [[French 75 (cocktail)|''French 75'']] is a Champagne-based drink and a classic mixture of Gin, lemon juice and sugar syrup, while the ''Honey Bee'' consists of white rum, honey and lemon juice<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rense|first=Sarah|date=15 May 2020|title=How to make a Honey Bee|url=https://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3770/honey-bee-drink-recipe/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=esquire.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150215020034/http://www.esquire.com/food-drink/drinks/recipes/a3770/honey-bee-drink-recipe/|archive-date=15 February 2015}}</ref> and therefore is akin to a [[Daiquiri]]. A modern cocktail which shares the ingredients rum, lime juice and champagne with the Airmail Cocktail is the [[Old Cuban]], which was created in 2001.

Most recipes feature a mixture ratio of 3 [[Litre|cl]] rum, 1.5 cl lime juice and 1.5 cl honey syrup,<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /> which are then topped up with 3 cl champagne<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web|date=6 May 2021|title=Airmail Cocktail|url=https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/recipe-airmail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=imbibemagazine.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927230258/https://imbibemagazine.com/recipe/recipe-airmail/ |archive-date=2020-09-27 }}</ref> and either garnished with a slice of lime on the rim of the glass<ref name=":4" /> or not garnished at all<ref name=":5" /> - as usual for cocktails based on sparkling wine. The magazine ''[[Imbibe Magazine|Imbibe]]'' recommends a dash of [[Angostura bitters|Angostura]] (bitters) and a mint leaf,<ref name=":7" /> while the rum manufacturer [[Bacardi|Bacardí]] recommends a postage stamp as garnish.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Air Mail|url=https://www.bacardi.com/de/de/rum-cocktails/air-mail/|url-status=live|access-date=17 June 2021|website=bacardi.com|language=German|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422142859/https://www.bacardi.com/de/de/rum-cocktails/air-mail/ |archive-date=2021-04-22 }}</ref>

The Cocktail can be prepared with [[Rum#Grades|dark or white rum]]. Dark rum is best complemented with the addition of a comparatively [[Honey#Acid content and flavor effects|aromatic honey]], while white rum prefers the use of a mild honey like [[Honey#Floral source|Acacia blossom honey]].<ref name=":5" /> Cuban rum is often recommended. Substitution of the lime juice with lemon juice is possible.<ref name=":3" /> The honey syrup used for the cocktail is a mixture of 2 parts honey and 1 part water,<ref name=":4" /> which is easier to incorporate into mixtures and to add to taste than pure honey. In most cases, the cocktail is topped up with [[Champagne#Sweetness|dry champagne]], [[Sparkling wine#Crémant|Crémant]] or [[sparkling wine]] (less so with [[Prosecco]]).<ref name=":7" />

It is usually served [[Bartending terminology#Straight, up, and straight up|straight up]] in a pre-cooled [[Champagne glass#Flute|champagne flute]] or [[Champagne glass#Coupe|coupe]].<ref name=":5" /> Some recipes call for much larger quantities of liquid and proportionally more sparkling wine which therefore suggests serving the cocktail in a [[Collins glass]].<ref name=":6" />
