{{legend|#654321|2008 batches}}
{{legend|#423629|2010 batches}}]]
Traditional preparation of yerba mate leaves involves [[Smoking (cooking)|smoking]] them and for this reason they contain a high number of [[polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons]] (PAHs), such as [[benzo(a)pyrene]], which are [[carcinogen]]ic.<ref name="Golozar-2012">{{cite journal |last1=Golozar |first1=Asieh |last2=Fagundes |first2=Renato B. |last3=Etemadi |first3=Arash |last4=Schantz |first4=Michele M. |last5=Kamangar |first5=Farin |last6=Abnet |first6=Christian C. |last7=Dawsey |first7=Sanford M. |title=Significant Variation in the Concentration of Carcinogenic Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons in ''Yerba Maté'' Samples by Brand, Batch, and Processing Method |journal=[[Environmental Science & Technology]] |date=18 December 2012 |volume=46 |issue=24 |pages=13488–13493 |doi=10.1021/es303494s |pmid=23101992 |pmc=3525749|bibcode=2012EnST...4613488G }}</ref> It has been suggested that this may explain cancers associated with mate consumption, such as [[Lung cancer|lung]] and [[bladder cancer]], that cannot be attributed to its hot temperature. Instead, the hot temperature of mate (above 65°C) is specifically linked to [[oesophageal cancer]].<ref name="Oranuba-2018">{{cite journal |last1=Oranuba |first1=Ebele |last2=Deng |first2=Hua |last3=Peng |first3=Jiangnan |last4=Dawsey |first4=Sanford M |last5=Kamangar |first5=Farin |title=Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons as a potential source of carcinogenicity of mate |journal=[[Journal of Environmental Science and Health, Part C]] |date=2 January 2019 |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=26–41 |doi=10.1080/10590501.2019.1555323 |pmid=30596334 |pmc=6443446|bibcode=2019JESHC..37...26O }}</ref> However, the occurrence of PAHs in yerba mate leaves and infusion is based on small studies with non-representative sampling.<ref name="IARC-Book-2018">{{Cite book |title=Drinking Coffee, Mate, and Very Hot Beverages |year=2018 |publisher=International Agency for Research on Cancer |isbn=978-92-832-0183-0 |url=https://publications.iarc.fr/Book-And-Report-Series/Iarc-Monographs-On-The-Identification-Of-Carcinogenic-Hazards-To-Humans/Drinking-Coffee-Mate-And-Very-Hot-Beverages-2018 |format= |issn=1017-1606 |author-link=International Agency for Research on Cancer |access-date=2024-04-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240429063524/https://publications.iarc.fr/Book-And-Report-Series/Iarc-Monographs-On-The-Identification-Of-Carcinogenic-Hazards-To-Humans/Drinking-Coffee-Mate-And-Very-Hot-Beverages-2018 |archive-date=29 April 2024 |url-status=live |archive-format=}}</ref> In any case, the use of mate with potentially lower PAHs content, such as unsmoked mate, has been suggested as a preventive approach.<ref name="Golozar-2012"/><ref name="Oranuba-2018"/>[[File:Mate gaucho.jpg|thumb|Brazilian-style {{lang|pt|chimarrão}}]]

== Other properties ==

Mate is a rich source of [[caffeine]]. On average, mate tea contains 92 mg of [[chlorogenic acid]] per gram of dry leaves, and no [[catechin]]s, giving it a significantly different [[polyphenol]] profile from other teas.<ref name="Journal of Food Science">{{cite journal | doi = 10.1111/j.1750-3841.2007.00535.x | pmid = 18034743| title = Yerba Mate Tea: A Comprehensive Review on Chemistry, Health Implications, and Technological Considerations| journal = Journal of Food Science | date = 17 October 2007 | volume=72| issue = 9| pages = R138-51| last1 = Heck| first1 = C. I.| last2 = De Mejia| first2 = E. G.| s2cid = 32413555| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1111/j.1750-3841.2007.00535.x | pmid = 18034743| title = Polyphenols in green tea, black tea, and Mate tea| journal = Journal of Food Science | date = 17 October 2007 | volume=72 | issue = 9| pages=R138–R151| last1 = Heck| first1 = C. I.| last2 = De Mejia| first2 = E. G.| s2cid = 32413555| doi-access = free}}</ref>

{{anchor|Mateína}}According to Argentine culture in part promoted by marketers, the stimulant in mate is actually a substance called '''{{lang|es|mateína}}'''<!-- Bolded because [[Mateína]] redirects here. --> (named after the drink). However, analysis of the active [[Yerba mate#Chemical composition and properties|chemicals in yerba mate]] has found that {{lang|es|mateína}} is caffeine.<ref>{{Cite web|date=14 October 2011|title=La mateína no existe|url=https://www.unl.edu.ar/noticias/leer/8809/La_mateina_no_existe.html|access-date=23 July 2020|website=[[Universidad Nacional del Litoral]]}}</ref>

== Legendary origins ==
{{see also|Guaraní creation myth}}

The Guaraní people started drinking mate in a region that currently includes Paraguay, southern Brazil, southeastern Bolivia, northeastern Argentina and Uruguay. They have a legend that the Goddesses of the Moon and the Cloud came to visit the Earth one day. An old man saved them from a {{lang|es|yaguareté}} ([[jaguar]]) that was going to attack them. The goddesses gave him a new kind of plant, from which he could prepare a "drink of friendship" as compensation for his actions.<ref name="Preedy" />

== Variants ==

[[File:Mate cocido frio.jpg|thumb|Iced {{lang|es|[[mate cocido]]}}]]
There various types of yerba mate used to make the drink, depending on the processing and composition. Some key types include:

* {{lang|es|Con palo}} – a mix of stems and ground leaf
* {{lang|es|Sin palo}} – despalada: without stems or very little stem content
* {{lang|es|Compuesta}} – Mixed with other herbs and plants, like mint
* {{lang|es|Saborizada}} – in which the leaf has been flavored with flavorings and [[Food additive|food additives]]
* {{lang|es|Para tereré}} – made specifically for {{lang|es|[[tereré]]}}, usually with other herbs like mint etc
* {{lang|es|Barbacuá}} – toasted mate
* {{lang|es|Cocido/Saquitos}} – bagged, similar to tea bags

Another drink can be prepared with specially cut dry leaves, very cold water, and, optionally, [[lemon]] or another fruit juice, called {{lang|es|[[tereré]]}}. It is very common in Paraguay, northeastern Argentina and in the state of [[Mato Grosso do Sul]], Brazil. After pouring the water, it is considered proper to "wait while the saint has a sip" before the first person takes a drink. In southern Brazil, {{lang|pt|tererê}} is sometimes used as a derogatory term for a not hot enough {{lang|pt|chimarrão}}.

In Uruguay and Brazil, the traditional gourd is usually big with a corresponding large hole. In Argentina (especially in the capital [[Buenos Aires]]), the gourd is small and has a small hole and people sometimes add sugar for flavor.

In Uruguay, people commonly walk around the streets toting a {{lang|es|mate}} and a [[vacuum flask|thermos]] with hot water. In some parts of Argentina, gas stations sponsored by yerba mate producers provide free hot water to travelers, specifically for the purpose of drinking during the journey. Disposable mate sets with a plastic mate and straw and sets with a thermos flask and stacking containers for the yerba mate and sugar inside a fitted case are available.

In Argentina, {{lang|es|[[mate cocido]]}} (boiled mate), in Brazil, {{lang|pt-BR|chá mate}}, is made with a [[tea bag]] or leaves and drunk from a cup or mug, with or without sugar and milk. Companies such as Cabrales from [[Mar del Plata]] and [[Establecimiento Las Marías]] produce tea bags for export to Europe.<ref>[http://www.lanacion.com.ar/nota.asp?nota_id=340787 ''Cabrales abrirá locales en la Capital''] [[La Nación (Buenos Aires)|La Nación]] online, 6 October 2001 {{in lang|es}}.</ref>

[[File:A bottle of an ice tea variataion of mate and a glass of it.jpg|thumbnail|upright=.8|Mate is consumed as an ice tea in various regions of Brazil, in both artisanal and industrial forms. This is a bottle of industrialized mate ice tea, bought from a local supermarket in Rio de Janeiro.]]
Travel narratives, such as [[Maria Graham]]'s ''Journal of a Residence in Chile'', show a long history of mate-drinking in central Chile. Many rural Chileans drink mate, in particular in the southern regions, particularly [[Magallanes Region of Chile|Magallanes]], [[Aysén Region|Aysén]] and [[Chiloé Archipelago|Chiloé]].

In Peru, mate is widespread throughout the north and south, first being introduced to [[Lima]] in the 17th century. It is widespread in [[Rural area|rural zones]], and it is prepared with coca (plant) or in a sweetened tea form with small slices of lemon or orange.''<ref>{{Cite book|title=EL MATE Arte de Cebar|last=Villanueva|first=Amaro|publisher=La compañia general fabril financiera S. A.|year=1960|location=Buenos Aires|pages=200 (In Spanish)}}</ref>''

In some parts of Syria, Lebanon and other Eastern Mediterranean countries, drinking mate is also common. The custom came from Syrians and Lebanese who moved to South America during the late 19th and early parts of the 20th century, adopted the tradition, and kept it after returning to Western Asia. Syria is the biggest importer of yerba mate in the world, importing 15,000 tons a year. Mostly, the [[Druze]] communities in Syria and Lebanon maintain the culture and practice of mate.<ref name="donald" /><ref name="Middle East Online" />

According to a major retailer of mate in [[San Luis Obispo, California]], by 2004, mate had grown to about 5% of the overall natural tea market in North America.<ref>{{cite press release |title=Guayaki Honored With 2004 Socially Responsible Business Award |date=28 October 2004 |publisher=Guayaki |url=http://www.csrwire.com/News/3184.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120723173128/http://www.csrwire.com/News/3184.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 July 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |first=Laura |last=Everage |title=Trends in Tea |work=The Gourmet Retailer |date=1 November 2004 |url=http://www.gourmetretailer.com/gourmetretailer/magazine/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1000696346 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061105141723/http://www.gourmetretailer.com/gourmetretailer/magazine/article_display.jsp?vnu_content_id=1000696346 |archive-date=5 November 2006 }}</ref> Loose mate is commercially available in much of North America. Bottled mate is increasingly available in the United States. Canadian bottlers have introduced a cane sugar-sweetened, carbonated variety, similar to soda pop. One brand, Sol Mate, produces {{convert|10|usfloz|ml|adj=on}} glass bottles available at Canadian and U.S. retailers, making use of the translingual pun (English 'soul mate'; Spanish/Portuguese 'sun mate') for the sake of marketing.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/graphic/2007/01/19/GR2007011900577.html | title = Tip Sheet: Lowdown on Liquid Power-Ups | access-date = 29 May 2011 | last = Rude | first = Justin | date = 19 January 2007 | newspaper=The Washington Post }}</ref>

In some parts of the [[Southern Cone]] bitter mate is preferred, especially in Paraguay, Uruguay, the south of Brazil, and parts of Argentina and Bolivia. This is referred to in Brazil and a large part of Argentina as {{lang|es|cimarrón}} –which also an archaic name for wild cattle, especially, to a horse that was very attached to a cowboy – which is understood as unsweetened mate.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://circleofdrink.com/yerba-mate-terms-and-glossary|title=Mate Terms and Glossary|website=Circle of Drink|access-date=22 February 2019}}</ref> Many people are of the opinion that mate should be drunk in this form.

Unlike bitter mate, in every preparation of {{lang|es|mate dulce}}, or sweet mate, sugar is incorporated according to the taste of the drinker. This form of preparation is very widespread in various regions of Argentina, like in the [[Santiago del Estero]] province, [[Córdoba, Argentina|Córdoba]], [[Cuyo (Argentina)|Cuyo]], and [[Greater Buenos Aires|the metropolitan region of Buenos Aires]], among others. In Chile, this form of mate preparation is widespread in mostly [[Rural area|rural zones]]. The spoonful of sugar or honey should fall on the edge of the cavity that the straw forms in the {{lang|es|yerba}}, not all over the {{lang|es|mate}}. One variation is to sweeten only the first mate preparation in order to cut the bitterness of the first sip, thus softening the rest. In Paraguay, a variant of {{lang|es|mate dulce}} is prepared by first caramelizing refined sugar in a pot then adding milk. The mixture is heated and placed in a thermos and used in place of water. Often, chamomile ({{lang|es|manzanilla}}, in Spanish) and coconut are added to {{lang|es|yerba}} in the gumpa.

In the sweet version [[sugar substitute|artificial sweeteners]] are also often added. As an alternative sweetener, natural {{lang|gn|ka'á he'é}} (''[[Stevia rebaudiana]]'') is preferred, which is an herb whose leaves are added in order to give a touch of sweetness. This is used principally in Paraguay.

The gourd in which bitter mate is drunk is not used to consume sweet mate due to the idea that the taste of the sugar would be detrimental to its later use to prepare and drink bitter mate, as it is said that it ruins the flavor of the mate.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1988-08-10-mn-143-story.html|title=More Than a Drink : Yerba Mate: Argentina's Cultural Rite|last=SMITH|first=JAMES F.|date=10 August 1988|work=Los Angeles Times|access-date=22 February 2019|issn=0458-3035}}</ref>

[[Materva]] is a sweet, carbonated [[soft drink]] based on yerba mate. Developed in Cuba in 1920, and produced since the 1960s in [[Miami, Florida]], it is a staple of the Cuban culture in Miami.<ref name="Wong-2014">{{cite news |last=Wong |first=Samantha |title=Materva: Un Buchito de Cuba |url=http://www.jwu.edu/uploadedFiles/Documents/Academics/studentwork/JWUStuFoodWritingNMI.pdf |access-date=10 September 2020 |newspaper=Johnson and Wales: Student Food Writing |page=8 (PDF p. 11) |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140113000105/https://www.jwu.edu/uploadedFiles/Documents/Academics/studentwork/JWUStuFoodWritingNMI.pdf |archive-date=13 January 2014}}</ref><ref name="Roque-2011">{{Cite book |title=The Cuban Kitchen |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vmJlvl1mVUgC&pg=PA6 |first=Raquel Rábade |last=Roque |date=2011 |edition=1st |page=6 |publisher=Alfred A. Knopf |access-date=10 September 2020 |isbn=9780375711961 |language=en}}</ref>

Hoppy (drink):
{{Short description|Low-alcohol beer-flavored beverage}}
{{Refimprove|date=April 2010}}

[[File:Hoppy-20190908.JPG|thumb|right|A glass of Hoppy mixed with ''shōchū'']]
{{nihongo|'''Hoppy'''|ホッピー|Hoppii}} is a beer-flavored almost [[soft drink|non-alcoholic]] drink (0.8% alcohol) that Kokuka Beverage Company began producing and selling in [[Japan]] in 1948; it is most available in and associated with [[Tokyo]].<ref name=cnn /> Kokuka subsequently changed its name to Hoppy Beverage Co., Ltd. Hoppy is a registered [[trademark]] of Hoppy Beverage Co., Ltd.

Despite its beer-like flavor, Hoppy contains no [[purines|purine bases]].<ref name=r01>[http://www.hoppy-happy.com/products/hoppy.html "Product guide"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100506005153/http://www.hoppy-happy.com/products/hoppy.html |date=2010-05-06 }} {{in lang|ja}}, Hoppy Beverage Co., Ltd. (Retrieved on April 29, 2010)</ref>

At the time of its launch, Hoppy mixed with ''[[shōchū]]'' (a Japanese distilled beverage) was considered a substitute for [[beer]], which was beyond the reach of ordinary people. The mixed drink is referred to as Hoppy as well. It is still a staple among some Tokyo residents, and has experienced a retro revival of late.<ref name=cnn>"[http://travel.cnn.com/tokyo/drink/hoppy-denki-bran-and-hoisu-3-unique-tokyo-drinks-543636 Hoppy, Denki Bran and Hoisu: 3 unique Tokyo drinks]", ''CNN Travel'', by Matt Alt, 27 November, 2009</ref> It is a popular item at [[izakaya]] (Japanese-style pubs), especially within the suburban old town area along the [[Keisei Main Line]].{{Citation needed|date=December 2009}}

== Products ==
* Hoppy (original)
* Black Hoppy (tastes bitter and sweet with aroma)
* 55 Hoppy (memorialized with its 55th birthday)
* Hoppy 330 (bottled in a single-use bottle for home use)
* Hoppy Black (same as Black Hoppy for home use)

== Recommended use ==
Legally speaking, Hoppy is a non-alcoholic drink; however, it does contain about 0.8 percent alcohol.<ref name=r01/> It is often added to ''shōchū'', a Japanese distilled beverage.  The company recommends a detailed way of using it as follows:<ref>[http://www.hoppy-happy.com/gourmet-recipe/howtodrink/ "The way of drinking Hoppy (Three coolings)"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720104913/http://www.hoppy-happy.com/gourmet-recipe/howtodrink/ |date=2011-07-20 }} {{in lang|ja}}, Hoppy Beverage Co., Ltd. (Retrieved on May 1, 2010)</ref>

#''Shōchū'' should be ''[[Shochu#Multiply-distilled_sh.C5.8Dch.C5.AB|kōrui shōchū]]'' (or ''shōchū kōrui'', 焼酎甲類), which is distilled two or more times, and should contain 25 percent alcohol.
#Beforehand, the Hoppy and ''shōchū'' should be chilled in a refrigerator, and glasses should be chilled in a freezer. The company calls this "''sanrei''" (三冷, literally "three coolings").
#Five parts Hoppy should be added to one part ''shōchū''. This will give a resultant drink which has about 5 percent alcohol.
#The ''Shōchū'' should be ready in glasses first, and Hoppy should be added vigorously so that the drink foams up, without stirring, which is not recommended.
#Ice should not be added, because it detracts from the taste of the drink.

When Hoppy is ordered at a pub, a glass or mug of shōchū is brought along with a bottle of Hoppy.  The shochu will be referred to as {{nihongo|"naka"|中|lit. "inside"}}, and the Hoppy will be called {{nihongo|"soto"|外|lit. "outside"}}. If another bottle of Hoppy is needed, the phrase "another 'soto'" is used. It is also possible to order just "naka," in which case a shōchū shot will be served on its own.{{Citation needed|date=December 2009}}

Some establishments will place the mug and shōchū in a freezer and allow it to turn into a frozen slush before serving it with Hoppy.  The use of ice is sometimes looked down upon, but it is possible to find places that serve Hoppy and shōchū with ice.

'''Joseph "Joe" Gilmore''' (19 May 1922 – 18 December 2015)<ref>{{cite web |last=Nincevich |first=Stefano |date=23 December 2015 |title=Peter Dorelli e il "suo" Joe Gilmore |url=http://www.bargiornale.it/hey-joe-peter-dorelli-ricorda-il-suo-mentore-joe-gilmore/ |access-date=28 January 2017}}</ref> was a renowned bartender and famous mixologist during the 20th century. He was Head Barman at The [[Savoy Hotel]]'s American Bar from 1954 to 1976 and is recognised as the creator of numerous cocktails to mark special events and important guests, a longstanding tradition at the American Bar. Gilmore's most famous creations include Moonwalk, Link-Up, The Corpse Reviver, Lorraine, and Missouri Mule.

== Early life ==
Joseph Patrick Gilmore was born on 19 May 1922 in [[Belfast]], [[Northern Ireland]] to John Gilmore, a [[tobacconist]], and Margaret O'Connor, a tailoress, from [[Belfast]], [[Ireland]].

He was the third of nine children.

In 1938, aged 16, Gilmore moved to [[London]] looking for work and "adventure".<ref name="obit">{{cite web |date=January 15, 2016 |title=Joe Gilmore, barman - obituary |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/12102090/Joe-Gilmore-barman-obituary.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=January 28, 2017 |website=The Telegraph}}</ref> He began working as a wallpaper packer at the [[Arthur Sanderson & Sons|Arthur Sanderson & Son]]'s factory in [[Perivale]], London, later taking up work as a kitchen hand.<ref name="irishnews.com">{{Cite web |date=2016-01-16 |title=Cocktail king Joe Gilmore, Belfast's barman to the stars |url=http://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |access-date=2023-02-09 |website=The Irish News |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210141840/https://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Gilmore began his early bartender training at La Coquille, a French restaurant on [[St Martin's Lane]], [[Covent Garden]], among other places.<ref name="irishnews.com" /> While working at The Olde Bell he met and served Welsh millionaire steel-baron Kenneth Davies and the aviator [[Amy Johnson|Amy Johnston]]. The couple reportedly asked Gilmore for a dry martini, which he attempted unsuccessfully. Despite his attempt being enjoyed by the couple, Davies and Johnston politely demonstrated how to make one. Gilmore cited this interaction as the spark that fuelled his passion of cocktail mixology.<ref name="irishnews.com" /> After this first encounter, Davies and Gilmore became life long friends.<ref name="irishnews.com" />

== Career ==
Gilmore first began working at [[Savoy Hotel|The Savoy]] as a commis waiter at The American Bar of the Savoy Hotel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joe Gilmore |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/2886/people/joe-gilmore |access-date=2023-02-10 |website=www.diffordsguide.com |language=en}}</ref> By 1940, aged 18, he was promoted to trainee barman and began his apprenticeship with [[Harry Craddock]], earning [[Pound sterling|£]]3.10[[Shilling|s]] a week.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-16 |title=Cocktail king Joe Gilmore, Belfast's barman to the stars |url=http://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |access-date=2023-02-10 |website=The Irish News |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210141840/https://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Bartender to royals, politicians, world leaders and celebrities |language=en-GB |work=Belfast News Letter |url=https://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/bartender-royals-politicians-world-leaders-and-celebrities-1276443 |access-date=2023-02-10}}</ref>

In 1954, Gilmore took over as head bartender. Over the following two decades Gilmore created new cocktails, especially to honour special occasions and important guests, including [[Diana, Princess of Wales|Princess Diana]], [[Prince William, Duke of Cambridge|Prince William]], [[Anne, Princess Royal|Anne, The Princess Royal]], [[Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother|The Queen Mother]], [[Winston Churchill|Sir Winston Churchill]], and American Presidents [[Harry S. Truman]] and [[Richard Nixon]].

In addition to serving five generations of royals at private receptions and parties, Gilmore frequently served [[Errol Flynn]], [[Laurel and Hardy]], [[Charlie Chaplin]], [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]], [[Grace Kelly]], [[George Bernard Shaw]], [[Ernest Hemingway]], [[Noël Coward]], [[Agatha Christie]], [[Alice Faye]], [[Ingrid Bergman]], [[Julie Andrews]], [[Laurence Olivier]], [[Joan Crawford]], [[Judy Garland]], [[Liza Minnelli]], [[Bing Crosby]] and [[Frank Sinatra]] and [[Winston Churchill]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-16 |title=Cocktail king Joe Gilmore, Belfast's barman to the stars |url=http://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |access-date=2023-02-10 |website=The Irish News |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210141840/https://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1969, he created one of his most famous cocktails, the "Moonwalk", to commemorate the [[Apollo 11]] Moon landing. The cocktail is a combination of grapefruit juice, orange liqueur and rose water, topped with champagne. This was the first drink astronauts [[Neil Armstrong]] and [[Buzz Aldrin]] had upon returning to Earth.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-03-18 |title=Moonwalk |url=https://www.saveur.com/article/Recipes/Moonwalk-Cocktail/ |access-date=2023-02-13 |website=Saveur |language=en}}</ref>

Frank Sinatra was a frequent guest to the American Bar whenever he was in London and insisted only Gilmore was to serve him. It is widely believed the line from Sinatra’s One For My Baby "set’em up Joe" is in reference to Gilmore.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A final toast to Ireland's cocktail king |url=https://www.irishecho.com/2016/1/a-final-toast-to-irelands-cocktail-king |access-date=2023-02-13 |website=Irish Echo Newspaper |language=en}}</ref>

Gilmore retired from the Savoy in 1976.<ref name="obit" />

== Personal life ==
Gilmore married Marie Jeanne Zambelli in 1943. They had three sons.

During [[The Blitz]], Gilmore helped protect The Savoy by working as a fire warden from its roof.

Gilmore never returned to Ireland, but "...{{nbsp}}never forgot his Irish roots or family background and never lost his soft Belfast accent."<ref>{{Cite web |last=The Newsroom |date=2016-01-20 |title=Bartender to royals, politicians, world leaders and celebrities |url=https://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/bartender-royals-politicians-world-leaders-and-celebrities-1276443 |access-date=2023-02-09 |website=newsletter.co.uk}}</ref> He remained a [[Roman Catholic]] throughout his life, and died on 18 December 2015, aged 93.<ref>{{cite web | last=McDaid | first=Laura | title=Belfast barman who served cocktails to the stars dies aged 93 | publisher=[[BBC News]] | date=January 25, 2016 | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-northern-ireland-35399125 | access-date=January 28, 2017}}</ref>

An '''Incredible Hulk''', '''Green Eyed Monster''', '''Shrock''',  or '''Hip and Hen''' is a green-colored [[cocktail]] made by equal parts (2 fl oz each)<ref name="Hpnotiq.com">[http://www.hpnotiq.com/ Hpnotiq.com official recipe] → Drink Recipes → Exotiq Cocktails → Incredible Hulk ''(No direct link is available due to the [[Adobe Flash]] interface.)'' Retrieved 2007-01-15.</ref><ref name="Tabari">McCoy, Tabari (2004-04-15). "[http://www.intakeweekly.com/articles/6/020082-6886-151.html Drink Like a Rapper] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060721182024/http://www.intakeweekly.com/articles/6/020082-6886-151.html |date=2006-07-21 }}". ''Intake Weekly''. Retrieved 2006-12-20.</ref><ref name="Gibson">Gibson, Ashley M. (2004-05-07). "[http://charlotte.bizjournals.com/charlotte/stories/2004/05/10/tidbits1.html?page=5 Table Talk]". ''Charlotte Business Journal''. Retrieved 2006-12-20.</ref> of the fruit liqueur [[Hpnotiq]] and [[Hennessy]] brand [[cognac (drink)|cognac]] poured over ice. It is named after the [[Marvel Comics]] character [[Hulk]], who is sometimes referred to as the Incredible Hulk.

==History==
The drink was created at a Hpnotiq launch event by a restaurant bartender at [[Sean Combs]]' New York City restaurant, Justin's. A Hpnotiq employee noticed many women but few men drinking his company's liquor, because the men considered the blue, fruity drink to be too effeminate. Victor Alvarez, a bartender at the restaurant, mixed Hennessy with Hpnotiq to dilute the fruity flavor, resulting in a green beverage that quickly became a hit.<ref name="Govinda">Govinda, Pamela (2002). [http://www.beveragenet.net/cheers/2004/0404/0404ml.asp "The Millennials At the Bar"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060429054245/http://www.beveragenet.net/cheers/2004/0404/0404ml.asp |date=2006-04-29 }}. ''Adams Beverage Group''. Retrieved 2006-12-20.</ref>

==Variations==
The name 'Incredible Hulk' is also widely used amongst students in the North of England to describe a cocktail consisting of equal parts of [[WKD Original Vodka|WKD Blue]] and [[lager]].

==Culture==
The Incredible Hulk cocktail has been referenced in songs such as "Incredible Hulk" by the Memphis rap group Stress Free Fam and has appeared in [[music video]]s. It was also mentioned in ''[[The Boondocks (TV series)|The Boondocks]]'' episode "[[The Story of Thugnificent]]".<ref name="Tabari"/> ''[[Epic Meal Time]]'', a [[YouTube]] cooking show, featured cocktail at the start of the episode "Masta Pasta" with Muscles Glasses being punched repeatedly in the chest. As Dave's punching stops to complain that his hand hurts, someone off-camera says, "That's what Incredible Hulk does to you."<ref name="Epic Meal Time">"[http://www.epicmealtime.com/videos/2011/6/14/masta-pasta.html Epic Meal Time - Masta Pasta] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110617211908/http://www.epicmealtime.com/videos/2011/6/14/masta-pasta.html |date=2011-06-17 }}"</ref>
It can also be seen in the [[post-credits scene]] of [[The Incredible Hulk (film)|The Incredible Hulk]] where [[Thunderbolt Ross|General Ross]] is drinking a glass of the cocktail at a bar.

|url=https://www.lesechos.fr/travailler-mieux/vie-au-travail/qui-est-tropico-la-1ere-marque-francaise-rachetee-par-coca-cola-1176895?_x_tr_sl=fr&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en&_x_tr_pto=sc |website=[[Les Echos (France)|Les Echos]] |language=fr}} As of 2023, it is also the "number one juice drinks brand" in Britain.{{Cite press release |title=Oasis refreshes Summer lunches with return of fruity campaign |date=23 June 2023 |url=https://grocerytrader.co.uk/oasis-refreshes-summer-lunches-with-return-of-fruity-campaign/ |language=en-US |last= |access-date=14 September 2025 |work=Grocery Trader}} In May 2013, Oasis was exported to stores and supermarkets around the [[Ivory Coast]], and by the end of 2013, to stores and supermarkets around [[Madagascar]].{{citation needed|date=September 2012}} == Advertising == === Britain === Advertising campaigns for Oasis target adults and promote the drink as an alternative to water. Guaro (drink):
{{Short description|Liquor made in many places in Latin America}}
{{About|an alcoholic drink||Guaro (disambiguation){{!}}Guaro}}
[[File:Guaro Sour, Quepos.jpg|thumb|A guaro [[Sour (cocktail)|sour]] served in [[Quepos]], Costa Rica]]

'''Guaro''' is a [[liquor]] made in many places in [[Latin America]]. A clear liquid distilled from [[sugar cane]] juices, it has a slightly sweeter taste than comparable liquors. It is traditionally 60 proof or 30% alcohol, although recently 70 proof and 80 proof versions are produced.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://theculturetrip.com/central-america/costa-rica/articles/a-brief-history-of-guaro-costa-ricas-national-liquor/|title=A Brief History of Guaro: Costa Rica's National Liquor|last=Parker|first=Jenn|website=Culture Trip|date=24 May 2017 |access-date=2019-07-26}}</ref> It is popular in [[Colombia]], [[Costa Rica]], [[Ecuador]], [[El Salvador]], [[Guatemala]], [[Honduras]], [[Nicaragua]], and [[Panama]], although in many places the word "guaro" can refer to almost any liquor.

The name "guaro" came from [[Central America]]. Colombians call it [[aguardiente]]. Sometimes it is referred to as a "soft vodka" because it has a lower alcohol content than vodka.{{citation needed|date=January 2015}}

== History ==
In Costa Rica, the government nationalized its manufacture in 1851 in an effort to quell the clandestine production of liquor.<ref name=":0" /> The ''Fabrica Nacional de Licores'' (National Liquor Factory) was founded for this reason, and since 1980<ref name="news.co.cr">{{Cite news|url=https://news.co.cr/the-traditional-drink-of-costa-rica-cacique-guaro/23077/|title=The Traditional Drink of Costa Rica: Cacique Guaro|date=2013-07-14|website=Costa Rica Star News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-07-26}}</ref> produces the only legal brand, [[Cacique Guaro]].<ref name=":0" />

==Clandestine and fraudulent production==
Clandestine liquor production is still prevalent, but it is seen more as a tradition than a business as it would be difficult to compete with the nationally produced guaro. The illegal version of the product is often called ''guaro de contrabando'' ("smuggled guaro") and is produced by various methods, all through distillation, but with different base ingredients, typically fruits or sweets from other sources, molasses from sugarcane, or simply sugar.

===Deaths===
In 2019 multiple deaths were reported caused by drinking adulterated counterfeit guaro produced by various criminal organizations.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Murphy |first1=Heather |title=19 Deaths in Costa Rica Tied to Tainted Alcohol, Officials Say |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/07/22/world/americas/costa-rica-tainted-alcohol.html |work=The New York Times |date=22 July 2019}}</ref>

==Export==

Guaro LLC began exporting guaro to California in the United States.<ref>[http://www.amcostarica.com/042104.htm Humble guaro goes to West Coast to be a star]  ''A.M. Oghi (drink):
{{Short description|Armenian distilled fruit spirit}}
{{Italic title}}
'''Oghi''' (sometimes '''oghee''', {{langx|hy|[[wikt:օղի|օղի]]}} ''òġi''; colloquially '''aragh''') is an [[Armenia]]n [[distilled beverage|spirit]] distilled from fruits or berries. It is widely produced as [[moonshine]] from home-grown garden fruits all across Armenia, where it is served as a popular welcome drink to guests and is routinely drunk during meals.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.road-to-armenia.com/scenes/journal3.html |title=Oghi, an Armenian fruit vodka |access-date=2008-12-12 |archive-date=2008-10-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081008031938/http://www.road-to-armenia.com/scenes/journal3.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> Arguably, Armenian oghi is not "vodka" at all (see [[Vodka war]]) and merely became thought of as such during the Soviet era in Armenia.

Mulberry oghi is commercially produced and exported under the brand name ''Artsakh'' by the Artsakh-Alco Brandy Company in [[Askeran Region|Askeran District]] in the [[Republic of Artsakh]].<ref>[http://www.topliquor.com/store/Artsakh-Gold-Mulberry-Barrel-Aged-Armenian-Vodka-750-ml-p-67100.html Artsakh mulberry vodka]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.spyur.am/artsakhalco.htm |title=Artsakh-Alco Brandy Company |access-date=2008-12-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091025220413/http://www.spyur.am/artsakhalco.htm |archive-date=2009-10-25 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Varieties==
*''Tuti oghi'' – mulberry oghi (commercial brand name ''Artsakh'', from Nagorno-Karabakh)
*''Honi oghi'' – from hon, a small red berry ([[European Cornel|cornelian cherry]])
*''Tsirani oghi'' – from apricots
*''Tandzi oghi'' – from pears
*''Khaghoghi oghi'' – from grapes
*''Salori oghi'' – from plums
*''Moshi oghi''  – from blackberry
*''Tzi oghi'' – from figs
*''Khundzori oghi'' – from apples

==Oghi in the Armenian Diaspora==
In the [[Armenian Diaspora]], ''oghi'' refers to the aniseed-flavored distilled alcoholic drink called [[arak (drink)|arak]] in the [[Middle East]], [[rakı]] in Turkey, or [[ouzo]] in [[Greece]].<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=QdxTnaqOywIC&dq=%22armenian+diaspora%22+oghi&pg=PA131 ''Western Armenian Dictionary and Phrasebook''], by Nicholas Awde and Vazken-Khatchig Davidian, Hippocrene Books, 2006, p. 131; {{ISBN|0-7818-1048-5}}, {{ISBN|978-0-7818-1048-7}}</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=GmtPLvnrc38C&dq=oghi+raki+arak&pg=PA815 ''The Heritage of Armenian Literature''], Vol. III, p. 815, by Agop Jack Hacikyan, Gabriel Basmajian, Edward S. Franchuk, Nourhan Ouzounian, Wayne State University Press, 2000, {{ISBN|0-8143-3221-8}}</ref> In the Prohibition-Era United States, Armenians produced bootleg Oghi from raisins and flavored it with anise. In the old country of [[Western Armenia]], the oghi was often made from grape [[pomace]], or from [[Morus (plant)|mulberries]], and was sometimes flavored with [[anise]], [[mastic (plant resin)|mastic]], or even [[cardamom]] or orange peel, as well as other herbs or spices. In the region of [[Kharpert]] as well as nearby Chnkoosh, oghi was usually made from mulberries.

Margarita machine:
{{Short description|Margarita dispensing device}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=January 2024}}
[[Image:A margarita machine in Wakefield MA.jpg|thumb|right|250px|A margarita machine in [[Wakefield, Massachusetts]]]]
A '''margarita machine,''' also known as a '''frozen drink machine''' is a piece of commercial foodservice equipment which dispenses a frozen [[margarita]]. A margarita mix, traditionally lime flavored, is poured into the hopper,<ref>{{Cite web |title=POPUP |url=https://smservice.spacemanusa.com/portal/en/kb/articles/sog-fb-introduction |access-date=2023-02-27 |website=smservice.spacemanusa.com |archive-date=2023-02-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230227210407/https://smservice.spacemanusa.com/portal/en/kb/articles/sog-fb-introduction |url-status=live }}</ref> which can be refrigerated, and may contain a spinning [[Agitator (device)|agitator]].  From the hopper, the product flows into the freezing cylinder, where it is frozen and kept at the proper viscosity to serve.  The user is able to dispense margaritas from such a device for extended periods of time without losing any quality in the taste of the margaritas. A margarita machine may be purchased from a [[foodservice distributor]] and is manufactured by companies such as [[Spaceman USA]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.spacemanusa.com/|title=Spaceman Soft Serve and Frozen Beverage Machines|website=Spaceman|access-date=2023-02-27|archive-date=2023-02-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230227211037/https://www.spacemanusa.com/|url-status=live}}</ref> and [[Taylor Company]].

==History==
The invention of the world's first frozen margarita machine in 1971 by Mariano Martinez, a Dallas restaurateur, marked a significant milestone in cocktail history. This development was a response to the challenges faced in his restaurant, Mariano's Mexican Cuisine, due to the high demand for margaritas.

Before the advent of the margarita machine, frozen margaritas were typically made using a blender. This method was popularized by the introduction of the Waring Blendor in 1937, invented by Fred Waring.<ref name="Smithsonian Origins">{{cite web |title=The Uniquely Texan Origins of the Frozen Margarita |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smithsonian-institution/the-uniquely-texan-origins-of-the-frozen-margarita-180975243/ |access-date=2023-12-04 |publisher=Smithsonian Magazine}}</ref> Mariano's father used a traditional recipe he learned while working at a San Antonio speakeasy in 1938, which included ice, triple sec, hand-muddled limes, 100 percent blue agave tequila, and a splash of simple syrup.

The legalization of liquor by the drink in Texas in 1970, following a state constitutional amendment, enabled Martinez to open his restaurant. The popularity of his family's margarita recipe was initially met with enthusiasm, but the labor-intensive process of making them in a blender led to challenges.<ref name="Smithsonian Origins" />

Martinez's innovation came when he realized the potential of using a machine for a more consistent margarita. Initially considering a Slurpee machine, he eventually adapted a secondhand soft-serve ice cream machine to make his margaritas. This adaptation involved tweaking the traditional Recipe to create a uniform slush without diluting the alcohol's flavor.<ref name="Smithsonian Origins" />

In 2005, the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History acknowledged the cultural and historical significance of Martinez's invention by acquiring his original frozen margarita machine. This acquisition highlights the margarita machine's role in transforming the frozen margarita from a regional specialty to a national favorite cocktail.<ref name="Smithsonian Acquisition">{{cite web |title=National Museum of American History Acquires Frozen Margarita Machine |url=https://americanhistory.si.edu/press/releases/national-museum-american-history-acquires-frozen-margarita-machine |access-date=2023-12-04 |publisher=Smithsonian Institution}}</ref>

The invention of the frozen margarita machine by Mariano Martinez in 1971 not only revolutionized the way margaritas were made but also had a significant impact on the popularity of Tex-Mex food and the structure of Tex-Mex restaurants.<ref name="Smithsonian Origins" />

==Characteristics==
Margarita machines remove heat from a drink mix using a [[Vapor-compression refrigeration]] system (VCRS).  The product is fed into the freezing cylinder where it is agitated by an beater or auger, and frozen.  The freezing cylinder is also referred to as the evaporator.  Once the product is frozen, it can be dispensed through the discharge door by manually pulling the handle.  Margarita machines can use any combination of ingredients, as long as the [[brix]] value is between 12 and 18.

A brix below 12 will lead to over freezing and a brix of over 18 will be hard to freeze and too sweet.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Spaceman |first=Made by |date=July 27, 2022 |title=All You Need to Know About Frozen Drink Machines |url=https://www.spacemanusa.com/all-you-need-to-know-about-frozen-drink-machines/ |access-date=2023-02-27 |website=Spaceman |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-02-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230227210408/https://www.spacemanusa.com/all-you-need-to-know-about-frozen-drink-machines/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

'''Jaffa''' is a popular carbonated soft drink produced in [[Finland]] by [[Hartwall]]. Jaffa is usually [[orange soft drink|orange flavoured]], however different flavours are sold. 

The brand is also notable for the numerous popular posters and designs created for it by graphic designer [[Erik Bruun]].<ref name="hu">{{cite news |last1=Nupponen |first1=Sakari |title=Muistatko tämän Jaffa-mainoksen – 90-vuotias tekijä on täydessä vedossa |url=https://www.helsinginuutiset.fi/paikalliset/1561934 |access-date=16 July 2020 |work=Helsingin Uutiset |date=19 July 2016}}</ref><ref name="mtv">{{cite news |last1=Tuominen |first1=Petra |title=Legendaarinen juoma, josta tuli Suomessa välitön hitti – muistatko vielä nämä Jaffa-pullot? |url=https://www.mtvuutiset.fi/makuja/artikkeli/legendaarinen-juoma-josta-tuli-suomessa-valiton-hitti-muistatko-viela-nama-jaffa-pullot/7414712 |access-date=16 July 2020 |work=MTV Uutiset |date=20 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="cision">{{cite web |title=Hartwall Jaffa onnittelee graafikko Erik Bruunia katukuvassa |url=https://news.cision.com/fi/oy-hartwall-ab |website=Hartwall |access-date=16 July 2020 |date=31 March 2016}}</ref><ref name="ruokatieto">{{cite web |title=50-vuotias Hartwall Jaffa maistuu kaikenikäisille |url=https://www.ruokatieto.fi/uutiset/50-vuotias-hartwall-jaffa-maistuu-kaikenikaisille |website=Ruokatieto |access-date=16 July 2020 |date=20 May 1999 |archive-date=17 July 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200717125018/https://www.ruokatieto.fi/uutiset/50-vuotias-hartwall-jaffa-maistuu-kaikenikaisille |url-status=dead }}</ref>

'''Manhattan Special''' is a beverage company located in [[Brooklyn]], New York. The company was founded in 1895 and is located in the neighborhood of [[Williamsburg, Brooklyn|Williamsburg]]. Their most famous product is their Espresso Coffee Soda, made with espresso beans, seltzer water, and sugar. The name of the company originated from the location of its plant on [[Manhattan Avenue (Brooklyn)|Manhattan Avenue]].<ref>{{cite news |last=Lukas |first=Paul |date=July 23, 2003 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/07/23/dining/surviving-by-fizzy-logic.html |title=Surviving by Fizzy Logic |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Wilson |first=Michael |date=July 7, 2008 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/07/07/nyregion/07coffee.html |title=A Modern Comeback for a Taste of Brooklyn |work=The New York Times}}</ref>

Although best known for their coffee beverages, Manhattan Special also produces a line of more traditional sodas. It uses all natural flavors.  Flavors include vanilla [[cream soda]], cherry, [[sarsaparilla (soft drink)|sarsaparilla]], orange, and gassosa (lemon/lime).

Manhattan Special is mentioned in the film ''[[Sing Sing (2023 film)|Sing Sing]]'' as a beverage one of the prisoners loved to drink with his wife before his incarceration.

Krambambula (drink):
{{Short description|Type of cocktail from Belarus}}
[[File:Belorussian Krambambulya.jpg|thumb|Belarusian Krambambula in a Moscow restaurant]]
'''Krambambula''' is a Belarusian alcoholic mix drink or [[cocktail]] that typically consists of [[red wine]], and various kinds of liquor, including [[gin]], [[vodka]], or [[rum]] - there are many different recipes.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kuechengoetter.de/rezepte/verschiedenes/Krambambuli-331279.html |title=Krambambuli |author= |date= |publisher=Kűchengötter |accessdate=October 8, 2012}} (in German)</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kochbar.de/rezepte/krambambuli.html |title= 4 Krambambuli Rezepte |author=|date= |publisher= kochbar|accessdate= October 8, 2012}} (in German)</ref> Commercially produced versions are also available in some areas.

==Etymology==
The name is probably derived from the [[Old High German]] word ''Kranawitu'' or ''chranawita'' ("croaker timber," another name for [[juniper]]) and from the [[Rotwelsch]] word ''Blamp'' (alcoholic drink). 

==History==
[[File:Gdańsk Główne Miasto - ul. Szeroka (Dom Pod Łososiem).JPG|thumb|Pod Łososiem (The Salmon) restaurant in Gdańsk]]
A red-colored cherry [[liqueur]] called ''Krambambuli'' was formerly produced by a distillery in [[Gdańsk|Danzig]] (Gdańsk) established by Ambrosius Vermöllen, a [[Mennonite]] immigrant from [[De Lier]] in [[County of Holland|Holland]], who received Danzig citizenship on 6 July 1598.

Moose milk (cocktail):
{{Short description|Canadian alcoholic mixed drink}}
{{Canadian cuisine}}

'''Moose milk''' is a traditional [[Canadian cuisine|Canadian]] alcoholic mixed drink with roots in the historic celebratory events of the [[Canadian Armed Forces]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rummel |first=Rachel |date=2020-12-07 |title=Meet 'Moose Milk,' the Wintry Cocktail of the Canadian Military |url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/what-is-moose-milk-canadian-holiday-cocktail |access-date=2024-04-17 |website=[[Atlas Obscura]] |language=en}}</ref> It is also served at the [[Levée (event)|levée]], a [[New Year's Day]] celebration held all levels of the [[Canadian government]]al administrations to honour the member of the armed forces, from the federal level to municipalities.<ref name="cbn">{{Cite web| title = NEW YEAR'S LEVEE AND MOOSE MILK| work = Cape Breton News| accessdate = 2016-08-25| date = 2010-12-31| url = https://caperfrasers.wordpress.com/2010/12/31/new-year-levee-and-moose-milk/}}</ref><ref name="swg">{{Cite web| title = The History of Moose Milk| work = Shooters Woodfire Grill| accessdate = 2016-08-25| url = http://www.shooterswoodfiregrill.com/blog/2014/06/the-history-of-moose-milk/| archive-date = 2016-08-26| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160826090338/http://www.shooterswoodfiregrill.com/blog/2014/06/the-history-of-moose-milk/| url-status = dead}}</ref> The term was first recorded used to describe the cocktail in the 1915–1920.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dictionary.com/browse/moose--milk|title=the definition of moose milk|website=www.dictionary.com|language=en|access-date=2019-02-02}}</ref>

==Culture==
The [[Royal Canadian Navy]], [[Royal Canadian Air Force]], and [[Canadian Army]] all claim as the originator of the drink.<ref name="cbn"/><ref name="swg"/><ref name="f">
{{Cite web| title = Moose Milk Recipe - Food.com| accessdate = 2016-08-25| url = http://www.food.com/recipe/moose-milk-80943}}</ref>

Events or parties held in the Royal Canadian Navy serving moose milk, are known as "moosers".<ref>{{Cite book| edition = 1| publisher = Mark Nelson| isbn = 978-0-9732825-3-5| last = Nelson| first = Mark R.| title = Jackspeak of the Royal Canadian Navy: A Glossary of Canadian Naval Terminology| date = 2014-10-29}}</ref> The navy also serves the drink on-board on Sundays while the ships are in port, the phrase "moose is loose" is used to refer to the presence of the drink at various locations (e.g. "The moose is loose in the main cafeteria").<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://hamiltonnaval.ca/naval-traditions/moosemilk/|title=Moosemilk {{!}} Hamilton Naval Heritage Association|language=en-CA|access-date=2019-02-02}}</ref>

==Components==
Moose milk is composed of five different classes of ingredients:<ref name="iroq">{{Cite web| title = Navy Moose Milk Drink Recipe |date=28 May 2013|publisher=Liverpool Ships and Sailors| accessdate = 2016-08-25| url = http://www.liverpoolshipsandsailors.com/2013/05/28/navy-moose-milk-drink-recipe/}}</ref><ref name="rcaf">{{Cite web| first=Otteray |last=Scribe |title = Royal Canadian Air Force Moose Milk Recipe| work = Daily Kos| accessdate = 2016-08-25| url = http://www.dailykos.com/story/2013/12/31/1266338/-Royal-Canadian-Air-Force-Moose-Milk-Recipe}}</ref><ref name="tdk">{{Cite web| title = Moose's Milk| work = The Drink Kings| accessdate = 2016-08-25| date = 2014-11-05| url = http://www.thedrinkkings.com/mooses-milk-recipe/}}</ref>
* ''[[Hard liquor|Spirit]]'': typically a combination of [[Canadian whisky]], [[vodka]], or dark [[rum]]
* ''[[Coffee]] beverage'': [[Kahlúa]] and occasionally prepared coffee
* ''Dairy'': a combination of whole [[milk]], [[cream]], [[condensed milk]], [[eggnog]], or vanilla [[ice cream]]
* ''Sweetener'': [[maple syrup]] or [[sugar]]
* ''Spice'': [[nutmeg]] and occasionally [[cinnamon]]
[[Egg yolk]]s are sometimes used directly or indirectly through eggnog or ice cream to prevent separation of the drink.<ref name="tdk" />

Nutcracker (drink):
{{short description|Illicit alcoholic drinks sold in New York City}}
[[File:Lightning Hopkins, nutcracker style cocktail, Peaches on Lewis.jpg|thumbnail|upright|Nutcrackers are traditionally sold in juice bottles; more recently, legal to-go cocktails are sold in the same format.]]
A '''nutcracker''' is a type of [[cocktail]] consisting of a mixture of  [[hard liquor]] and sugary beverages such as [[fruit juice]].<ref name="Huffington Post 20 May 2011">{{cite news |last1=Zanoni |first1=Carla |title=Cops Crack Down On Sale Of Alcoholic 'Nutcracker' Drinks |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/nutcracker-drinks-have-co_n_864955 |work=Huffington Post |date=20 May 2011 |language=en}}</ref> Nutcrackers originated and are typically made and sold in [[New York City]].<ref name="NYT 17 August 2019">{{cite news |last1=Randle |first1=Aaron |title=Banned on the Beach? It's Still Nutcracker Summer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/08/17/nyregion/banned-on-the-beach-its-still-nutcracker-summer.html |work=The New York Times |date=17 August 2019}}</ref> Originally sold via word-of-mouth by street vendors, nutcrackers have also been offered as "to-go cocktails" by establishments such as bars and restaurants.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Maurer|first=Daniel|url=https://bedfordandbowery.com/2020/05/bars-are-now-selling-nycs-favorite-illicit-street-drink-nutcracker/|title = Bars Are Now Selling NYC's Favorite Illicit Street Drink, Nutcracker|date = 29 May 2020|website=Bedford + Bowery}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Cherie|first=Ariel|url=https://theurbandaily.com/2940354/nutcracker-drink-recipes/|title = 5 Nutcracker Recipes for You to Try This Summer|date = 2 June 2014|website=The Urban Daily}}</ref>

Nutcrackers frequently consist of liquors such as vodka, rum, tequila and cognac, mixed with fruit juice, [[Kool-Aid]] or candy. They are sold mainly during the summer on the streets and on the beaches, and come in cups or small plastic bottles.<ref name="NYT 17 August 2019" /><ref name="Huffington Post 20 May 2011" />

==History==
Nutcrackers are thought to have been first made in 1993 or 1994 in the [[Dominican Americans|Dominican]] areas of [[Washington Heights, Manhattan|Washington Heights]], specifically as a cocktail at the Flor de Mayo restaurant, which styles the drink as the "Nut Cracker", and claims to be the original version.<ref name="grubstreet">{{cite web |last=Herbert |first=David Gauvey |title=On the Trail of New York's Nutcracker Kings |url=https://www.grubstreet.com/2019/06/on-the-trail-of-nyc-nutcracker-kings.html |work=Grub Street |date=2019-06-13}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |website=Flor de Mayo |title=Drinks Drinks Drinks... |url=http://www.flordemayo.com/drinks.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150206030104/http://www.flordemayo.com/drinks.pdf |archive-date=2015-02-06}}</ref> The "Nut Cracker" cocktail was invented by José Chu, a restaurant manager, and "Juice", a drug dealer, who requested a new cocktail, and was named for ''[[The Nutcracker]]'' ballet, due to a New York City Ballet ad on TV at the time.<ref name="grubstreet" /> It consisted of Bacardi 151, Southern Comfort, Amaretto, pineapple juice, grenadine, and Rose's Sour Lime, and is described as strong, syrupy, sweet, and tart.<ref name="grubstreet" /> 

From 1999, the cocktail was then bottled and sold for $10 each by "Fatyuil", a Dominican-American hairdresser, out of her apartment on St. Nicholas Avenue, and became popular. From 2000, it was further popularized by Freddy Tejada, who sold drinks out of a barbershop on [[Audubon Avenue]], and featured the drink in a program on a [[Manhattan Neighborhood Network]] (public access television) program, ''Dominican USA''.<ref name="grubstreet" /> It then became popular in [[Harlem]] and across the city.<ref name="NYT 17 August 2019" />

== Legality ==
The sale of nutcrackers without a license violates New York law, and the police have on occasion attempted to sanction it.<ref name="Huffington Post 20 May 2011" /> 

In 2010, Black community leaders including [[Al Sharpton]] spoke out against the sale of nutcrackers because of the unregulated drinks' potential dangers to health and to children. In 2011, the "nutcracker bill" ([https://assembly.state.ny.us/leg/?default_fld=&bn=A06324&term=2011&Summary=Y&Actions=Y&Text=Y&Committee&nbspVotes=Y&Floor&nbspVotes=Y A06324]) sponsored by State Senator [[Adriano Espaillat]] (D – Manhattan/Bronx) and Assemblyman [[Nelson Castro (politician)|Nelson Castro]] (D – Bronx) and signed by Governor [[Andrew Cuomo]] stripped barbershops of their license if they were convicted of selling alcohol to minors.<ref name="grubstreet" /><ref>{{cite press release |title=Gov. Cuomo Signs Sen. Espaillat's Bill to Crackdown on Dangerous "Nutcracker" Alcoholic Drink |first=Adriano |last=Espaillat |date=2011-08-19 |url=https://www.nysenate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/adriano-espaillat/gov-cuomo-signs-sen-espaillats-bill-crackdown-dangerous |website=New York State Senate}}</ref> 

Some nutcracker vendors have attempted to professionalize and legalize their business in order to assuage such concerns.<ref name="NYT 17 August 2019" />

In 2020, the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and resulting closure of dine-in bars and restaurants, and the newly-legal sale of alcohol to-go resulted in increased competition with traditional nutcracker sales; some to-go cocktails were sold in the same traditional juice bottle format as nutcrackers.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/20/nyregion/coronavirus-nutcrackers-cocktails-nyc.html |title=The Nutcracker Hustle: Why Selling Buried Cocktails Just Got Harder |first=Margot |last=Boyer-Dry|newspaper=The New York Times |date=20 June 2020 }}</ref>

== Popular culture ==
Nutcrackers have been mentioned in popular culture since as early as [[Loaded Lux]], "Nut Cracker" (2006),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://youtube.com/watch?v=SFZpJ8AVkp4|website = [[YouTube]]| title=Loaded Lux: Nut Cracker }}</ref> and popularized in [[N.O.R.E.]], "Nutcracker" (2010).<ref name="grubstreet" />

Izze (drink):
{{Short description|American sparkling juice brand}}
{{Infobox brand|name=Izze|country=United States|introduced=February 2002|producttype=Sparkling juice|currentowner=[[PepsiCo]]|image=Izze drink logo.png}}

'''Izze''', stylized in all caps, is an American [[Sparkling water|sparkling juice]] brand produced by the '''Izze Beverage Company''', which is owned by [[PepsiCo]]. The company is based in [[Boulder, Colorado]]. It was founded in Boulder in 2002 by Greg Stroh and Todd Woloson, and was purchased by PepsiCo in 2006. 

== Varieties ==
As of 2024, Izze is available in can and bottle forms. In can form, the flavors are: Apple, Blackberry, Cherry Lime, Clementine, Grapefruit, Mango, Peach, Pomegranate, Strawberry, Watermelon and Pineapple. In bottle form, the flavors are: Blackberry, Cherry Lime, Clementine, Grapefruit, Peach, and Pomegranate.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Meet Our Flavors – IZZE Sparkling Juice Drink |url=https://izze.com/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=izze.com |language=en}}</ref> The flavors are sometimes sold in variety packs.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Corte |first=Michael La |date=2022-12-29 |title=The 8 best beverages to buy at Costco |url=https://www.salon.com/2022/12/29/the-8-best-beverages-to-buy-at-costco/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Salon |language=en}}</ref> The brand was also previously available as Izze esque, which has fewer calories; Izze Fortified, which has more vitamins; and Izze Fusions, a mix between sparkling water, sparkling soda, and juice.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=May 24, 2012 |title=IZZE® Brings Back A Summertime Sparkler: Lemon |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/izze-brings-back-a-summertime-sparkler-lemon-153609885.html |access-date=July 30, 2024 |website=PR Newswire}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=IZZE Fusions {{!}} Details - BevNET.com Brand Database |url=http://www.bevnet.com/brands/izze-fusions |access-date=2025-07-17 |website=www.bevnet.com |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Izze Esque {{!}} Details - BevNET.com Brand Database |url=http://www.bevnet.com/brands/izze_esque |access-date=2025-07-17 |website=www.bevnet.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Izze Beverage Company also markets the brand as an [[alcohol mixer]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=March 21, 2017 |title=Why PepsiCo and TBWA are staying fuzzy on details in new Izze Fusions push |url=https://www.campaignlive.com/article/why-pepsico-tbwa-staying-fuzzy-details-new-izze-fusions-push/1427990 |access-date=July 31, 2024 |website=Campaign Live}}</ref>

== History ==
Izze was created by Greg Stroh and Todd Woloson in [[Boulder, Colorado]], in February 2002. It was inspired by the "Sundance Natural Juice Sparklers" sparkling fruit juice produced by the [[Stroh Brewery Company|Stroh Brewery]], which was the Stroh family business. Izze was an alternative to the carbonated soft drinks and juices on the market at the time. It grew in popularity through its placement in large retailers like [[King Soopers]], [[Target Corporation|Target]], [[Starbucks]], and [[Whole Foods Market|Whole Foods]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dolan |first=Kerry A. |title=How To Blow $9 Billion: The Fallen Stroh Family |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/kerryadolan/2014/07/08/how-the-stroh-family-lost-the-largest-private-beer-fortune-in-the-u-s/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2008-03-21 |title=Industry vet dances to health tune |url=https://www.denverpost.com/2008/03/21/industry-vet-dances-to-health-tune/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=The Denver Post |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Izze Beverage Co.: Spreading Good Karma {{!}} Beverage Industry |url=https://www.bevindustry.com/articles/83964-izze-beverage-co-spreading-good-karma |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=www.bevindustry.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Dolan |first=Kerry A. |title=From Stroh Brewery To Izze Soda And Beyond: One Stroh Family Member's Entrepreneurial Path |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/kerryadolan/2014/07/10/from-stroh-brewery-to-izze-soda-and-beyond-one-stroh-family-members-entrepreneurial-path/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref> Izze was first released in four flavors: Blackberry, Grapefruit, Lemon, and Pear.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> Local bars in Colorado initially showed support to the company by serving the drink mixed with alcohol.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hamilton |first=William L. |date=2004-07-04 |title=SHAKEN AND STIRRED; Fruity Fizz for Adults |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/07/04/style/shaken-and-stirred-fruity-fizz-for-adults.html |access-date=2024-07-31 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Woloson served as the President and CEO of the Izze Beverage Company until its purchase in 2006.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |date=2011-10-06 |title=IZZE Founder Todd Woloson to Speak at BevNET Live |url=https://www.bevnet.com/news/events/live-winter11/izze-founder-todd-woloson-to-speak-at-bevnet-live |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=BevNET.com |language=en-US}}</ref> In 2005, Izze began being released in 12-packs of 8.4-ounce cans, intended for distribution in schools, which became popular purchases at Target and [[Tesco]] stores.<ref name=":4" />

[[PepsiCo]] had been in talks to purchase Izze since around March 2005, and the purchase for $75 million<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Camera |first=Daily |date=2009-08-13 |title=The Final Word – Oct. 9 |url=https://www.dailycamera.com/ci_13065189/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Boulder Daily Camera |language=en-US}}</ref> was announced on September 26, 2006. PepsiCo had been declining in sales, partially because consumers had started moving towards healthier "natural beverage" brands like Izze. PepsiCo chose Izze as it was one of the top "natural beverage" brands in the country. Izze, which had 29 employees at the time, stayed in Colorado, and a Pepsi executive moved to area to help grow the brand. The two companies agreed to maintain Izze's brand as a small company.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Post |first=Kimberly S. Johnson {{!}} The Denver |date=2006-09-26 |title=PepsiCo taking big swig of Izze |url=https://www.denverpost.com/2006/09/26/pepsico-taking-big-swig-of-izze/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=The Denver Post |language=en-US}}</ref> The brand was put under PepsiCo's [[Naked Juice]] division.<ref name=":5" /> In 2009, it was reported that Izze was putting much of their marketing efforts into [[product placement]] in movies and TV shows, such as the show ''[[Grey's Anatomy]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Steinberg |first=Brian |date=April 1, 2009 |title=Getting Izze to Izzie on 'Grey's Anatomy' |url=https://adage.com/article/madisonvine-news/pepsico-s-free-izze-product-placement-grey-s-anatomy/135712 |access-date=July 30, 2024 |website=Ad Age}}</ref> 

In 2016, PepsiCo was sued in a [[class action lawsuit]] that alleged the original Izze brand was [[Deceptive marketing|deceptively marketed]], as it claimed to have "no [[Preservative|preservatives]]" and had "two servings of fruit based on [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]]’s 2010 [[Dietary Guidelines for Americans|Dietary Guidelines]]"; the [[Plaintiff|plaintiffs]] alleged the drinks fit neither of these descriptions.<ref name=":3" /> In July 2017, PepsiCo launched Izze Fusions, and promoted the version to teenagers by sponsoring the "Camp Izze" music festival on April 8, which was the start of musician [[Shawn Mendes]]' [[Illuminate World Tour|worldwide tour]] that year.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=PepsiCo |title=New IZZE FUSIONS Will Not Be Defined |url=https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/new-izze-fusions-will-not-be-defined-300426197.html |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=www.prnewswire.com |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Kell |first=John |title=PepsiCo Debuts Two New Drinks as Part of Its Health Overhaul |url=https://fortune.com/2017/03/03/pepsico-new-healthier-drinks/ |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=Fortune |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-05-08 |title=See Izze’s Teen-Focused Product Launch |url=https://www.bizbash.com/catering-design/beverages/media-gallery/13482193/see-izzes-teenfocused-product-launch |access-date=2024-07-31 |website=BizBash |language=en-us}}</ref> The company is partnered with Stroh and Woloson's Global Education Fund [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit]].<ref name=":6" /><ref name=":4" />

An '''Incredible Hulk''', '''Green Eyed Monster''', '''Shrock''',  or '''Hip and Hen''' is a green-colored [[cocktail]] made by equal parts (2 fl oz each)<ref name="Hpnotiq.com">[http://www.hpnotiq.com/ Hpnotiq.com official recipe] → Drink Recipes → Exotiq Cocktails → Incredible Hulk ''(No direct link is available due to the [[Adobe Flash]] interface.)'' Retrieved 2007-01-15.</ref><ref name="Tabari">McCoy, Tabari (2004-04-15). "[http://www.intakeweekly.com/articles/6/020082-6886-151.html Drink Like a Rapper] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060721182024/http://www.intakeweekly.com/articles/6/020082-6886-151.html |date=2006-07-21 }}". ''Intake Weekly''. Retrieved 2006-12-20.</ref><ref name="Gibson">Gibson, Ashley M. (2004-05-07). "[http://charlotte.bizjournals.com/charlotte/stories/2004/05/10/tidbits1.html?page=5 Table Talk]". ''Charlotte Business Journal''. Retrieved 2006-12-20.</ref> of the fruit liqueur [[Hpnotiq]] and [[Hennessy]] brand [[cognac (drink)|cognac]] poured over ice. It is named after the [[Marvel Comics]] character [[Hulk]], who is sometimes referred to as the Incredible Hulk.

==History==
The drink was created at a Hpnotiq launch event by a restaurant bartender at [[Sean Combs]]' New York City restaurant, Justin's. A Hpnotiq employee noticed many women but few men drinking his company's liquor, because the men considered the blue, fruity drink to be too effeminate. Victor Alvarez, a bartender at the restaurant, mixed Hennessy with Hpnotiq to dilute the fruity flavor, resulting in a green beverage that quickly became a hit.<ref name="Govinda">Govinda, Pamela (2002). [http://www.beveragenet.net/cheers/2004/0404/0404ml.asp "The Millennials At the Bar"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060429054245/http://www.beveragenet.net/cheers/2004/0404/0404ml.asp |date=2006-04-29 }}. ''Adams Beverage Group''. Retrieved 2006-12-20.</ref>

==Variations==
The name 'Incredible Hulk' is also widely used amongst students in the North of England to describe a cocktail consisting of equal parts of [[WKD Original Vodka|WKD Blue]] and [[lager]].

==Culture==
The Incredible Hulk cocktail has been referenced in songs such as "Incredible Hulk" by the Memphis rap group Stress Free Fam and has appeared in [[music video]]s. It was also mentioned in ''[[The Boondocks (TV series)|The Boondocks]]'' episode "[[The Story of Thugnificent]]".<ref name="Tabari"/> ''[[Epic Meal Time]]'', a [[YouTube]] cooking show, featured cocktail at the start of the episode "Masta Pasta" with Muscles Glasses being punched repeatedly in the chest. As Dave's punching stops to complain that his hand hurts, someone off-camera says, "That's what Incredible Hulk does to you."<ref name="Epic Meal Time">"[http://www.epicmealtime.com/videos/2011/6/14/masta-pasta.html Epic Meal Time - Masta Pasta] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110617211908/http://www.epicmealtime.com/videos/2011/6/14/masta-pasta.html |date=2011-06-17 }}"</ref>
It can also be seen in the [[post-credits scene]] of [[The Incredible Hulk (film)|The Incredible Hulk]] where [[Thunderbolt Ross|General Ross]] is drinking a glass of the cocktail at a bar.

'''Joseph "Joe" Gilmore''' (19 May 1922 – 18 December 2015)<ref>{{cite web |last=Nincevich |first=Stefano |date=23 December 2015 |title=Peter Dorelli e il "suo" Joe Gilmore |url=http://www.bargiornale.it/hey-joe-peter-dorelli-ricorda-il-suo-mentore-joe-gilmore/ |access-date=28 January 2017}}</ref> was a renowned bartender and famous mixologist during the 20th century. He was Head Barman at The [[Savoy Hotel]]'s American Bar from 1954 to 1976 and is recognised as the creator of numerous cocktails to mark special events and important guests, a longstanding tradition at the American Bar. Gilmore's most famous creations include Moonwalk, Link-Up, The Corpse Reviver, Lorraine, and Missouri Mule.

== Early life ==
Joseph Patrick Gilmore was born on 19 May 1922 in [[Belfast]], [[Northern Ireland]] to John Gilmore, a [[tobacconist]], and Margaret O'Connor, a tailoress, from [[Belfast]], [[Ireland]].

He was the third of nine children.

In 1938, aged 16, Gilmore moved to [[London]] looking for work and "adventure".<ref name="obit">{{cite web |date=January 15, 2016 |title=Joe Gilmore, barman - obituary |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/12102090/Joe-Gilmore-barman-obituary.html |url-access=subscription |access-date=January 28, 2017 |website=The Telegraph}}</ref> He began working as a wallpaper packer at the [[Arthur Sanderson & Sons|Arthur Sanderson & Son]]'s factory in [[Perivale]], London, later taking up work as a kitchen hand.<ref name="irishnews.com">{{Cite web |date=2016-01-16 |title=Cocktail king Joe Gilmore, Belfast's barman to the stars |url=http://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |access-date=2023-02-09 |website=The Irish News |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210141840/https://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Gilmore began his early bartender training at La Coquille, a French restaurant on [[St Martin's Lane]], [[Covent Garden]], among other places.<ref name="irishnews.com" /> While working at The Olde Bell he met and served Welsh millionaire steel-baron Kenneth Davies and the aviator [[Amy Johnson|Amy Johnston]]. The couple reportedly asked Gilmore for a dry martini, which he attempted unsuccessfully. Despite his attempt being enjoyed by the couple, Davies and Johnston politely demonstrated how to make one. Gilmore cited this interaction as the spark that fuelled his passion of cocktail mixology.<ref name="irishnews.com" /> After this first encounter, Davies and Gilmore became life long friends.<ref name="irishnews.com" />

== Career ==
Gilmore first began working at [[Savoy Hotel|The Savoy]] as a commis waiter at The American Bar of the Savoy Hotel.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Joe Gilmore |url=https://www.diffordsguide.com/encyclopedia/2886/people/joe-gilmore |access-date=2023-02-10 |website=www.diffordsguide.com |language=en}}</ref> By 1940, aged 18, he was promoted to trainee barman and began his apprenticeship with [[Harry Craddock]], earning [[Pound sterling|£]]3.10[[Shilling|s]] a week.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-16 |title=Cocktail king Joe Gilmore, Belfast's barman to the stars |url=http://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |access-date=2023-02-10 |website=The Irish News |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210141840/https://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |title=Bartender to royals, politicians, world leaders and celebrities |language=en-GB |work=Belfast News Letter |url=https://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/bartender-royals-politicians-world-leaders-and-celebrities-1276443 |access-date=2023-02-10}}</ref>

In 1954, Gilmore took over as head bartender. Over the following two decades Gilmore created new cocktails, especially to honour special occasions and important guests, including [[Diana, Princess of Wales|Princess Diana]], [[Prince William, Duke of Cambridge|Prince William]], [[Anne, Princess Royal|Anne, The Princess Royal]], [[Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother|The Queen Mother]], [[Winston Churchill|Sir Winston Churchill]], and American Presidents [[Harry S. Truman]] and [[Richard Nixon]].

In addition to serving five generations of royals at private receptions and parties, Gilmore frequently served [[Errol Flynn]], [[Laurel and Hardy]], [[Charlie Chaplin]], [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]], [[Grace Kelly]], [[George Bernard Shaw]], [[Ernest Hemingway]], [[Noël Coward]], [[Agatha Christie]], [[Alice Faye]], [[Ingrid Bergman]], [[Julie Andrews]], [[Laurence Olivier]], [[Joan Crawford]], [[Judy Garland]], [[Liza Minnelli]], [[Bing Crosby]] and [[Frank Sinatra]] and [[Winston Churchill]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-01-16 |title=Cocktail king Joe Gilmore, Belfast's barman to the stars |url=http://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |access-date=2023-02-10 |website=The Irish News |language=en |archive-date=10 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230210141840/https://www.irishnews.com/notices/livesremembered/2016/01/16/news/cocktail-king-joe-gilmore-belfast-s-barman-to-the-stars-382007/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 1969, he created one of his most famous cocktails, the "Moonwalk", to commemorate the [[Apollo 11]] Moon landing. The cocktail is a combination of grapefruit juice, orange liqueur and rose water, topped with champagne. This was the first drink astronauts [[Neil Armstrong]] and [[Buzz Aldrin]] had upon returning to Earth.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-03-18 |title=Moonwalk |url=https://www.saveur.com/article/Recipes/Moonwalk-Cocktail/ |access-date=2023-02-13 |website=Saveur |language=en}}</ref>

Frank Sinatra was a frequent guest to the American Bar whenever he was in London and insisted only Gilmore was to serve him. It is widely believed the line from Sinatra’s One For My Baby "set’em up Joe" is in reference to Gilmore.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A final toast to Ireland's cocktail king |url=https://www.irishecho.com/2016/1/a-final-toast-to-irelands-cocktail-king |access-date=2023-02-13 |website=Irish Echo Newspaper |language=en}}</ref>

Gilmore retired from the Savoy in 1976.<ref name="obit" />

== Personal life ==
Gilmore married Marie Jeanne Zambelli in 1943. They had three sons.

During [[The Blitz]], Gilmore helped protect The Savoy by working as a fire warden from its roof.

Gilmore never returned to Ireland, but "...{{nbsp}}never forgot his Irish roots or family background and never lost his soft Belfast accent."<ref>{{Cite web |last=The Newsroom |date=2016-01-20 |title=Bartender to royals, politicians, world leaders and celebrities |url=https://www.newsletter.co.uk/news/bartender-royals-politicians-world-leaders-and-celebrities-1276443 |access-date=2023-02-09 |website=newsletter.co.uk}}</ref> He remained a [[Roman Catholic]] throughout his life, and died on 18 December 2015, aged 93.<ref>{{cite web | last=McDaid | first=Laura | title=Belfast barman who served cocktails to the stars dies aged 93 | publisher=[[BBC News]] | date=January 25, 2016 | url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-northern-ireland-35399125 | access-date=January 28, 2017}}</ref>
