'''Sazerac Company, Inc.''', is a privately held American [[alcoholic beverage]] company headquartered in [[Metairie, Louisiana|Metairie]] in the [[New Orleans metropolitan area|metropolitan area]] of [[New Orleans|New Orleans, Louisiana]], but with its principal office in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].<ref name="SazeracWeb">{{Cite web |title=The Sazerac Company {{!}} Our Story |url=https://www.sazerac.com/our-company/our-story.html |access-date=2021-07-23 |website=Sazerac |language=en}}</ref> The company is owned by [[William Goldring (businessman)|William Goldring]] and his family. {{As of|2017}}, it operated nine [[distillery|distilleries]], had 2,000 employees, and operated in 112 countries. It is one of the two largest spirits companies in the United States, with annual revenue of about $1 billion made from selling about 300 beverage brands.<ref name="dynasty">{{Cite web |date=Summer 2017 |title=Bourbon Dynasty |url=http://freemanmag.tulane.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/123/2017/09/Freemanmagazinesummer2017.pdf |access-date=April 17, 2018 |website=Freeman – The alumni magazine of the A.B. Freeman School of Business at Tulane University |page=8 |archive-date=January 5, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230105142917/https://freemanmag.tulane.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/123/2017/09/Freemanmagazinesummer2017.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="cheap liquor">{{Cite news |last=Coffey |first=Brendan |date=December 16, 2016 |title=Cheap-Liquor Billionaire Looks Abroad as Sales Slow |work=[[Bloomberg L.P.|Bloomberg]] |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2016-12-16/america-s-cheap-liquor-billionaire-looks-abroad-as-growth-slows |url-access=subscription |access-date=April 17, 2018}}</ref><ref name="billionaire">{{Cite news |date=December 16, 2016 |title=New Orleans liquor billionaire looks abroad as US market slows |work=Greater Baton Rouge Business Report |url=https://www.businessreport.com/article/new-orleans-liquor-billionaire-looks-abroad-us-market-slows |access-date=April 17, 2018}}</ref>

==History==
The company was founded in 1869 after the purchase by Thomas H. Handy of the Sazerac Coffee House, a bar and importer of a brand of cognac named ''Sazerac de Forge''.<ref name = SazeracWeb/> The coffee house itself had been established in 1850.<ref name="cheap liquor" /> After its purchase, Handy's company began to acquire and market more brands of liquor. According to the company, the Sazerac Coffee House had been named after a [[cocktail]] called the [[Sazerac]] that was created in the mid-1800s by the immigrant Antoine Amédée Peychaud, who operated a [[apothecary|pharmacy]] on [[Royal Street, New Orleans|Royal Street]] in the [[French Quarter]] of New Orleans in 1838.<ref name = SazeracWeb/> The company publishes a Sazerac recipe and produces a [[Peychaud's Bitters]] named after Peychaud, which is an ingredient in the traditional Sazerac cocktail.<ref>{{Cite web |date=26 June 2008 |title=New Orleans Declares Sazerac Its Cocktail of Choice |url=https://www.npr.org/2008/06/26/91912549/new-orleans-declares-sazerac-its-cocktail-of-choice |website=npr}}</ref><ref name="SazeracRecipe">{{Cite web |title=The Sazerac – Official Cocktail of New Orleans: How the Sazerac Cocktail Came to Be |url=https://www.sazerac.com/cocktail.aspx |access-date=December 6, 2010 |website=The Sazerac Company official website}}</ref>

William Goldring began buying shares of the company in 1984, and eventually purchased the entire company.<ref name="cheap liquor" />

In 2009, the company's principal office was moved to Louisville, Kentucky, reflecting an increased company focus on [[bourbon whiskey]] production. However, the Sazerac Company still maintains an active presence in the New Orleans area, and it also has operations in [[Carson, California|Carson]]<ref name="SazeracWeb" /> and [[Loomis, California|Loomis]],<ref name="LCA" /> [[California]]; [[Baltimore, Maryland]]; [[Chicago, Illinois]];<ref name="CHI">{{Cite web |title=Definition of Mezcal |url=https://www.liquor.com/spirit/mezcal/ |access-date=2018-04-14}}</ref> [[Bardstown, Kentucky|Bardstown]],<ref name="BKYOKY">{{Cite web |date=March 26, 2009 |title=Sazerac buys Kentucky bourbon brands, distillery |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/louisville/stories/2009/03/23/daily34.html |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref> [[Frankfort, Kentucky|Frankfort]],<ref name="FKY" /> and [[Owensboro, Kentucky]];<ref name="BKYOKY" /> [[Fredericksburg, Virginia]];<ref name="FVA" /> [[Montreal, Quebec]], Canada;<ref name="MCA">{{Cite web |date=September 27, 2011 |title=Corby Distilleries sells Montreal plant, 17 brands to Sazerac for $32.9-million |url=https://globalnews.ca/news/159771/corby-distilleries-sells-montreal-plant-17-brands-to-sazerac-for-32-9-million/ |access-date=April 12, 2018}}</ref> [[Lewiston, Maine]];<ref name="LME">{{Cite web |date=October 17, 2013 |title=Lewiston liquor bottling facility sold to Sazerac, jobs saved |url=https://www.bangordailynews.com/2013/10/16/business/lewiston-liquor-bottling-facility-sold-jobs-saved/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180414174035/https://amp.bangordailynews.com/2013/10/16/business/lewiston-liquor-bottling-facility-sold-jobs-saved/ |archive-date=April 14, 2018 |access-date=April 12, 2014}}</ref> [[Londonderry, New Hampshire]]; [[Newport, Tennessee]];<ref name="NTN">{{Cite web |date=December 22, 2016 |title=Sazerac Expanding into Tennessee Whiskey with Distillery Purchase |url=https://whiskycast.com/sazerac-expanding-into-tennessee-whiskey-with-distillery-purchase/ |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref> and [[Segonzac, Charente|Segonzac, France]].<ref name="FRA">{{Cite web |date=December 23, 2016 |title=Sazerac Purchases Domaine Breuil de Segonzac Cognac |url=http://beveragedynamics.com/2016/12/23/sazerac-purchases-domaine-breuil-de-segonzac-cognac/ |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref>

In 2014, Sazerac announced the creation of the Bond & Royal Company, located in Chicago, Illinois, to take over the specialty and craft segment of its brands from the Gemini Spirits and Wine portfolio including Dimmi, an Italian liqueur,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2012-05-10 |title=Review: Dimmi Liquore di Milano |url=https://www.drinkhacker.com/2012/05/10/review-dimmi-liquore-di-milano/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180415190445/https://www.drinkhacker.com/2012/05/10/review-dimmi-liquore-di-milano/amp/ |archive-date=April 15, 2018 |access-date=2018-04-14}}</ref> and the Casa San Matias, manufacturer of Corazón tequila.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 11, 2014 |title=Sazerac creates dedicated craft spirits division |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2014/09/sazerac-creates-dedicated-craft-spirits-division/ |access-date=2018-04-14 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In 2016, the company had an estimated revenue of $1 billion per year and a market valuation estimate of $4.5 billion.<ref name="cheap liquor" /> The valuation placed Goldring in the [[Bloomberg Billionaires Index]] with an estimated net worth of $3.9 billion.<ref name="cheap liquor" />

In October 2019, Sazerac opened The Sazerac House, a museum and distillery in New Orleans.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Paulus |first=Caroline |date=2020-01-06 |title=The Sazerac House in New Orleans is A Must-See Whiskey History Destination {{!}} The Bourbon Review |url=https://www.gobourbon.com/sazerac-house/ |access-date=2025-03-19 |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Acquisitions and partnerships ==
In 1989, Sazerac acquired several brands from [[Seagram]], including [[McAfee's Benchmark]] and [[Eagle Rare]] (Kentucky straight bourbon), [[Nikolai (vodka)|Nikolai]] (vodka), [[Dr. McGillicuddy's]], (liqueur) and [[Fireball Cinnamon Whisky]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 29, 1989 |title=Seagram to Sell Rights to 17 Brands |work=The New York Times |url=https://mobile.nytimes.com/1989/03/29/business/company-news-seagram-to-sell-rights-to-17-brands.html |access-date=April 14, 2018}}</ref>

In 1992, Sazerac acquired the [[George T. Stagg]] Distillery in Frankfort, Kentucky, at which time the company's primary focus became the production of bourbon whiskey, a product that is primarily distilled, aged, and bottled in Kentucky, later changing its name to the [[Buffalo Trace Distillery]] in 1999.<ref name="FKY">{{Cite web |title=Bourbon Company, Bourbon Man Buffalo Trace Distillery & Mark Brown |url=http://www.maltadvocate.com/classics-bourbon-buffalo.asp |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080120111607/http://www.maltadvocate.com/classics-bourbon-buffalo.asp |archive-date=January 20, 2008 |access-date=April 14, 2018 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>

In 1994, Sazerac acquired Monsieur Henri, a wine and specialty spirits company.{{Citation needed|date=July 2024}} In 2007, it was announced that they were changing its name to Gemini Spirits and Wine; it is headquartered in [[Loomis, California]].<ref name="LCA">{{Cite web |date=2007-06-03 |title=A New Star In The Spirits & Wine Industry – Monsieur Henri becomes Gemini Spirits & Wine Company |url=https://www.geminispiritswine.com/news_monsieur.asp |access-date=2018-04-11}}{{Dead link|date=December 2023|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref>

In 1999, Sazerac acquired the [[W.L. Weller]] bourbon brands.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Emen |first=Jake |date=March 14, 2016 |title=Vintage Whiskey: Getting Hold of the Really, Really Old Stuff |url=https://thewhiskeywash.com/whiskey-styles/bourbon/vintage-whiskey-primer-need-know-vintage-whiskey |access-date=April 16, 2018 |website=The Whiskey Wash}}</ref>

In 2002, Sazerac entered an agreement with the Van Winkle family to produce its [[Pappy Van Winkle's Family Reserve]] and [[Old Rip Van Winkle]] bourbon and rye whisky brands at its Buffalo Trace Distillery.<ref>{{Cite web |date=July 30, 2014 |title=Liquor Of Legend: The Distillery Behind Buffalo Trace Bourbon, Blanton's--And Pappy Van Winkle |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/abrambrown/2014/07/30/liquor-of-legend-the-distillery-behind-buffalo-trace-bourbon-blantons-and-pappy-van-winkle/ |access-date=April 16, 2018 |website=[[Forbes]]}}</ref>

In 2003, Sazerac acquired the [[A. Smith Bowman Distillery]], located in Fredericksburg, Virginia. [[Virginia Gentleman]], a bourbon whiskey, is distilled there.<ref name="FVA">{{Cite web |date=June 9, 2014 |title=Virginia Gentleman Small Batch Bourbon Review |url=https://modernthirst.com/2014/06/09/bourbon-review-virginia-gentleman-small-batch/ |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref>

In March 2009, Sazerac completed its acquisition of [[Constellation Brands]] value-priced spirit assets. The purchase included [[Very Old Barton]] and several other bourbon brands, a distillery in Bardstown, Kentucky, and a bottling and warehousing facility in Owensboro, Kentucky.<ref>{{Citation |last=Lawrence |first=Keith |title=Constellation Spirits sold in Sazerac deal |date=2009-01-13 |url=http://edc.owensboro.com/documents/ConstellationSpiritssold.pdf |work=Messenger-Inquirer |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090320115514/http://edc.owensboro.com/documents/ConstellationSpiritssold.pdf |url-status=dead |archive-date=2009-03-20}}</ref> In June 2009, Sazerac acquired the [[Old Taylor]] Bourbon label and barrel inventory from [[Beam Global Spirits & Wine]], now known as [[Suntory Global Spirits]]<ref>{{Cite press release |title=Beam Global Spirits & Wine Acquires Effen Vodka |date=June 23, 2009 |publisher=Business Wire |url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20090623006189/en/Beam-Global-Spirits-Wine-Acquires-EFFEN%C2%AE-Vodka |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref>

In June 2009, Sazerac sold Effen Vodka to [[Fortune Brands (1969–2011)|Fortune Brands]]. After a restructuring of Fortune Brands and an acquisition by [[Suntory]], Effen has since become a [[Suntory Global Spirits]] brand.<ref>{{Cite web |date=April 14, 2018 |title=Effen vodka to get profile boost with Fortune Brands as owner |url=https://articles.chicagotribune.com/2009-08-31/news/0908300342_1_vodka-market-fortune-brands-effen|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100918045321/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/2009-08-31/news/0908300342_1_vodka-market-fortune-brands-effen|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 18, 2010}}</ref>

In September 2011, Sazerac entered into an agreement with [[Corby Spirit and Wine|Corby Distilleries Limited]], to purchase 17 Corby owned brands as part of the agreement made with the other brands acquired from Corby Distilleries Limited.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 28, 2011 |title=Sazerac Acquires McGuinness Silk Tassel Canadian Whisky |url=http://www.canadianwhisky.org/news-views/sazerac-acquires-mcguinness-silk-tassel-canadian-whisky.html |access-date=April 16, 2018 |archive-date=April 14, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180414172218/https://www.canadianwhisky.org/news-views/sazerac-acquires-mcguinness-silk-tassel-canadian-whisky.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> The deal also included shares of Corby's manufacturing and bottling facilities in Montreal.<ref name="MCA" /> The distillery was eventually renamed as the Old Montreal Distillery, and distillation of new spirit was resumed there.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 1, 2017 |title=Sazerac returns Canadian whisky distilling to Montreal |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2017/03/sazerac-returns-canadian-whisky-distilling-to-montreal |access-date=2018-04-13 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In October 2011, Sazerac acquired 32 brands from White Rock Distillery, most notably Ryan's Irish cream liqueur.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 5, 2011 |title=Sazerac Buys 32 Brands Of White Rock Distilleries |url=http://www.boozenews.com/industry/sazerac-buys-32-brands-of-white-rock-distilleries/ |access-date=2018-04-14 |archive-date=September 25, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200925081949/http://www.boozenews.com/industry/sazerac-buys-32-brands-of-white-rock-distilleries/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Clouser |first=Stephanie |date=1 September 2011 |title=Sazerac to purchase number of brands |url=https://www.bizjournals.com/louisville/news/2011/09/01/sazerac-to-purchase-number-of-brands.html |access-date=8 July 2024 |website=bizjournals.com}}</ref>

In May 2012, Sazerac acquired several more brands from White Rock Distillery including Tenure England vodka.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 18, 2012 |title=Sazerac buys more spirit brands from White Rock |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2012/05/sazerac-buys-more-spirit-brands-from-white-rock/ |access-date=2018-04-13 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In October 2012, Sazerac acquired Gran Gala, a liqueur brand, from [[Stock Spirits]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 22, 2012 |title=Stock Spirits sells Gran Gala brand to Sazerac |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2012/10/stock-spirits-sells-gran-gala-brand-to-sazerac/ |access-date=April 13, 2018 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In October 2013, Sazerac bought a distillery, including land and equipment in Lewiston, Maine, from Beam Inc. (now known as Suntory Global Spirits).<ref name="LME" /> By 2017, the name of the distillery was changed to Boston Brands of Maine. The [[Mr. Boston|Mr. Boston premium spirits]] line of Brandies is distilled there.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 9, 2017 |title=Sazerac plans US$1 million expansion at Lewiston plant |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2017/12/sazerac-plans-1-million-expansion-at-lewiston-plant |access-date=2018-04-12 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In 2014, Sazerac entered into a licensing and distribution agreement with [[The Wine Group]], to market its Big House Bourbon, [[Concannon Vineyard|Concannon Irish Whiskey]], and Piedra Azul Tequila.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 24, 2014 |title=Sazerac is to begin distribution of Big House Bourbon, Concannon Irish Whiskey and Piedra Azul Tequila following a licensing agreement with The Wine Group |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2014/02/sazerac-takes-on-irish-whiskey-tequila-and-bourbon-brands/ |access-date=April 13, 2018 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In October 2015, Sazerac acquired Michael Collins, an Irish whiskey from the Sidney Frank Importing Company.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 2015 |title=Sazerac acquires Michael Collins Irish whiskey |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2015/10/sazerac-acquires-michael-collins-irish-whiskey/ |access-date=2018-04-13 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref> Also in 2015, Sazerac added Van Gogh Imports, changing its name to 375 Park Avenue Spirits, as an independent, but fully integrated, division in its portfolio.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 27, 2015 |title=Van Gogh Imports Joins Sazerac Co., Changes Name To 375 Park Avenue Spirits |url=https://www.shankennewsdaily.com/index.php/2015/01/27/11600/van-gogh-imports-joins-sazerac-co-changes-name-to-375-park-avenue-spirits/ |access-date=April 16, 2018}}</ref> The company also entered an agreement with [[La Martiniquaise]] to be the US distributor of its Saint-Vivant [[Armagnac (brandy)|Armagnac]] brand, produced in [[France]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 9, 2015 |title=Sazerac to expand Saint-Vivant Armagnac in US |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2015/12/sazerac-to-expand-saint-vivant-armagnac-in-us/ |access-date=2018-04-13 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In 2016, Sazerac entered into an agreement with [[Arcus (company)|ArcusGruppen]] to be the US distributor of its Lysholm Linie, Aalborg Taffel, and Aalborg Jubilaeums [[Akvavit|Aquavit]] brands produced in [[Norway]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 22, 2016 |title=Sazerac Partners with Arcus Gruppen for U.S. Imports |url=https://www.bevnet.com/news/spirits/2016/sazerac-partners-arcus-gruppen-u-s-imports/ |access-date=2018-04-15}}</ref>

In March 2016, Sazerac completed the purchase of the [[Southern Comfort]] and [[Tuaca]] brands from [[Brown-Forman, Inc.]]<ref>{{Cite news |date=March 2, 2016 |title=Brown-Forman finalises Southern Comfort sale |work=[[The Spirits Business]] |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2016/03/brown-forman-finalises-southern-comfort-sale/ |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref> That same month, Sazerac acquired Hi-Spirits to take over the distribution of its products in the UK.<ref>{{Cite news |date=October 19, 2016 |title=Sazerac Ceo Confirms Hi-Spirits Acquisition |work=[[The Spirits Business]] |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2016/10/sazerac-ceo-confirms-hi-spirits-acquisition/ |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref>

On May 31, 2016, Sazerac entered a long-term Canadian national distribution agreement with Charton Hobbs, Inc. a wine and spirits company.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 31, 2016 |title=Sazerac signs Canada-wide distribution agreement |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/new_orleans/news/business/article_096c005e-a96c-51ca-9ba2-35966415f92f.html |access-date=2018-04-15}}</ref>

In May 2016, Sazerac announced that had finalized a deal with [[Pernod Ricard]]'s [[Irish Distillers]] to acquire its [[Paddy Whiskey]] brand.<ref>{{Cite web |date=May 17, 2016 |title=Irish Distillers finalizes Paddy sale to Sazerac |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2016/05/irish-distillers-finalises-paddy-sale-to-sazerac/ |access-date=April 11, 2018 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In September 2016, Sazerac acquired The Last Drop Distillers, an [[independent bottler]] of Scotch whiskey,<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 6, 2016 |title=The Sazerac Company has acquired The Last Drop Distillers Limited, a British family-run spirits bottler, for an undisclosed sum. |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2016/09/sazerac-acquires-the-last-drop-distillers/ |access-date=April 12, 2018}}</ref> and Australian spirit maker South Trade International.<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 16, 2016 |title=Sazerac acquires South Trade International |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2016/09/sazerac-acquires-southtrade-international/ |access-date=April 11, 2018 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In October 2016, Sazerac acquired [[Frïs Vodka]] from [[Pernod Ricard]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 3, 2016 |title=Sazerac buys Frïs Vodka from Pernod |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2016/10/sazerac-buys-fris-vodka-from-pernod/ |access-date=2018-04-14 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In December 2016, Sazerac announced its acquisition of The Popcorn Sutton Distillery in Newport, Tennessee.<ref name="NTN" />

In December 2016, Sazerac announced that had acquired Domaine Breuil de Segonzac Cognac, including property located near the town of [[Segonzac, Charente|Segonzac, France]], near [[Cognac, France|Cognac]].<ref name="FRA" />

On March 3, 2017, it was announced that Sazerac entered a joint venture with [[Bittermens]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 6, 2017 |title=Sazerac buys stake in cocktail bitters company |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2017/03/sazerac-buys-stake-in-cocktail-bitters-company/ |access-date=June 23, 2018 |website=[[The Spirits Business]]}}</ref>

In June 2017, it was announced that Sazerac had entered agreement with [[Dictador]] to be the US distributor of its Rum products through its 375 Spirits division.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 28, 2017 |title=Dictador Rum Appoints 375 Park Avenue Spirits as U.S. Importer |url=https://www.bevnet.com/news/spirits/2017/dictador-rum-appoints-375-park-avenue-spirits-u-s-importer/ |access-date=2018-04-15}}</ref>

In October 2017, it was announced that Sazerac entered an agreement with [[John Distilleries]] Private Limited (JDPL) the manufacturer of [[Paul John (whisky)|Paul John Whisky]]  to enter the India market.<ref>{{Cite web |date=October 20, 2017 |title=The Sazerac Company Invests in John Distilleries |url=https://www.bevnet.com/news/spirits/2017/sazerac-company-invests-john-distilleries/ |access-date=April 11, 2018}}</ref>

In November 2018, Sazerac announced it would acquire 19 spirits brands from [[Diageo]] Plc, including John Begg blended Scotch, Seagram's V.O. Canadian whisky, [[Myers's Rum|Myers's]] rum, Parrot Bay rum liqueur, Romana Sambuca, [[Popov (vodka)|Popov]] vodka, [[Yukon Jack (liqueur)|Yukon Jack]] whisky liqueur, [[Goldschläger]] cinnamon liqueur, Peligroso tequila, Grind liqueur and [[Booth's Gin|Booth's]] gin.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 12, 2018 |title=Diageo sells portfolio of brands to Sazerac |url=https://www.diageo.com/en/news-and-media/press-releases/diageo-sells-portfolio-of-brands-to-sazerac/ |access-date=February 14, 2019 |archive-date=June 28, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220628062516/https://www.diageo.com/en/news-and-media/press-releases/diageo-sells-portfolio-of-brands-to-sazerac/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=November 12, 2018 |title=Diageo to sell 19 brands to U.S.-based Sazerac for $550 million |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-diageo-divestment/diageo-to-sell-19-brands-to-u-s-based-sazerac-for-550-million |access-date=February 14, 2019 |website=[[Reuters]]}}{{dead link|date=July 2021|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>

In June 2020, the company announced it would acquire [[Early Times (whiskey)|Early Times]] and [[Canadian Mist]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carruthers |first=Nicola |date=2020-08-04 |title=Brown-Forman completes sale of Canadian Mist to Sazerac |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2020/08/brown-forman-completes-sale-of-canadian-mist-to-sazerac/ |access-date=2024-07-08 |website=The Spirits Business |language=en-US}}</ref> including the latter's distillery in Ontario, from Brown-Forman. The acquisition included the barrel aging stocks related to the different brands as well.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 10, 2020 |title=Brown-Forman sells Early Times and Canadian Mist to Sazerac |url=https://www.thespiritsbusiness.com/2020/06/brown-forman-sells-early-times-and-canadian-mist-to-sazerac/ |access-date=July 11, 2020}}</ref>

In March 2024, Sazerac announced plans to acquire [[BuzzBallz]], a ready-to-drink cocktail brand.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Fireball maker Sazerac acquires RTD cocktail brand BuzzBallz |url=https://www.fooddive.com/news/fireball-maker-sazerac-acquires-rtd-cocktail-maker-buzzballz-spirits-alcohol-market/711116/ |access-date=2024-07-08 |website=Food Dive |language=en-US}}</ref> The acquisition was complete in May 2024.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Thomas |first=Louis |date=2024-05-02 |title=Sazerac completes BuzzBallz acquistion |url=https://www.thedrinksbusiness.com/2024/05/sazerac-completes-buzzballz-acquistion/ |access-date=2024-07-08 |website=The Drinks Business |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Sarsaparilla (drink):
{{short description|Soft drink}}
[[File:Sioux City sarsaparilla bottles.jpg|thumb|upright|For decades, until the 2010s, the iconic [[Sioux City (soft drink)|Sioux City]] sarsaparilla bottle was sold in retail stores in the United States.]]
{{Cookbook|Sarsaparilla}}
'''Sarsaparilla''' ({{IPAc-en|UK|ˌ|s|ɑːr|s|p|ə|ˈ|r|ɪ|l|ə}}, {{IPAc-en|USalso|ˌ|s|æ|s|p|ə|ˈ|r|ɪ|l|ə}} {{Respell|sas|pə|RI|lə}})<ref>{{cite LPD|3}}</ref><ref>{{cite EPD|18}}</ref> is a [[soft drink]] originally made from the vine ''[[Smilax ornata]]'' (also called 'sarsaparilla') or other species of ''[[Smilax]]'' such as ''[[Smilax officinalis]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Smilax+officinalis |title=Useful Tropical Plants ''Smilax officinalis'' |last=Fern |first=Ken |date=30 July 2021 |website=tropical.theferns.info |publisher=Tropical Plants Database |access-date=20 March 2022 }}</ref> In most [[Southeast Asia]]n countries, it is known by the common name '''sarsi''', and the trademarks '''Sarsi''' and '''Sarsae'''. It is similar in flavor to [[root beer]]. In the US, sarsaparilla is traditionally made with [[birch oil]] rather than the tropical plant.

==Etymology==
''[[Smilax ornata]]'', a perennial trailing vine with prickly stems that is native to Mexico and Central America, is often used as the basis for the soft drink sarsaparilla.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/?name_id=288960|title=Plants of the World Online | Kew Science|website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref> Common names include sarsaparilla, Honduran sarsaparilla, and Jamaican sarsaparilla.<ref>{{GRIN|id=400333|access-date=29 May 2023}}</ref>

It is known in [[Spanish language|Spanish]] as ''{{lang|es|[[wikt:zarzaparrilla|zarzaparrilla]]}}'', which is derived from the words ''{{linktext|zarza|lang=es}}'' meaning "bramble" (from preroman ''sarza''), and ''{{linktext|parrilla|lang=es}}'', meaning "little grape vine".<ref>{{Cite web |title=sarsaparilla | Etymology, origin and meaning of sarsaparilla by etymonline |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/sarsaparilla |website=etymonline.com}}</ref><ref>Davidse, G. & al. (eds.) (1994). Flora Mesoamericana 6: 1–543. Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, México, D.F.</ref><ref>Balick, M.J., Nee, M.H. & Atha, D.E. (2000). Checklist of the Vascular Plants of Belize with Common Names an Uses: 1–246. New York Botanic Garden Press, New York.</ref><ref>Espejo Serena, A. & López-Ferrari, A.R. (2000). Las Monocotiledóneas Mexicanas una Sinopsis Florística 1(9–11): 1–337. Consejo Nacional de la Flora de México, México D.F.</ref><ref>Nelson Sutherland, C.H. (2008). Catálogo de las plantes vasculares de Honduras. Espermatofitas: 1–1576. SERNA/Guaymuras, Tegucigalpa, Honduras.</ref>

==History in the US==
Sarsaparilla was popular in the United States in the 19th century. According to advertisements for [[patent medicines]] of the period, it was considered to be a remedy for skin and blood problems.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hood's Sarsaparilla|url=http://lcdl.library.cofc.edu/lcdl/catalog/lcdl:60541|website=Lowcountry Digital Library|access-date=1 September 2014|archive-date=15 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141015021640/http://lcdl.library.cofc.edu/lcdl/catalog/lcdl:60541|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>[https://archive.org/details/ayersamericanalm00ayer James Cook Ayer, ''Ayer's American Almanac'', 1878]</ref> ''The Oxford Companion to American Food and Drink'' notes that it evokes images of "languid [[Southern belle|belles]] and parched [[cowboy]]s".<ref>{{cite book|chapter=Sarsaparilla|last=Tobias|first=Ruth|editor-first=Andrew F|editor-last=Smith|title=The Oxford Companion to American Food and Drink|year=2007|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|page=550|isbn=9780195307962|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AoWlCmNDA3QC&pg=PT550}}</ref>

Sarsaparilla is sometimes considered to be a type of [[root beer]]. Dozens of brands of sarsaparilla are made by microbreweries, mainly in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sarsaparilla Reviews|date=29 November 2021 |url=https://rootbeerbarrel.com/category/sarsaparillas/}}</ref>

==Availability==
Sarsaparilla is not readily available in most countries; however, many [[Bar_(establishment)|bars]] and most major supermarket chains in the Philippines, Taiwan, Singapore and Australia stock sarsaparilla-flavored soft drinks, and sarsaparilla remains available in the United Kingdom as a legacy of the [[temperance movement]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sarsaparilla |author= |website=Foods of England |url=https://www.foodsofengland.info/sarsaparilla.html |access-date=17 April 2025 }}</ref>

===United States===
[[File:"This is all right. Hood's Sarsaparilla can't fool me twice." "Be sure you are right," is this old man's motto. (front) - 8558173634.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Trade card]], 1886]]
The classic sarsaparilla was not made from the extract of the sarsaparilla plant, a tropical vine distantly related to the lily. It was originally made from a blend of birch oil and [[sassafras]], the dried root bark of the sassafras tree. In this context, sassafras should not be confused with common sassafras seasoning, [[Filé powder|filé]], used in [[Cajun cooking]] and made from dried and ground sassafras leaves. Sassafras was widely used as a home remedy in the 19th century; taken in sufficient doses it induces sweating, which some people thought had health benefits. Sarsaparilla made its debut as a patent medicine, an easy-to-take form of sassafras, much as [[Coca-Cola]] was first marketed in 1885 as a remedy for hangovers, headaches and morphine addiction.<ref>[https://www.straightdope.com/columns/read/319/whatever-happened-to-the-soft-drink-sarsaparilla Whatever happened to the soft drink sarsaparilla?] December 16, 1977 by Cecil Adams, retrieved 2013-04-30</ref> Besides the effects of the ingredients, sodas were popular in the United States at the time, due to the belief that [[carbonated water]] had health benefits.<ref>{{cite web |title=Themes for Coca-Cola Advertising (1886–1999) |url=http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/ccmphtml/colatime1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010124072300/http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/ccmphtml/colatime1.html |archive-date=24 January 2001 |access-date=2007-02-11}}</ref> In 1960 the FDA banned the use of sassafras oil in foodstuffs after evidence accumulated showing that the main constituent, [[safrole]], was carcinogenic.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dietz|first1=Birgit|last2=Bolton|first2=Judy L.|date=2007-04-01|title=Botanical Dietary Supplements Gone Bad|journal=Chemical Research in Toxicology|volume=20|issue=4|pages=586–590|doi=10.1021/tx7000527|issn=0893-228X|pmc=2504026|pmid=17362034}}</ref> Safrole is also found in filé, nutmeg, mace, cinnamon, anise, black pepper and sweet basil, but in low enough concentration to be deemed safe.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dietz|first1=Birgit|last2=Bolton|first2=Judy L.|date=April 2007|title=Botanical Dietary Supplements Gone Bad|journal=Chemical Research in Toxicology|volume=20|issue=4|pages=586–590|doi=10.1021/tx7000527|issn=0893-228X|pmc=2504026|pmid=17362034}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Real Food Encyclopedia {{!}} Sassafras and Filé|url=https://foodprint.org/real-food/sassafras-and-file/|access-date=2021-01-24|website=FoodPrint|language=en-US}}</ref>

===East Asia===

====Taiwan====
[[HeySong Sarsaparilla]] ({{zh|t=黑松沙士}}) is the most popular brand of sarsaparilla drink in Taiwan. It is manufactured by [[HeySong Corporation]].<ref>Jinn's Publishers et al. "Omoshiro Temakan Meguri No.4: HeySong Soft Drink Museum". Nãruhodo The Taiwan. Vol. 235. October 2006.</ref>

===Southeast Asia===
====Cambodia====
In Cambodia, sarsaparilla is one of the flavors sold under the [[Fanta]] brand, bottled and distributed by Cambodia Beverage Company Ltd., a unit of the Coca-Cola SABCO Group.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phnompenhpost.com/special-reports/coca-cola-celebrates-125th-anniversary|title=Coca-Cola celebrates 125th Anniversary|publisher=The Phnom Penh Post|date=3 July 2011|access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref>

====Indonesia====
There are two well known sarsaparilla brands in Indonesia, [[Badak]] (from [[North Sumatra]]) and Indo Saparella (from the [[Special Region of Yogyakarta]]). Badak was established by a Swiss national named Heinrich Surbeck in 1916 in [[Pematangsiantar]], [[North Sumatra]] and Indo Saparella was established in 1960 in [[Yogyakarta]]. There is also Agung Ngoro a local soft drink brand who produces traditional sarsaparilla in a glass bottle.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.genpi.co/travel/3545/ini-tiga-merek-saparela-yang-pernah-hits-di-indonesia|title=Three Sarsaparilla Brands That Were Hits In Indonesia (2018)|date=26 November 2018|access-date=7 April 2020}}</ref>

====Thailand====
Hi-Mark by [[Green Spot (Thailand)|Green Spot]]{{citation needed|date=June 2012}} was the domestic sarsaparilla drink in Thailand, but was discontinued in 2000. [[Fraser and Neave|F&N]] Sarsi has been produced in Thailand by Sermsuk Public Company Limited since 2018, reviving a brand last sold locally in the 1990s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://positioningmag.com/1182613 |title=สิ้นสุดการรอคอย! "ซาสี่" มาแล้ว ขอท้าชิงแชร์ตลาดน้ำอัดลมหมื่นล้านแล้ว!|date=9 August 2018 |publisher=Positioning |access-date=2023-04-02 |language=th }}</ref>

==Sarsi (brand)==
[[Image:Fnnsarsi.JPG|upright=0.5|thumb|A can of F&N Sarsi from Singapore]]

===Philippines===
In the Philippines, Sarsi is a brand name for a sarsaparilla drink originally manufactured by Cosmos Bottling Corporation, a local company that is now a subsidiary of [[Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines|Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines, Inc.]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.philstar.com/business/2013/04/05/927003/cosmos-sets-delisting-psei|title=Cosmos sets delisting from PSEi|first=Neil Jerome C.|last=Morales|website=[[The Philippine STAR]] |access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref> Cosmos Bottling Corporation was established in 1918 as Manila Aerated Water Company.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2479&dat=20010912&id=OKhjAAAAIBAJ&pg=833,34120272|title=Philippine Daily Inquirer – Google News Archive Search|access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref> Sarsi was originally branded as Cosmos Sarsaparilla until the 1970s. The unique taste that distinguishes the current version of Sarsi from other sarsaparilla-based soft drinks is attributed to the sugar substitute [[saccharin]], although its "regular" formula contains [[high-fructose corn syrup]] or cane sugar.

===Singapore===
In Singapore, F&N Sarsi (originally branded as Sarsi) is a brand name for a sarsaparilla drink manufactured by the Singaporean company [[Fraser and Neave|F&N Group]] (Fraser and Neave). It is unrelated to the brand established in the Philippines.

==Sarsae (brand)==
===Mainland China===
[[File:Bottle of Asia Sarsae.jpg|thumb|upright|A bottle of Asia Sarsae sold in [[Guangzhou]], [[Guangdong]], China]]

In mainland China, the drink's introduction can be traced back to the 1920s, when [[AS Watson]] began producing its sarsaparilla drink in Shanghai and other Chinese cities. In the 1940s, Li Zhiyang (李智扬), Li Guanling (李冠玲), Huang Youtong (黄油桶), Liang Hanqi (梁汉奇) and Wang Zhensan (王震山) were among eleven people who had worked in Watson's Canton and founded Asian Waters in Guangzhou to continue producing Sarsae there and in other mainland Chinese locations.<ref>{{cite news|author=Judy|title=亚洲（汽水）|url=https://news.dayoo.com/guangzhou/120336/120341/201208/15/120341_25631936.htm|access-date=15 August 2012|newspaper=Guangzhou Daily}} {{dead link|date=November 2017}}</ref>

[[Asia (soft drink brand)|Asia Sarsae]] (亚洲沙示) is now produced by [[Xiangxue Pharmaceutical]].

===Hong Kong===
In Hong Kong, Sarsae (沙示) is the most popular brand of sarsaparilla drink. It is manufactured and distributed by the [[A.S. Watson Group|A. S. Watson Group]], which pioneered in carbonated beverages in Hong Kong.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://www.hutchison-whampoa.com/upload/en/about/journal/Sphere17-Then_and_Now_E.pdf|title=Thirst Quenchers|page=32|magazine=Sphere|access-date=29 May 2023}}</ref> The drink was the central [[plot device]] of a 1985 film called ''It's a Drink, It's a Bomb'' (starring [[George Lam]], [[John Sham]] and [[Maggie Cheung]]), about a [[hand grenade]] disguised as a Sarsae cola, detonated by releasing its [[Drink can|ringpull]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lovehkfilm.com/reviews/its_a_drink.htm|title=It's a Drink, It's a Bomb (1985)|access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref>

Rossini (cocktail):
{{Short description|Cocktail}}
[[File:Un Rossini, grazie (467053126).jpg|thumb]]
The '''Rossini''' is a type of [[Alcoholic beverage|alcoholic mixed drink]] made with sweet [[sparkling wine]] ([[Prosecco]]) and [[purée]]d [[strawberry|strawberries]].<ref>[http://www.saveur.com/article/Recipes/Classic-Rossini Rossini Cocktail]. Saveur.com September 2012. Retrieved 2012-09-03.</ref> The cocktail is the most popular alternative to the classic [[Bellini (cocktail)|Bellini]].<ref>[http://familystylefood.com/2013/05/strawberry-and-prosecco-rossini/ Strawberry and Prosecco Rossini]. Familystylefood.com. Retrieved 2014-09-03.</ref>

== Origin of the name ==
The drink was named after the 19th century Italian composer [[Gioachino Rossini]].<ref name= osipova>[http://www.kakuteru.ru/rossini.html?lang=en Rossini]. Kakuteru.ru. Retrieved 2014-09-03.</ref>

== Preparation ==
Being a variation of the Bellini cocktail, Rossini is based on the same preparation.<ref>[http://www.cellartours.com/blog/italy/10-iconic-italian-cocktails 10 Iconic Italian Cocktails]. Cellartours.com. Retrieved 2014-09-03.</ref> Cut two thick slices from one strawberry and reserve. Purée the remaining strawberries and pour into two Champagne flutes. Top up with Prosecco and serve with the strawberry slice on the rim of the glass.<ref>[http://www.femalefirst.co.uk/foodanddrink/strawberry-rossini-cocktail-298849.html Strawberry Rossini Cocktail]. Femalefirst.co.uk. Retrieved 2014-09-03.</ref>

== Variations ==
* Bellini. [[Peach]] juice or purée are used instead of strawberry syrup and purée
* [[Mimosa (cocktail)|Mimosa]]. Strawberry component is replaced by [[orange juice]]
* Tintoretto. Consists of [[Champagne]] and [[pomegranate]] juice
* Puccini. Similar to the Mimosa, but contains [[tangerine]] or [[mandarin orange|mandarin]] juice

Sharbat (drink):
{{Short description|Sweet drinks}}

{{Distinguish | Sherbet (frozen dessert)| Sorbet}}
[[File:Sharbat.JPG|thumb|Two kinds of Iranian ''sharbat'' (center is lemon and right is cherry ''sharbat'') along with Iranian tea (left)]]
'''Sharbat''' ({{langx|fa|شربت}}, {{IPA|fa|ʃæɾˈbæt|pron}}; also transliterated or written as ''shorbot'', ''šerbet'', ''şerbet'' or ''sherbet'') is a drink prepared from fruit or flower [[petals]].<ref>{{cite book |title= Persian Pilgrimages |last= Molavi |first= Afshin |year= 2002 |publisher= W. W. Norton & Company |isbn= 0-393-05119-6 |url= https://archive.org/details/persianpilgrimag00afsh/page/113 |page= [https://archive.org/details/persianpilgrimag00afsh/page/113 113] |url-access= registration }}</ref> It is a sweet [[Squash (drink)|cordial]], and usually served chilled. It can be served in concentrated form and eaten with a spoon or diluted with water to create the drink. 

Popular ''sharbats'' are made of one or more of the following: [[basil seeds]],golāb ([[rose water|rose water)]], fresh rose petals, [[sandalwood]], ''[[Aegle marmelos|bael]]'', [[hibiscus]], [[lemon]], [[Orange (fruit)|orange]], [[mango]], [[pineapple]], [[grape]], ''[[falsa]]'' (''Grewia asiatica'') and [[chia seed]]s.

''Sharbat'' is common in homes of [[Iran]], [[Armenia]], [[Turkey]], [[Bosnia]], [[Arab world]], [[Afghanistan]], [[Pakistan]], [[Bangladesh]] and [[India]]. It is also popular with Muslims when breaking their daily [[fasting|fasts]] during the month of [[Ramadan]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://muslimheritage.com/article/world%E2%80%99s-first-soft-drink|title=The World's First Soft Drink|website=Muslim Heritage|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161224200942/http://www.muslimheritage.com/article/world%E2%80%99s-first-soft-drink|archive-date=2016-12-24|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Organic Rose Sharbat in Merdzavan, Armenia |url=https://orgayouth.com/organic-rose-sharbat-in-merdzavan-armenia?utm_ |website=Orgayouth}}</ref>

==Etymology==
[[File:Afza Syrup (Lal sharbat).JPG|thumb|[[Rooh Afza]] sharbat or shorbot drink made from fruit and herbs formulated in 1906 in [[Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh]], India, and launched from [[Old Delhi, India]]]]
The term comes from the Persian word ''sharbat'' (شربت),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/sherbet|title=Sherbet {{!}} frozen dessert|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|language=en|access-date=2019-07-23|quote=The word sherbet derives from the Persian sharbat, an iced fruit drink; iced desserts were introduced to the West via the Middle East. In the late 20th century there was a revival of the practice of serving a tart sherbet or sorbet between the courses of an elaborate meal to refresh the palate.}}</ref> meaning a drink of sugar and water. This in turn came from the [[Arabic]] word ''shariba'', "to drink".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wain |first1=Harry |title=The story behind the word: some interesting origins of medical terms |date=1958 |publisher=Thomas |oclc=630688 |page=288 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MGFrAAAAMAAJ&q=sharbat+meaning}}</ref> By the late [[Middle Ages]], the [[Arabic]] word ''sharāb'' (شراب) had come to mean "alcoholic beverage" and the alternate form sharbāt (شربات) and its [[Persian language|Persian]] and [[Turkish language|Turkish]] variations, ''sharbat'' (شربت), and ''şerbet'' respectively, took on the meaning of a sweet non-alcoholic beverage.<ref name=weir>{{Cite book| publisher = Oxford University Press| isbn = 978-0-19-931339-6| last1 = Weir| first1 = Robin| last2 = Quinzio| first2 = Jeri| title = The Oxford Companion to Sugar and Sweets| chapter = Sherbet| access-date = 2018-07-20| date = 2015-07-23| chapter-url = http://www.oxfordreference.com/view/10.1093/acref/9780199313396.001.0001/acref-9780199313396-e-463 |via=[[Oxford Reference]] }}</ref> The word is reported to have been first used in English vocabulary in 1603, and referenced by philosopher Francis Bacon in 1626.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-17 |title=Definition of SHERBET |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/sherbet |access-date=2026-04-22 |website=www.merriam-webster.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Saudi Aramco World : The World’s First Soft Drink |url=https://archive.aramcoworld.com/issue/200505/the.world.s.first.soft.drink.htm |access-date=2026-04-22 |website=archive.aramcoworld.com}}</ref>

==History==
It is believed that sharbats originated in [[Iran]] ([[Name of Iran|Persia]]).<ref name="weir" /><ref>{{Cite book|last=Marks|first=Gil|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gFK_yx7Ps7cC&pg=PT1|title=Encyclopedia of Jewish Food|date=2010-11-17|publisher=HMH|isbn=978-0-544-18631-6|language=en|quote=Sharbat is a fruit syrup. Origin: Persia}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Farrokh |first=Dr Kaveh |title=The Unknown Origins of Ice Cream in Ancient Iran |url=https://www.kavehfarrokh.com/ancient-prehistory-651-a-d/achaemenids/the-unknown-origins-of-ice-cream-in-ancient-iran/ |access-date=2023-04-05 |website=Dr. Kaveh Farrokh |language=en-US|quote=It is believed that Arabs who had conquered Persian Empire at the time took the age-old Persian refreshment called Sharbat and enriched the existing mix of fruit syrup and snow chilled honey with milk and sugar. This was the conception of the modern day granita and gelato.}}</ref><ref name="Cousineau">{{Cite book |last=Cousineau |first=Phil |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7g3yC_EI310C&q=sorbet+originated+in+persia&pg=PT255 |title=The Painted Word: A Treasure Chest of Remarkable Words and Their Origins |date=2012-09-11 |publisher=Simon and Schuster |isbn=9781936740253 |language=en |quote=The ancient Persians created a delicious and cooling concoction called sharbat}}</ref><ref name="Dishoom: From Bombay with Love">{{Cite book |last1=Thakrar |first1=Shamil |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4cqQDwAAQBAJ&q=sharbat+persian+origin&pg=PA23-IA120 |title=Dishoom: From Bombay with Love |last2=Thakrar |first2=Kavi |last3=Nasir |first3=Naved |date=2019-09-05 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing |isbn=9781408890660 |language=en |quote=Sharbat is a soft drink with Persian origins}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zcNdB_sl2JkC&q=sharbat+origin+persian&pg=PA80|title=National & Regional Styles of Cookery: Proceedings : Oxford Symposium 1981|last=Davidson|first=Alan|date=1981-01-01|publisher=Oxford Symposium|isbn=9780907325079|language=en|page=80}}</ref> Several syrups are listed in the 11th-century ''[[Canon of Medicine]]'' by Persian scholar [[Ibn Sīnā]].<ref>{{Cite web| title = 100 farklı Osmanlı şerbeti bir kitapta toplandı| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = http://www.trthaber.com/haber/kultur-sanat/100-farkli-osmanli-serbeti-bir-kitapta-toplandi-316442.html| website=trt haber| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171207194711/http://www.trthaber.com/haber/kultur-sanat/100-farkli-osmanli-serbeti-bir-kitapta-toplandi-316442.html| archive-date = 2017-12-07| url-status = live}}</ref> In the 12th century, [[Persian language|Persian]] book of [[Zakhireye Khwarazmshahi]], [[Ismail Gorgani|Gorgani]] describes different types of Sharbats in [[Iran]], including Ghoore, Anar, Sekanjebin, etc.

The first Western mention of sharbat is an Italian reference to something that [[Ottoman Turks|Turks]] drink. The word enters Italian as ''sorbetti'' which later became ''sorbet'' in French.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-07-19 |title=Des « sharbats » de la Perse aux sorbets, une histoire longue et glacée |url=https://www.lorientlejour.com/article/1306073/des-sharbats-de-la-perse-aux-sorbets-une-histoire-longue-et-glacee.html |access-date=2026-04-22 |website=L'Orient-Le Jour |language=fr}}</ref> In the 17th-century, England began importing "sherbet powders" made from dried fruit and flowers mixed with sugar. In the modern era [[Sherbet (powder)|sherbet powder]] is still popular in the [[UK]], though Oxford Reference distinguishes this earlier drink from the later use of effervescent “sherbet powder” in English.<ref>{{Cite web |title=sherbet |url=https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100501373 |access-date=2026-04-22}}</ref> A contemporary [[George Sandys|English writer]] traveling in the Middle East wrote of "sundry sherbets … some made of sugar and lemons, some of violets, and the like." When [[European people|Europeans]] figured out how to [[Endothermic process|freeze sherbet]] they began making ''[[sorbet]]to'' by adding fruit juices and flavorings to a frozen simple syrup base. In the US sherbet generally meant an ice milk, but recipes from early soda fountain manuals include ingredients like gelatin, beaten egg whites, cream, or milk.<ref name=weir />

Sharbat was traditionally made with [[cane juice]], but in modern times it is commonly made at home with sugar and water. Lime is sometimes added to improve the texture and flavor of the sharbat.<ref name=ndtv>{{Cite web| title = Sharbat| work = NDTV Food| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://food.ndtv.com/ingredient/sharbat-701174| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171101001914/http://food.ndtv.com/ingredient/sharbat-701174| archive-date = 2017-11-01| url-status = live}}</ref> Honey is also commonly used as a sweetener. Sharbet comes in many flavors including lemon, pomegranate, quince, strawberry, cherry, orange, rose, orange blossom, tamarind, mulberry and violet.<ref name=weir /> One sharbat recorded in the 19th-century cookbook by [[Friedrich Unger]] is called ''gülgülü tiryaki şerbet'' which means "pink [[opium]]-eater's sherbet".<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Kegan Paul| isbn = 978-0-7103-0936-5| last = Unger| first = Friedrich| title = A King's Confectioner in the Orient: Friedrich Unger, Court Confectioner to King Otto I of Greece| date = 2003 |page=74}}</ref>

==Varieties==
[[File:Imli Aloo Bukharay Sharbat.jpg|thumb|[[Tamarind]] and [[plum]] sharbat]]
[[Tamarind]] sherbet is a popular non-alcoholic beverage in Muslim countries that is commonly prepared during [[Ramadan]]. In Turkey tamarind sherbet, called ''demirhindi şerbeti'', might be flavored with [[cloves]], [[cardamom]], fresh [[ginger]], a [[cinnamon]] stick, [[honey]], [[Salvia officinalis|sage]] and dried [[Tilia|linden]] flowers.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Demirhindi Şerbeti| work = Arda'nın Mutfağı| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = http://www.ardaninmutfagi.com/yemek-tarifleri/tatlilar/demirhindi-serbeti| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180104182140/http://www.ardaninmutfagi.com/yemek-tarifleri/tatlilar/demirhindi-serbeti| archive-date = 2018-01-04| url-status = live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title = Demirhindi şerbeti tarifi| work = Milliyet Haber| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = http://www.milliyet.com.tr/demirhindi-serbeti-tarifi-pembenar-detay-icecekler-2263537/| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170125030700/http://www.milliyet.com.tr/demirhindi-serbeti-tarifi-pembenar-detay-icecekler-2263537/| archive-date = 2017-01-25| url-status = live}}</ref> In [[Hindustani language|Hindi-Urdu]], tamarind is called ''imli'' and is commonly paired with dried plums (''aaloo bukhara'').<ref>{{cite web |title=इमली |url=https://www.shabdkosh.com/dictionary/hindi-english/%E0%A4%87%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B2%E0%A5%80/%E0%A4%87%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%B2%E0%A5%80-meaning-in-english |publisher=Shabdkosh |access-date=16 April 2026 |date=2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title = Health benefits of Imli and Aaloo Bukhara drink| work = Samaa TV| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = http://www.samaa.tv/uncategorized/2017/06/health-benefits-of-imli-and-aaloo-bukhara-drink/}}</ref>

Almond sherbet is probably of Persian origin<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zcNdB_sl2JkC&q=sharbat+originated+in+persia&pg=PA80|title=National & Regional Styles of Cookery: Proceedings : Oxford Symposium 1981|last=Davidson|first=Alan|date=1981-01-01|publisher=Oxford Symposium|isbn=9780907325079|language=en|page=80}}</ref> and can be spiced with [[cardamom]] and [[kewra]].<ref>{{Cite web| title = Badaam ka Sharbat Recipe by Niru Gupta| work = NDTV Food| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-badaam-ka-sharbat-1-483347| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180307135627/https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-badaam-ka-sharbat-1-483347| archive-date = 2018-03-07| url-status = live}}</ref> Another version of almond sherbet is made with milk and [[saffron]] and [[musk melon]] seeds are sometimes added.<ref>{{Cite news | title = Make this cooling almond sharbat this summer| work = The Indian Express| access-date = 2018-07-19| date = 2016-06-03| url = http://indianexpress.com/article/lifestyle/food-wine/make-this-cooling-almond-sharbat-this-summer-foodie-2833088/| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170821130405/http://indianexpress.com/article/lifestyle/food-wine/make-this-cooling-almond-sharbat-this-summer-foodie-2833088/| archive-date = 2017-08-21| url-status = live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news | title = Recipe: Badam ka sharbat (almond-saffron milk) | work = The Boston Globe | access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://www.bostonglobe.com/lifestyle/food-dining/2017/05/29/recipe-badam-sharbat-almond-saffron-milk/Mpr7hJytDvCXhObd4A7O8M/story.html| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170708094322/http://www.bostonglobe.com/lifestyle/food-dining/2017/05/29/recipe-badam-sharbat-almond-saffron-milk/Mpr7hJytDvCXhObd4A7O8M/story.html| archive-date = 2017-07-08| url-status = live}}</ref>

[[File:Bael_Sherbat_Indian_Beverage.jpg|thumb|[[Bela Pana]]]]
Wood apple sharbat can be flavored with salt, pepper and [[mentha]] or simply sugar and [[lemon]] juice.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Here Is How You Can Make Bael Sherbet At Home| work = NDTV Food| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://food.ndtv.com/food-drinks/here-is-how-you-can-make-bael-sharbat-at-home-1851998| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180514221836/https://food.ndtv.com/food-drinks/here-is-how-you-can-make-bael-sharbat-at-home-1851998| archive-date = 2018-05-14| url-status = live}}</ref> Called ''[[Aegle marmelos|bael]] ka sharbat'' it is one of the most popular beverages in [[India]] and was discussed in the 1894 ''Agricultural Gazette of New South Wales''.<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Springer Science & Business Media| isbn = 978-3-662-07774-0| last = Bajaj| first = Y. P. S.| title = High-Tech and Micropropagation V| date = 2013-03-09| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=-FzxCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA273| access-date = 2018-07-19| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://books.google.com/books?id=-FzxCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA273| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Government printer.| title = Agricultural Gazette of New South Wales| date = 1894| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=4znuAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA156| access-date = 2018-07-19| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://books.google.com/books?id=4znuAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA156| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref> Another sharbat variation from India is made with powdered [[sandalwood]] (''chandan'') and sugared milk.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Chandan ka Sharbat Recipe by Niru Gupta| work = NDTV Food| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-chandan-ka-sherbet-100545| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-chandan-ka-sherbet-100545| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref> [[Phalsa]] berries are another base for some varieties of south Asian sherbet.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Phalse Ka Sharbat Recipe| work = NDTV Food| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-phalse-ka-sharbat-218026| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180625090947/https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-phalse-ka-sharbat-218026| archive-date = 2018-06-25| url-status = live}}</ref> Some sour sharbet variations might make use of citrus fruits, tamarind, or ''[[Amla (fruit)|amla]]'' berries. An Indian lemonade called ''nimbu pani'' is made with fresh squeezed lemon or lime juice with additional flavorings like ginger, mint, saffron, kewra or even crushed black pepper.<ref name=guardian />

[[Vetiver]] sherbet (''khus'' syrup) can be made by adding ''khus'' essence to sugar and water. The ''khus'' essence itself is made from the roots of vetiver grass. Vetiver sherbet can be used as a flavoring for milkshakes, [[lassi]] and other yogurt drinks, ice cream, [[Shirley Temple (drink)|Shirley Temples]] and other mixed beverages. It can also be used as a general purpose dessert topping.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Khus ka Sharbat Recipe by Niru Gupta| work = NDTV Food| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://food.ndtv.com/recipe-khus-ka-sharbat-100543| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20171119055039/http://food.ndtv.com/recipe-khus-ka-sharbat-100543| archive-date = 2017-11-19| url-status = live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Springer| isbn = 978-3-319-26062-4| last = Lim| first = T. K.| title = Edible Medicinal and Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 11 Modified Stems, Roots, Bulbs| date = 2016-02-08 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-4WMCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA200}}</ref>

The most common sharbat flavor is probably [[rose]].<ref name=ndtv /> Rose sharbat can be used as a topping for the milk pudding ''[[muhallebi]]''. One Turkish method of making rose sharbat involves kneading fresh rose petals with a little [[citric acid]] or sugar to release their fragrance. (If sugar is used the petals are left in the fridge overnight and a small amount of lemon juice is added the following day.) This petal mixture is called ''gül mayası'' and can be added to a sharbat base of sugar and water to make a rose sharbat topping that can be used to flavor desserts like ''muhallebi'', and other cookies and cakes.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Gül Şerbetli Su Muhallebisi {{!}} Kolay Tatlılar| work = www.showtv.com.tr| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://www.showtv.com.tr/yemek-tarifleri/tatlilar/492799-gul-serbetli-su-muhallebisi| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180719093135/https://www.showtv.com.tr/yemek-tarifleri/tatlilar/492799-gul-serbetli-su-muhallebisi| archive-date = 2018-07-19| url-status = live}}</ref>

=== Middle East ===
[[File:Kunefe and dondurma.jpg|thumb|[[Knafeh]], dessert made from ''[[Kadayif (pastry)|kadayif]]'' soaked in sh''erbet'', served with [[dondurma]]]] 
Many Ottoman Muslims did not have a custom of consuming or serving alcoholic beverages, which contributed to the popularity of sherbet during the [[Middle Ages]]. In the Ottoman period, palace sherbet production took place in the Helvahane and that sherbet commonly consisted of fruit and water, enhanced with sugar, rose water, and spices.<ref name=":0" /> Sherbet could take three forms: syrups, pastes called ''çevirme'' and tablets. Ottoman confectioners would create concentrated essences out of fresh ingredients that could be diluted to make sherbet. In 17<sup>th</sup> century [[Istanbul]] about 500 people worked in the sherbet trade across 300 shops, rising to around 1100 when certain itinerant sellers are included. These Ottoman-era sherbets were produced year-round and served cold in summer and hot in winter, with hot and spicy sherbets widely consumed during colder months. <ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Studies on Ottoman Sherbets from the Past to Present |url=https://dergipark.org.tr/en/download/article-file/3930008 |access-date=2026-04-22}}</ref> In modern times, sherbet production has declined but in some regions of Turkey syrups are still made. Pastes are rare and can only be found in speciality shops; most commercially available pastes today are limited to [[bergamot orange|bergamot]] or [[Mastic (plant resin)|mastic]] flavors. Tablets were a specialty item, even during Ottoman Times, made only by confectioner's in professional shops. To make the tablets, fruit juices and essential oils, like [[rose]] or [[cinnamon]], were added to boiling sugared water and stirred against the sides of the pan until the sugar began to crystallize. Spices, ground nuts, and herbs might be added to the mixture, which was poured onto a large marble slab and allowed to set.<ref name=isin>{{Cite book| publisher = I.B.Tauris| isbn = 978-1-84885-898-5| last = Isin| first = Mary| title = Sherbet and Spice: The Complete Story of Turkish Sweets and Desserts| date = 2013-01-08}}</ref>

In the 19th-century Isaac Edrehi wrote about a shopkeeper named Mustafa who made two types of beverages called sherbet and khoshâb:<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = I. Edrehi| last = Edrehi| first = Moses|author-link=Moses Edrehi| title = History of the capital of Asia and the Turks: together with an account of the domestic manners of the Turks in Turkey| date = 1855| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=nUQLAAAAIAAJ&pg=RA2-PA53| access-date = 2018-07-19| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://books.google.com/books?id=nUQLAAAAIAAJ&pg=RA2-PA53| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref>
<blockquote>One of the dainties on the happy mixture of which Hadjy Mustafa prides himself is khoshâb. This beverage, though nearly related to, must not be confounded with, sherbet. The latter is slightly acidulated, and in general made of fresh lemon, [[quince]], orange or [[cherry juice]], or of candied grapes, mulberries, and [[Damson|Damascus plums]], squeezed or diluted in cold water, and thus drank at all hours. But the khoshâb (agreeable water) forms the termination of all orthodox dinners, and is composed of preserved fruits or syrups, such as Aidin pomegranates, Mardin plums, Damascus and Bokhara apricots, Rodosto peaches, Scala Nuova cherries, Beybek strawberries, Adrianople roses, tamarinds, and so forth."</blockquote>

The Ottoman writer [[Evliya Çelebi]] records that the Merchants of Khoshâb in [[Ottoman Egypt]] made khoshâb, which he calls "a kind of sherbet", from "the juice of the most excellent fruits, such as apricots of Bokhara, plums of Mardin, pears of Azerbaijan, mulberries of Arabguir, grapes of Smyrna, sour cherries (aigriottes) of Rodosto, apples of Koja Ili, prunes of Temesvar, and peaches of Constantinople." According to this account the ''khoshâb'' is flavored with "amber and musk". He goes on to describe a different group of sherbet-merchants whose shops are decorated with "many thousand cups and bowls of China and Fayence, which are filled with sherbet, made of rhubarb, roses, lemons, lotus, tamarinds and grapes."<ref>{{Cite book| title = Oriental Translation Fund| date = 1834| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=Wl0PAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA154| access-date = 2018-07-19| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://books.google.com/books?id=Wl0PAQAAMAAJ&pg=RA1-PA154| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref>

The 15th-century Ottoman poem by [[Süleyman Çelebi]] wrote: "As I burned with raging thirst, They handed me a glass of sherbet" describing how the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]]{{'}}s mother was given a glass of sherbet while she was in labor.<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Oxford Symposium| isbn = 978-1-903018-89-7| last = McWilliams| first = Mark| title = Celebration: Proceedings of the Oxford Symposium on Food and Cookery 2011| date = 2012-07-01| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wTwQDgAAQBAJ&pg=PT150}}</ref> When a woman in Anatolia gives birth it is still customary to offer  a hot sherbet called ''[[lohusa şerbeti]]'' to guests.<ref name=isin /><ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Oxford Symposium| isbn = 978-0-907325-46-8| last = Walker| first = Harlan| title = Oxford Symposium on Food & Cookery, 1990: Feasting and Fasting : Proceedings| date = 1991| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=XseXnb98h90C&pg=PA104| access-date = 2018-07-19| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://books.google.com/books?id=XseXnb98h90C&pg=PA104| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref>

Common sharbat flavors include tamarind, [[pomegranate]], [[black mulberry]], sour grape, [[licorice]], [[morello cherry]], rose, honey.<ref>Özdoğan, Yahya, and Nermin Işık. "Geleneksel Türk Mutfağında Şerbet." (2008).</ref> One version uses fresh purple [[wisteria]] flowers. The petals are soaked in water for a full day and then strained through [[cheesecloth]]. The petals are bundled in the cheesecloth and their highly fragranced liquid is also squeezed into the bowl containing the scented water. Sugar is added and the sugared mixture is allowed to rest overnight.<ref>{{Cite AV media| people = Refika'nın Mutfağı| title = Refika'dan Kolay Mor Salkımlı Şerbet Tarifi| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=alk4aVTkQYM| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=alk4aVTkQYM| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref>
 
A simple sherbet of lemon, [[citric acid]] and water, without additional spices, is called ''nişan şerbeti'' or "betrothal sherbet" in [[Turkish language|Turkish]] and is traditionally served at engagement ceremonies.<ref>{{Cite book| publisher = Esform Ofset| isbn = 978-975-95385-4-5| last1 = Üçer| first1 = Müjgân| last2 = Akkaya| first2 = H. Suna Eretkin| title = Arapgir| date = 2008}}</ref> Some versions of lemon sherbet may be optionally flavored with honey and cloves.<ref>{{Cite AV media| people = Migros Türkiye| title = Limon Şerbeti Tarifi| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0QxNNT0wwVE| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0QxNNT0wwVE| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref> A similar sherbet flavored with cloves and lemon juice can also be made with fresh [[peach]]es.<ref>{{Cite AV media| people = Migros Türkiyeundefined (Director)| title = Şeftali Şerbeti| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ub_ebifmEk8| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ub_ebifmEk8| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref> Green apple and cinnamon is another possible flavor combination.<ref>{{Cite AV media| people = Migros Türkiye| title = Elma Şerbeti| access-date = 2018-07-19| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CBmPgG-rFL4}}</ref> One recipe for "Ottoman sherbet" calls for sugared sour cherries, dried plums, golden raisins, fresh ginger, cloves, cinnamon sticks to be simmered together.<ref>{{Cite AV media| people = Migros Türkiye| title = Osmanlı Şerbeti Nasıl Yapılır? {{!}} Osmanlı Şerbeti Tarifi| access-date = 2018-07-19| time = 48 seconds| url = https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mbJcKzXO5g4| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180720024941/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mbJcKzXO5g4| archive-date = 2018-07-20| url-status = live}}</ref>

=== India ===
Sharbat was introduced to [[India]] by the [[Mughal Empire|Mughal]]s in the 16th century.<ref name=guardian>{{Cite news| issn = 0261-3077| last = Sukhadwala| first = Sejal| title = Diwali drinks: sharbat to champagne| work = The Guardian| access-date = 2018-07-19| date = 2012-11-12| url = https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/wordofmouth/2012/nov/12/diwali-drinks-sharbat-to-champagne| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160722013053/https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/wordofmouth/2012/nov/12/diwali-drinks-sharbat-to-champagne| archive-date = 2016-07-22| url-status = live}}</ref> It was popularised in the [[Indian subcontinent]] by [[Babur]], who sent for frequent loads of ice from the [[Himalayas]] to make a cool refreshing drink.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.thehindu.com/thehindu/yw/2002/01/19/stories/2002011900260300.htm|title=Keeping cool|access-date=3 January 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161126092340/http://www.thehindu.com/thehindu/yw/2002/01/19/stories/2002011900260300.htm|archive-date=26 November 2016|url-status=dead|newspaper=[[The Hindu]]|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

===Algeria===
[[File:Cherbet.jpg|thumb|right|Lemon Cherbet]]
'''Cherbet''' ([[Arabic]]: شربات), also known as or '''charbet mazhar''', is a traditional Algerian drink. In Algerian weddings, the bride drinks a large quantity of this traditional beverage and then offers it to her female guests after the hammam ritual, along with brioche pastries called kâak bouchkara.<ref name="Kika" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=sirops de fruit {{!}} Cuisine Algerienne {{!}} Apprendre la gastronomie Algérienne |url=https://archive.wikiwix.com/cache/display2.php?url=http%3A%2F%2Fweb.archive.org%2Fweb%2F20131026202222%2Fhttp%3A%2F%2Fwww.cuisine-algerienne.com%2Frecettes%2Fsirops-de-fruits%2F |access-date=2023-06-27 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Bouayed">{{Cite book |last=Bouayed |first=Fatima-Zohra |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/1243890366 |title=Le livre de la cuisine d'Algérie |publisher=SNED |year=1981 |isbn=2201016488 |page=389}}</ref>

Its origin comes from the Algiers region, specifically from the city of Algiers. Its name comes from Algerian Arabic and means "drink made from orange blossom water.<ref name="Kika">{{Cite web |last=roudacuisine |date=2011-03-15 |title=Kikaats bouchkara revisitées (briochettes algériennes) كعيكعات بوشكارة |url=http://roudacuisine.over-blog.com/article-kikaat-bouchkara-revisitees-anneaux-brioches-53337884.html |access-date=2023-06-27 |website=Ma cuisine d'hier et d'aujourd'hui |language=fr}}</ref>

It is a syrup made of water, fresh cinnamon, a large amount of orange blossom water, and sugar according to taste.<ref name="Bouayed"/>

===Indonesia===

An [[Indonesia]]n, especially [[Java]]nese, drink called ''serbat'' is commonly found during the month of [[Ramadan]]. The most popular is made by mixing cold water, simple syrup, and shredded cantaloupe, popularly known as ''serbat blewah'' or cantaloupe sherbet.<ref>Riani, Asnida (2022-03-06). "3 Resep Es Blewah Segar untuk Hilangkan Dahaga". (in Indonesian). ''Liputan6''. Retrieved 2024-01-03.</ref>

'''Primo Brands Corporation''' (previously known as '''Cott Corporation''') is an American-Canadian water company offering multi-gallon bottled water, water dispensers, self-service refill water machines, and water filtration appliances. The company is headquartered in [[Tampa, Florida]], and services residential and commercial customers across the United States, Canada, Europe and Israel.

==Founding==
Cott Beverage Corporation was founded in 1923 by Solomon Cott, a Polish immigrant, with his sons Harry, Barney, Jack and Albert in [[Port Chester, New York]]. Harry Pencer, a clothier from [[Montreal]], [[Quebec]], began to import Cott [[Soft drink|soda]]s into Quebec in 1952. In 1955, Pencer acquired the Canadian rights to the Cott label and established Cott Beverages (Canada) Ltd., to bottle the Cott line of sodas. From 1976 to 1991, under the leadership of his son [[Gerry Pencer]], Cott expanded its distribution throughout Canada and back into the U.S. and into Europe.<ref>[http://www.fundinguniverse.com/company-histories/Cott-Corporation-Company-History.html History of Cott Corporation – FundingUniverse]. Fundinguniverse.com. Retrieved on July 24, 2012.</ref> In 1969, the name was changed to Cott Beverages Ltd., and in 1991 to Cott Corporation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Form 10-K |url=http://markets.financialcontent.com/stocks/action/getedgarwindow?accesscode=95014401003715 |author=Cott Corporation |date=March 7, 2001 |access-date=September 16, 2011|format=filing for the [[United States Securities and Exchange Commission]]}}</ref>

== Acquisitions ==
In October 2000, Concord Beverages, with its Vintage brand [[Carbonated water|seltzer water]], was acquired from Honickman Group.<ref>[http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_m0EIN/is_2000_Oct_18/ai_66198037 Cott Corporation Has Acquired Honickman Group's Concord Beverage To Strengthen U.S. Presence; Earnings, Excluding One-Time Gain, Triple In The 7th Profitable Quarter]. Findarticles.com. Retrieved on July 24, 2012.</ref> In July 2010, Cott announced its acquisition of [[Cliffstar]] Corporation, a US supplier of store-supplied and made juice beverages.<ref>{{cite news| url=https://www.thestar.com/business/article/833697--analyst-applauds-cott-s-acquisition | location=Toronto | work=The Star | title=Analyst applauds Cott's acquisition | first=David | last=Friend | date=July 8, 2010}}</ref>

Beginning in 2014, Cott expanded via acquisitions predominantly in the bottled water industry and exited the carbonated beverages business. In May 2014, Cott completed the acquisition of Aimia Foods (Holdings) Limited, a privately held producer and distributor of hot chocolate, coffee and powdered beverages, hot and cold cereal products located in [[Merseyside]], [[United Kingdom]].<ref>{{cite press release | publisher=Marketwired| date=30 May 2014| title=Cott Announces U.K. Business Unit's Acquisition of Aimia Foods | url=http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-uk-business-units-acquisition-of-aimia-foods-nyse-cot-1915642.htm}}</ref> In December 2014, Cott completed the acquisition of DSS Group, Inc. a bottled water and coffee direct-to-consumer home and office delivery services provider in the United States. The aggregate consideration was approximately $1.25 billion.<ref>{{cite press release | publisher=Marketwired| date=12 December 2014| title=Cott Announces Closing of DS Services Acquisition | url=http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-closing-of-ds-services-acquisition-nyse-cot-1976576.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150703064240/http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-closing-of-ds-services-acquisition-nyse-cot-1976576.htm|archive-date=2015-07-03|url-status=dead|access-date=2019-09-14}}</ref>

In January 2016, Cott completed the acquisition of Aquaterra, a Canadian bottled water and coffee delivery services provider, for approximately C$62 million.<ref>{{cite press release | publisher=Marketwired| date=5 January 2016| title=Cott Announces Closing of Aquaterra Acquisition | url=http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-closing-of-aquaterra-acquisition-nyse-cot-2085466.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307091824/http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-closing-of-aquaterra-acquisition-nyse-cot-2085466.htm|archive-date=2016-03-07|url-status=dead|access-date=2019-09-14}}</ref> Eight months later, Cott acquired [[Eden Springs]], a European water and coffee deliverer, for approximately €470 million,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.floridatrend.com/article/20453/eden-springs-to-be-acquired-by-cott-corporation-for-470-525-million|title=Eden Springs to be acquired by Cott Corporation for €470 ($525) million|date=2016-05-08|website=Florida Trend|access-date=2018-12-04}}</ref> and premium [[Coffee preparation|coffee roaster]] S&D Coffee and Tea, for approximately $355 million.<ref>{{cite press release | publisher=Marketwired| date=11 August 2016| title=Cott Announces Closing of S&D Acquisition and Date for Modeling Conference Call | url=http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-closing-of-s-d-acquisition-and-date-for-modeling-conference-call-tsx-bcb-2149968.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180406101839/http://www.marketwired.com/press-release/cott-announces-closing-of-s-d-acquisition-and-date-for-modeling-conference-call-tsx-bcb-2149968.htm|archive-date=2018-04-06|url-status=dead|access-date=2019-09-14}}</ref>

On January 30, 2018, Cott sold its carbonated soft drinks and juice bottling businesses to [[Refresco]] for US$1.25 billion.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Griffin |first1=Justine |title=Cott Corp. sells beverage manufacturing business for $1.25 billion |url=https://www.tampabay.com/news/business/cott-corp-sells-beverage-manufacturing-business-for-125-billion/2331422/ |access-date=November 21, 2019 |work=Tampa Bay Times |date=July 25, 2017 |language=en}}</ref> The transaction included the Cott business units in North America, [[United Kingdom|the UK]] and [[Mexico]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Arthur |first1=Rachel |title=Refresco completes acquisition of Cott's bottling activities |url=https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2018/01/31/Refresco-completes-acquisition-of-Cott-s-bottling-activities |access-date=November 21, 2019 |work=Beverage Daily |date=January 31, 2019}}</ref> That October, Cott announced the acquisition of [[Mountain Valley Spring Water|Mountain Valley Spring Company]] from Great Range Capital for $78.5 million<ref>{{Cite web|last=Schultz|first=Clark|date=2018-10-15|title=Cott acquires Mountain Valley Spring Company|url=https://seekingalpha.com/news/3397465-cott-acquires-mountain-valley-spring-company|access-date=2019-07-15|website=Seeking Alpha}}</ref>  The next February, Cott announced the sale of its soft drink concentrate production facility and RCI International division to Refresco for US$.25 billion.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2020-01-08 |title=Cott considering sale of its coffee and tea business to focus on water |url=https://calgary.citynews.ca/2020/01/08/cott-considering-sale-of-its-coffee-and-tea-business-to-focus-on-water/ |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=CityNews Calgary |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=May 2, 2019 |title=Cott Corp shares drop as it reports bigger than expected net loss |url=https://financialpost.com/pmn/business-pmn/cott-corp-shares-drop-as-it-reports-bigger-than-expected-net-loss |work=The Canadian Press}}</ref>

In January 2020, Cott sold S&D Coffee and Tea to [[WestRock|Westrock]] Coffee Company, LLC for US$405 million.<ref name=":0" />

On March 2, 2020, Cott completed its purchase of Primo Water Corporation for US$775 million.<ref>{{Cite press release|publisher=Primo Water|date=2020-01-13|title=Cott Announces the Acquisition of Primo Water Corporation and Continues its Transition Into a Pure-Play Water Solutions Provider|url=http://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2020/01/13/1969399/0/en/Cott-Announces-the-Acquisition-of-Primo-Water-Corporation-and-Continues-its-Transition-Into-a-Pure-Play-Water-Solutions-Provider.html|access-date=2021-01-14|website=GlobeNewswire News Room}}</ref> As part of the purchase agreement, Cott rebranded as Primo Water Corporation and changed its ticker symbols to NYSE:PRMW and TSX:PRMW.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-02-28 |title=Cott Corporation completed the acquisition of 82.2% stake in Primo Water Corporation from directors, officers and others for approximately $470 million |url=https://www.marketscreener.com/quote/stock/PRIMO-WATER-CORPORATION-6845440/news/Cott-Corporation-completed-the-acquisition-of-82-2-stake-in-Primo-Water-Corporation-from-directors-33968572/ |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=www.marketscreener.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

In July 2022, Primo Water Corporation acquired [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]-based Highland Mountain Water for an undisclosed sum.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Primo Water Corp. Acquires Highland Mountain Water |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/story/primo-water-corp-acquires-highland-mountain-water-271658140482 |access-date=2022-07-21 |website=MarketWatch |language=EN-US |archive-date=2022-07-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220721151231/https://www.marketwatch.com/story/primo-water-corp-acquires-highland-mountain-water-271658140482 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In November 2024, Primo Water merged with [[BlueTriton Brands]] ([[Nestlé Waters]]' North America subsidiary). The new company is known as Primo Brands.<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 5, 2024 |title=Primo Water Announces Shareowner Approval of Merger with Bluetriton Brands |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/primo-water-announces-shareowner-approval-211500494.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250211183413/https://finance.yahoo.com/news/primo-water-announces-shareowner-approval-211500494.html |archive-date=2025-02-11}}</ref>
