Sarsi (drink):
{{short description|Soft drink}}
[[File:Sioux City sarsaparilla bottles.jpg|thumb|upright|For decades, until the 2010s, the iconic [[Sioux City (soft drink)|Sioux City]] sarsaparilla bottle was sold in retail stores in the United States.]]
{{Cookbook|Sarsaparilla}}
'''Sarsaparilla''' ({{IPAc-en|UK|ˌ|s|ɑːr|s|p|ə|ˈ|r|ɪ|l|ə}}, {{IPAc-en|USalso|ˌ|s|æ|s|p|ə|ˈ|r|ɪ|l|ə}} {{Respell|sas|pə|RI|lə}})<ref>{{cite LPD|3}}</ref><ref>{{cite EPD|18}}</ref> is a [[soft drink]] originally made from the vine ''[[Smilax ornata]]'' (also called 'sarsaparilla') or other species of ''[[Smilax]]'' such as ''[[Smilax officinalis]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://tropical.theferns.info/viewtropical.php?id=Smilax+officinalis |title=Useful Tropical Plants ''Smilax officinalis'' |last=Fern |first=Ken |date=30 July 2021 |website=tropical.theferns.info |publisher=Tropical Plants Database |access-date=20 March 2022 }}</ref> In most [[Southeast Asia]]n countries, it is known by the common name '''sarsi''', and the trademarks '''Sarsi''' and '''Sarsae'''. It is similar in flavor to [[root beer]]. In the US, sarsaparilla is traditionally made with [[birch oil]] rather than the tropical plant.

==Etymology==
''[[Smilax ornata]]'', a perennial trailing vine with prickly stems that is native to Mexico and Central America, is often used as the basis for the soft drink sarsaparilla.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/?name_id=288960|title=Plants of the World Online | Kew Science|website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref> Common names include sarsaparilla, Honduran sarsaparilla, and Jamaican sarsaparilla.<ref>{{GRIN|id=400333|access-date=29 May 2023}}</ref>

It is known in [[Spanish language|Spanish]] as ''{{lang|es|[[wikt:zarzaparrilla|zarzaparrilla]]}}'', which is derived from the words ''{{linktext|zarza|lang=es}}'' meaning "bramble" (from preroman ''sarza''), and ''{{linktext|parrilla|lang=es}}'', meaning "little grape vine".<ref>{{Cite web |title=sarsaparilla | Etymology, origin and meaning of sarsaparilla by etymonline |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/sarsaparilla |website=etymonline.com}}</ref><ref>Davidse, G. & al. (eds.) (1994). Flora Mesoamericana 6: 1–543. Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, México, D.F.</ref><ref>Balick, M.J., Nee, M.H. & Atha, D.E. (2000). Checklist of the Vascular Plants of Belize with Common Names an Uses: 1–246. New York Botanic Garden Press, New York.</ref><ref>Espejo Serena, A. & López-Ferrari, A.R. (2000). Las Monocotiledóneas Mexicanas una Sinopsis Florística 1(9–11): 1–337. Consejo Nacional de la Flora de México, México D.F.</ref><ref>Nelson Sutherland, C.H. (2008). Catálogo de las plantes vasculares de Honduras. Espermatofitas: 1–1576. SERNA/Guaymuras, Tegucigalpa, Honduras.</ref>

==History in the US==
Sarsaparilla was popular in the United States in the 19th century. According to advertisements for [[patent medicines]] of the period, it was considered to be a remedy for skin and blood problems.<ref>{{cite web|title=Hood's Sarsaparilla|url=http://lcdl.library.cofc.edu/lcdl/catalog/lcdl:60541|website=Lowcountry Digital Library|access-date=1 September 2014|archive-date=15 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141015021640/http://lcdl.library.cofc.edu/lcdl/catalog/lcdl:60541|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>[https://archive.org/details/ayersamericanalm00ayer James Cook Ayer, ''Ayer's American Almanac'', 1878]</ref> ''The Oxford Companion to American Food and Drink'' notes that it evokes images of "languid [[Southern belle|belles]] and parched [[cowboy]]s".<ref>{{cite book|chapter=Sarsaparilla|last=Tobias|first=Ruth|editor-first=Andrew F|editor-last=Smith|title=The Oxford Companion to American Food and Drink|year=2007|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|page=550|isbn=9780195307962|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AoWlCmNDA3QC&pg=PT550}}</ref>

Sarsaparilla is sometimes considered to be a type of [[root beer]]. Dozens of brands of sarsaparilla are made by microbreweries, mainly in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sarsaparilla Reviews|date=29 November 2021 |url=https://rootbeerbarrel.com/category/sarsaparillas/}}</ref>

==Availability==
Sarsaparilla is not readily available in most countries; however, many [[Bar_(establishment)|bars]] and most major supermarket chains in the Philippines, Taiwan, Singapore and Australia stock sarsaparilla-flavored soft drinks, and sarsaparilla remains available in the United Kingdom as a legacy of the [[temperance movement]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Sarsaparilla |author= |website=Foods of England |url=https://www.foodsofengland.info/sarsaparilla.html |access-date=17 April 2025 }}</ref>

===United States===
[[File:"This is all right. Hood's Sarsaparilla can't fool me twice." "Be sure you are right," is this old man's motto. (front) - 8558173634.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Trade card]], 1886]]
The classic sarsaparilla was not made from the extract of the sarsaparilla plant, a tropical vine distantly related to the lily. It was originally made from a blend of birch oil and [[sassafras]], the dried root bark of the sassafras tree. In this context, sassafras should not be confused with common sassafras seasoning, [[Filé powder|filé]], used in [[Cajun cooking]] and made from dried and ground sassafras leaves. Sassafras was widely used as a home remedy in the 19th century; taken in sufficient doses it induces sweating, which some people thought had health benefits. Sarsaparilla made its debut as a patent medicine, an easy-to-take form of sassafras, much as [[Coca-Cola]] was first marketed in 1885 as a remedy for hangovers, headaches and morphine addiction.<ref>[https://www.straightdope.com/columns/read/319/whatever-happened-to-the-soft-drink-sarsaparilla Whatever happened to the soft drink sarsaparilla?] December 16, 1977 by Cecil Adams, retrieved 2013-04-30</ref> Besides the effects of the ingredients, sodas were popular in the United States at the time, due to the belief that [[carbonated water]] had health benefits.<ref>{{cite web |title=Themes for Coca-Cola Advertising (1886–1999) |url=http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/ccmphtml/colatime1.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010124072300/http://memory.loc.gov/ammem/ccmphtml/colatime1.html |archive-date=24 January 2001 |access-date=2007-02-11}}</ref> In 1960 the FDA banned the use of sassafras oil in foodstuffs after evidence accumulated showing that the main constituent, [[safrole]], was carcinogenic.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dietz|first1=Birgit|last2=Bolton|first2=Judy L.|date=2007-04-01|title=Botanical Dietary Supplements Gone Bad|journal=Chemical Research in Toxicology|volume=20|issue=4|pages=586–590|doi=10.1021/tx7000527|issn=0893-228X|pmc=2504026|pmid=17362034}}</ref> Safrole is also found in filé, nutmeg, mace, cinnamon, anise, black pepper and sweet basil, but in low enough concentration to be deemed safe.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dietz|first1=Birgit|last2=Bolton|first2=Judy L.|date=April 2007|title=Botanical Dietary Supplements Gone Bad|journal=Chemical Research in Toxicology|volume=20|issue=4|pages=586–590|doi=10.1021/tx7000527|issn=0893-228X|pmc=2504026|pmid=17362034}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Real Food Encyclopedia {{!}} Sassafras and Filé|url=https://foodprint.org/real-food/sassafras-and-file/|access-date=2021-01-24|website=FoodPrint|language=en-US}}</ref>

===East Asia===

====Taiwan====
[[HeySong Sarsaparilla]] ({{zh|t=黑松沙士}}) is the most popular brand of sarsaparilla drink in Taiwan. It is manufactured by [[HeySong Corporation]].<ref>Jinn's Publishers et al. "Omoshiro Temakan Meguri No.4: HeySong Soft Drink Museum". Nãruhodo The Taiwan. Vol. 235. October 2006.</ref>

===Southeast Asia===
====Cambodia====
In Cambodia, sarsaparilla is one of the flavors sold under the [[Fanta]] brand, bottled and distributed by Cambodia Beverage Company Ltd., a unit of the Coca-Cola SABCO Group.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.phnompenhpost.com/special-reports/coca-cola-celebrates-125th-anniversary|title=Coca-Cola celebrates 125th Anniversary|publisher=The Phnom Penh Post|date=3 July 2011|access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref>

====Indonesia====
There are two well known sarsaparilla brands in Indonesia, [[Badak]] (from [[North Sumatra]]) and Indo Saparella (from the [[Special Region of Yogyakarta]]). Badak was established by a Swiss national named Heinrich Surbeck in 1916 in [[Pematangsiantar]], [[North Sumatra]] and Indo Saparella was established in 1960 in [[Yogyakarta]]. There is also Agung Ngoro a local soft drink brand who produces traditional sarsaparilla in a glass bottle.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.genpi.co/travel/3545/ini-tiga-merek-saparela-yang-pernah-hits-di-indonesia|title=Three Sarsaparilla Brands That Were Hits In Indonesia (2018)|date=26 November 2018|access-date=7 April 2020}}</ref>

====Thailand====
Hi-Mark by [[Green Spot (Thailand)|Green Spot]]{{citation needed|date=June 2012}} was the domestic sarsaparilla drink in Thailand, but was discontinued in 2000. [[Fraser and Neave|F&N]] Sarsi has been produced in Thailand by Sermsuk Public Company Limited since 2018, reviving a brand last sold locally in the 1990s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://positioningmag.com/1182613 |title=สิ้นสุดการรอคอย! "ซาสี่" มาแล้ว ขอท้าชิงแชร์ตลาดน้ำอัดลมหมื่นล้านแล้ว!|date=9 August 2018 |publisher=Positioning |access-date=2023-04-02 |language=th }}</ref>

[[Image:Fnnsarsi.JPG|upright=0.5|thumb|A can of F&N Sarsi from Singapore]]

===Philippines===
In the Philippines, Sarsi is a brand name for a sarsaparilla drink originally manufactured by Cosmos Bottling Corporation, a local company that is now a subsidiary of [[Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines|Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines, Inc.]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.philstar.com/business/2013/04/05/927003/cosmos-sets-delisting-psei|title=Cosmos sets delisting from PSEi|first=Neil Jerome C.|last=Morales|website=[[The Philippine STAR]] |access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref> Cosmos Bottling Corporation was established in 1918 as Manila Aerated Water Company.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2479&dat=20010912&id=OKhjAAAAIBAJ&pg=833,34120272|title=Philippine Daily Inquirer – Google News Archive Search|access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref> Sarsi was originally branded as Cosmos Sarsaparilla until the 1970s. The unique taste that distinguishes the current version of Sarsi from other sarsaparilla-based soft drinks is attributed to the sugar substitute [[saccharin]], although its "regular" formula contains [[high-fructose corn syrup]] or cane sugar.

===Singapore===
In Singapore, F&N Sarsi (originally branded as Sarsi) is a brand name for a sarsaparilla drink manufactured by the Singaporean company [[Fraser and Neave|F&N Group]] (Fraser and Neave). It is unrelated to the brand established in the Philippines.

==Sarsae (brand)==
===Mainland China===
[[File:Bottle of Asia Sarsae.jpg|thumb|upright|A bottle of Asia Sarsae sold in [[Guangzhou]], [[Guangdong]], China]]

In mainland China, the drink's introduction can be traced back to the 1920s, when [[AS Watson]] began producing its sarsaparilla drink in Shanghai and other Chinese cities. In the 1940s, Li Zhiyang (李智扬), Li Guanling (李冠玲), Huang Youtong (黄油桶), Liang Hanqi (梁汉奇) and Wang Zhensan (王震山) were among eleven people who had worked in Watson's Canton and founded Asian Waters in Guangzhou to continue producing Sarsae there and in other mainland Chinese locations.<ref>{{cite news|author=Judy|title=亚洲（汽水）|url=https://news.dayoo.com/guangzhou/120336/120341/201208/15/120341_25631936.htm|access-date=15 August 2012|newspaper=Guangzhou Daily}} {{dead link|date=November 2017}}</ref>

[[Asia (soft drink brand)|Asia Sarsae]] (亚洲沙示) is now produced by [[Xiangxue Pharmaceutical]].

===Hong Kong===
In Hong Kong, Sarsae (沙示) is the most popular brand of sarsaparilla drink. It is manufactured and distributed by the [[A.S. Watson Group|A. S. Watson Group]], which pioneered in carbonated beverages in Hong Kong.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://www.hutchison-whampoa.com/upload/en/about/journal/Sphere17-Then_and_Now_E.pdf|title=Thirst Quenchers|page=32|magazine=Sphere|access-date=29 May 2023}}</ref> The drink was the central [[plot device]] of a 1985 film called ''It's a Drink, It's a Bomb'' (starring [[George Lam]], [[John Sham]] and [[Maggie Cheung]]), about a [[hand grenade]] disguised as a Sarsae cola, detonated by releasing its [[Drink can|ringpull]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lovehkfilm.com/reviews/its_a_drink.htm|title=It's a Drink, It's a Bomb (1985)|access-date=1 April 2017}}</ref>

Shooter (drink):
{{short description|Small serving of alcohol}}
{{refimprove|date=November 2012}}
[[File:Cocktail B52.jpg|thumb|right|A [[B-52 (cocktail)|B-52 shot]] served in a [[shot glass]]]]
[[File:Sake oyster shooter.jpg|thumb|A [[sake]] oyster shot]]

A '''shot''' (sometimes '''shooter''') is a small serving of [[Distilled beverage|spirits]] or a [[mixed drink]] (usually about {{convert|1.0|-|1.5|USoz|ml|disp=or}}), typically consumed quickly, often in a single gulp. It is common to serve a shot as a side to a larger drink.<ref name="DeGroff 2002">{{Cite book |title=The craft of the cocktail : everything you need to know to be a master bartender, with 500 recipes |last=DeGroff |first=Dale |date=2002 |publisher=Clarkson Potter/Publishers |isbn=9780307762276 |edition=1st |location=New York |oclc=669067001}}</ref>

Shots can be shaken, stirred, blended, layered, or simply poured. [[Shot glass]]es or [[Wine glass#Sherry glass|sherry glass]]es are the usual [[List of glassware#Drinkware|drinkware]] in which shots are served. They are most commonly served at [[Bar (establishment)|bars]], and some [[bartender]]s have their own signature shot.

The ingredients of shots vary from bartender to bartender and from region to region. Two shots can have the same name but different ingredients, resulting in two very different tastes.

Cerasus |species = cerasus |authority = [[L.]] 1753 |synonyms = {{Collapsible list |{{Plainlist | style = margin-left: 1em; text-indent: -1em; | * ''Cerasus acida'' (Ehrh.) Borkh. * ''Cerasus austera'' (L.) Borkh. * ''Cerasus austera'' (L.) M.Roem. * ''Cerasus collina'' Lej. & Courtois * ''Cerasus fruticosa'' Pall. * ''Cerasus vulgaris'' Mill. * ''Druparia cerasus'' (L.) Gaudin * ''Prunus recta'' (Liegel) K.Koch * ''Prunus semperflorens'' Ehrh. }} }} |synonyms_ref = {{cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/rjp-696|title=The Plant List: A Working List of All Plant Species |access-date=January 27, 2014}} }} '''''Prunus cerasus''''' ('''sour cherry''',{{PLANTS|id=PRCE|taxon=Prunus cerasus|access-date=14 October 2015}} '''tart cherry''', or '''dwarf cherry'''){{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}} is an Old World species of ''[[Prunus]]'' in the subgenus ''[[Prunus subg. Cerasus|Cerasus]]'' ([[cherries]]). It has two main groups of [[cultivar]]s: the dark-red [[Morello cherry]] and the lighter-red '''Amarelle cherry'''. The sour pulp is edible. ==Description== The tree is smaller than the sweet cherry (growing to a height of 4–10 m), has twiggy branches, and its crimson-to-near-black cherries are borne upon shorter stalks. It is closely related to the sweet cherry (''[[Prunus avium]]''), but has a [[fruit]] that is more [[acid]]ic. Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 17.4 days, and always bears 1 seed per fruit. Fruits average 84.9% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 39.7% [[carbohydrate]]s and 1.0% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}} ==Taxonomy== [[File:Illustration Prunus cerasus0.jpg|thumb|Illustration of Morello cherry]] [[File:Frühling blühender Kirschenbaum.jpg|thumb|A blooming sour cherry tree]] ''Prunus cerasus'', a [[tetraploid]] with 2n=32 chromosomes, is thought to have originated as a natural hybrid between ''[[Prunus avium]]'' and ''[[Prunus fruticosa]]'' in the [[Iranian Plateau]] or Eastern Europe where the two species come into contact. ''[[Prunus fruticosa]]'' is believed to have provided its smaller size and sour tasting fruit. The hybrids then stabilized and interbred to form a new, distinct species.{{cite journal|last=Stocks | first=Christopher | title=Britain's forgotten fruits | journal=Flora | volume=1 | pages=1–200 |date=2009 }} There are two main varieties (groups of [[cultivar]]s) of the sour cherry: the dark-red Morello cherry and the lighter-red Amarelle cherry.''Webster's New International Dictionary of the English Language''. Springfield, Massachusetts: G. & C. Merriam Co., 1913. See ''amarelle'' at p. 67. ==Distribution and habitat== It is distributed in much of [[Europe]], [[North Africa]] and [[West Asia]]. There are likely no truly wild occurrences. However, particularly the subspecies ''acida'' easily escapes cultivation and is naturalized throughout the growing area.{{Cite web | title=Portraits der im Capitulare de Villis aufgelisteten Pflanzen | url=https://biozac.de/biozac/capvil/Cvcerasu.htm | access-date=2025-08-08 | website=biozac.de}} == Cultivation == Cultivated sour cherries were selected from wild specimens of ''Prunus cerasus'' from around the [[Caspian Sea|Caspian]] and [[Black Sea]]s, and were known to the [[Greece|Greek]]s in 300 BC. They were also used by [[Persia]]ns and the [[Roman Empire|Romans]] who introduced them into [[Great Britain|Britain]] long before the 1st century AD.{{Citation needed|date=November 2022|reason= the Romans only arrived in Britain in the 1st century AD, so this is not possible?}} As early as the 12th Century, a Morello type sour cherry was grown in the Schaerbeek region of Belgium.https://www.beercity.brussels/home/50-objects-schaarbeekse-kriek-schaerbeekse Schaerbeek cherries were devastated by the Napoleonic and World Wars. Today there are efforts to reestablish Schaerbeek sour cherries, a defining component of [[Kriek lambic]] beer culture in Belgium recognized by UNESCO in 2016 as an "Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity." Although a "Morello type," Schaerbeek cherries are distinctive in that they are ovate on the horizontal axis, a deeper burgundy color when ripe, have a lower chill requirement to set fruit, and have a distinctive cinnamon aroma and flavor.https://lyonspeak.com/our-beers/ In England, sour cherry cultivation was popularized in the 16th century in the time of [[Henry VIII]]. They became a common crop amongst Kentish growers, and by 1640 over two dozen named [[cultivar]]s were recorded.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Before the [[Second World War]] there were more than fifty cultivars of sour cherry in cultivation in England; today, however, few are grown commercially, and despite the continuation of named cultivars such as 'Kentish Red', 'Amarelles', 'Griottes' and 'Flemish', only the generic Morello is offered by most nurseries. This is a late-flowering variety, and thus misses more frosts than its sweet counterpart and is therefore a more reliable cropper. The Morello cherry ripens in mid to late summer, toward the end of August in southern England. It is self-fertile, and would be a good [[pollenizer]] for other varieties if it did not flower so late in the season.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Sour cherries require similar cultivation conditions to [[pear]]s, that is, they prefer a rich, well-drained, moist [[soil]], although they demand more [[nitrogen]] and [[water]] than sweet cherries. Trees will do badly if waterlogged, but have greater tolerance of poor drainage than sweet varieties. As with sweet cherries, Morellos are traditionally cultivated by budding onto strong growing rootstocks, which produce trees too large for most gardens, although newer dwarfing rootstocks such as ''Colt'' and ''Gisella'' are now available. During spring, flowers should be protected, and trees weeded, mulched and sprayed with natural seaweed solution. This is also the time when any required [[pruning]] should be carried out (note that cherries should not be pruned during the dormant winter months). Morello cherry trees fruit on younger wood than sweet varieties, and thus can be pruned harder. They are usually grown as standards, but can be fan trained, cropping well even on cold walls, or grown as low bushes. Sour cherries suffer fewer pests and diseases than sweet cherries, although they are prone to heavy fruit losses from [[bird]]s. In summer, fruit should be protected with netting. When harvesting fruit, they should be cut from the tree rather than risking damage by pulling the stalks.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Unlike most sweet cherry varieties, sour cherries are [[self-fertile]] or self-[[pollenizer|pollenizing]]. Two implications of this are that seeds generally run true to the cultivar, and that much smaller [[pollinator]] populations are needed because pollen only has to be moved within individual flowers. In areas where pollinators are scarce, growers find that [[pollination management|stocking beehives]] in orchards improves yields.{{Cite web |url=https://www.oakgov.com/msu/Documents/publications/oc0089_cherries.pdf |title=Growing cherries|publisher=Michigan State University, Extension-Oakland County|date=2012 |access-date=2016-11-01 |archive-date=2017-02-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202001035/https://www.oakgov.com/msu/Documents/publications/oc0089_cherries.pdf |url-status=dead }} {| class="wikitable" style="float:right; 13em; text-align:center;" |+ Sour cherry production
2022, in tonnes[[Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database|FAOSTAT]] of the [[United Nations]]{{cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/QC|title=Production of sour cherries in 2022; Pick lists by Crops/Regions/Production Quantity/Year|date=2024|publisher=United Nations, [[Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database]]|access-date=10 July 2024}}
 |- |{{RUS}} ||297,200 |- |{{POL}} ||183,800 |- |{{UKR}} ||180,240 |- |{{TUR}} ||176,770 |- |{{SRB}} ||164,446 |- |{{IRN}} ||134,055 |- |{{USA}} ||110,770 |- |'''World''' ||'''1,593,025''' |} ==Production== In 2022, world production of sour cherries was 1.6 million [[tonne]]s, led by [[Russia]] with 19% of the total. Other major producers were [[Poland]], [[Ukraine]], and [[Turkey]]. ==Uses== ===Culinary=== The sour pulp is edible.{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region |publisher=Knopf |year=1980 |isbn=0-394-50760-6 |location=New York |page=498}} Dried sour cherries are used in cooking including [[soup]]s, [[pork]] dishes, [[cake]]s, [[tart]]s, and [[pie]]s. They are also used to make a jam/fruit spread.{{cite journal |last1=Bozhuyuk |first1=Mehmet R. |title=Morphological and Biochemical Characterization of Wild Sour Cherry (Prunus cerasus L.) Germplasm |journal=Erwerbs - Obstbau |date=2022 |volume=64 |issue=3 |page=357-363 |doi=10.1007/s10341-022-00656-z|url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/morphological-biochemical-characterization-wild/docview/2702345526/se-2|url-access=subscription }} Sour cherries are particularly common in Turkey, especially in the form of ''vişne suyu'' (sour cherry nectar), a widely consumed beverage, and ''vişne reçeli'' (sour cherry jam), often eaten as part of a traditional breakfast or mixed into plain [[yoghurt]].{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Sour cherries or sour cherry [[syrup]] are used in [[liqueur]]s and [[drinks]], such as the Romanian [[vișinată]] or the Portuguese [[ginjinha]]. In [[Iran]], [[Turkey]], [[Greece]] and [[Cyprus]], sour cherries are prized for making [[spoon sweets]] by slowly boiling pitted sour cherries and sugar; the syrup thereof is used for ''sharbat-e Albalou'', ''vişne şurubu'' or ''vyssináda'', a beverage made by diluting the syrup with ice-cold water. A particular use of sour cherries is in the production of [[kriek lambic]], a cherry-flavored variety of a naturally [[fermented]] [[beer]] made in Belgium.{{Cite book | last = Jackson | first = Michael | title = The Simon Schuster Pocket Guide to Beer | publisher = Simon and Schuster | date = 1997 | page = 80 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=p24Ktw6BDVoC&pg=PA80 | isbn = 978-0-684-84381-0}}{{Cite web|date=28 September 2021|title=Guinda|url=https://frutasdelbosque.org/guinda/|website=Frutasdelbosque.org|language=es}} In Germany and Austria, sour cherries are used for desserts such as the [[donauwelle]]. [[Cherry bounce]] is made by infusing sour cherries in old French brandy. ==Gallery== File:SourcherryYield.png|Worldwide sour cherry production, 2024 File:Ripe sour cherries on a branch.jpg|Ripe sour cherries, Hungary File:Black Che.jpg|Ripe sour cherries and their leaves, Iran File:Owoce Wiśnia.jpg|Sour cherries File:Kriek Beer 1.jpg|[[Kriek lambic]] is infused with sour cherries. ==Cultivars== Some notable cultivars are: * [[Morello cherry|Morello]] * [[Ostheim cherry]] * [[Stevnsbær]] * [[Pándy meggy]] * [[Amarena cherry]] (''Prunus cerasus'' var. ''amarena'') * [[Marasca cherry]] (''Prunus cerasus'' var. ''marasca'') * [[Griotte de Kleparow]] * [[Balaton cherry]] * [[Montmorency cherry]] * [[North Star cherry]], a [[dwarfing|dwarf]] variety For commercial production, "Morello" is the main cultivar grown in Central Europe, while the "Montmorency" variety is the most common in the US.José Quero-García, Amy Iezzoni, Gregorio López-Ortega, Cameron Peace, Mathieu Fouché, Elisabeth Dirlewanger, Mirko Schuster, 2019: Advances and challenges in cherry breeding, DOI 10.19103/AS.2018.0040.17 [[Kütahya cherry|Kütahya]] is the most important in Turkey, [[Oblačinska]] in Serbia. ==See also== * [[Fruit tree propagation]] * [[Ginjinha]], a Portuguese liqueur made from sour cherries * [[Kirsch]] * [[Kriek]], a traditional Belgian beer made with sour cherries * [[Pruning fruit trees]] * [[Sour cherry soup]] * ''[[Syzygium corynanthum]]'', an Australian [[rainforest]] tree also known as the sour cherry * [[Vișinată]], a Romanian liqueur made with sour cherries (''vișina'' in Romanian) ==References== {{Reflist}} ==Bibliography== * {{cite journal |date=1991 |first1=Johan |last1=Ehrlén |first2=Ove |last2=Eriksson |title=Phenological variation in fruit characteristics in vertebrate-dispersed plants |pages=463–470 |doi=10.1007/BF00318311 |journal=Oecologia |issn=0029-8549 |volume=86 |issue=4}} ==External links== {{commons category}} * {{PFAF|Prunus cerasus}} * {{PFAF|Prunus cerasus austera}} * {{PFAF|Prunus cerasus caproniana}} * {{PFAF|Prunus cerasus frutescens}} * {{PFAF|Prunus cerasus marasca}} {{Cherries}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q131517}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Cherries]] [[Category:Flora of Europe]] [[Category:Flora of Western Asia]] [[Category:Flora of the Caucasus]] [[Category:Plants described in 1753]] [[Category:Prunus|cerasus]] [[Category:Sour cherries]] [[Category:Sour fruits|Sour cherry (''Prunus cerasus'')]] [[Category:Fruit trees]] [[Category:Botanical taxa named by Carl Linnaeus]]

However, particularly the subspecies ''acida'' easily escapes cultivation and is naturalized throughout the growing area.{{Cite web | title=Portraits der im Capitulare de Villis aufgelisteten Pflanzen | url=https://biozac.de/biozac/capvil/Cvcerasu.htm | access-date=2025-08-08 | website=biozac.de}} == Cultivation == Cultivated sour cherries were selected from wild specimens of ''Prunus cerasus'' from around the [[Caspian Sea|Caspian]] and [[Black Sea]]s, and were known to the [[Greece|Greek]]s in 300 BC. They were also used by [[Persia]]ns and the [[Roman Empire|Romans]] who introduced them into [[Great Britain|Britain]] long before the 1st century AD.{{Citation needed|date=November 2022|reason= the Romans only arrived in Britain in the 1st century AD, so this is not possible?}} As early as the 12th Century, a Morello type sour cherry was grown in the Schaerbeek region of Belgium.https://www.beercity.brussels/home/50-objects-schaarbeekse-kriek-schaerbeekse Schaerbeek cherries were devastated by the Napoleonic and World Wars. Today there are efforts to reestablish Schaerbeek sour cherries, a defining component of [[Kriek lambic]] beer culture in Belgium recognized by UNESCO in 2016 as an "Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity." Although a "Morello type," Schaerbeek cherries are distinctive in that they are ovate on the horizontal axis, a deeper burgundy color when ripe, have a lower chill requirement to set fruit, and have a distinctive cinnamon aroma and flavor.https://lyonspeak.com/our-beers/ In England, sour cherry cultivation was popularized in the 16th century in the time of [[Henry VIII]]. They became a common crop amongst Kentish growers, and by 1640 over two dozen named [[cultivar]]s were recorded.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Before the [[Second World War]] there were more than fifty cultivars of sour cherry in cultivation in England; today, however, few are grown commercially, and despite the continuation of named cultivars such as 'Kentish Red', 'Amarelles', 'Griottes' and 'Flemish', only the generic Morello is offered by most nurseries. This is a late-flowering variety, and thus misses more frosts than its sweet counterpart and is therefore a more reliable cropper. The Morello cherry ripens in mid to late summer, toward the end of August in southern England. It is self-fertile, and would be a good [[pollenizer]] for other varieties if it did not flower so late in the season.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Sour cherries require similar cultivation conditions to [[pear]]s, that is, they prefer a rich, well-drained, moist [[soil]], although they demand more [[nitrogen]] and [[water]] than sweet cherries. Trees will do badly if waterlogged, but have greater tolerance of poor drainage than sweet varieties. As with sweet cherries, Morellos are traditionally cultivated by budding onto strong growing rootstocks, which produce trees too large for most gardens, although newer dwarfing rootstocks such as ''Colt'' and ''Gisella'' are now available. During spring, flowers should be protected, and trees weeded, mulched and sprayed with natural seaweed solution. This is also the time when any required [[pruning]] should be carried out (note that cherries should not be pruned during the dormant winter months). Morello cherry trees fruit on younger wood than sweet varieties, and thus can be pruned harder. They are usually grown as standards, but can be fan trained, cropping well even on cold walls, or grown as low bushes. Sour cherries suffer fewer pests and diseases than sweet cherries, although they are prone to heavy fruit losses from [[bird]]s. In summer, fruit should be protected with netting. When harvesting fruit, they should be cut from the tree rather than risking damage by pulling the stalks.{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Unlike most sweet cherry varieties, sour cherries are [[self-fertile]] or self-[[pollenizer|pollenizing]]. Two implications of this are that seeds generally run true to the cultivar, and that much smaller [[pollinator]] populations are needed because pollen only has to be moved within individual flowers. In areas where pollinators are scarce, growers find that [[pollination management|stocking beehives]] in orchards improves yields.{{Cite web |url=https://www.oakgov.com/msu/Documents/publications/oc0089_cherries.pdf |title=Growing cherries|publisher=Michigan State University, Extension-Oakland County|date=2012 |access-date=2016-11-01 |archive-date=2017-02-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202001035/https://www.oakgov.com/msu/Documents/publications/oc0089_cherries.pdf |url-status=dead }} {| class="wikitable" style="float:right; 13em; text-align:center;" |+ Sour cherry production
2022, in tonnes[[Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database|FAOSTAT]] of the [[United Nations]]{{cite web|url=http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#data/QC|title=Production of sour cherries in 2022; Pick lists by Crops/Regions/Production Quantity/Year|date=2024|publisher=United Nations, [[Food and Agriculture Organization Corporate Statistical Database]]|access-date=10 July 2024}}

Other major producers were [[Poland]], [[Ukraine]], and [[Turkey]]. ==Uses== ===Culinary=== The sour pulp is edible.{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region |publisher=Knopf |year=1980 |isbn=0-394-50760-6 |location=New York |page=498}} Dried sour cherries are used in cooking including [[soup]]s, [[pork]] dishes, [[cake]]s, [[tart]]s, and [[pie]]s. They are also used to make a jam/fruit spread.{{cite journal |last1=Bozhuyuk |first1=Mehmet R. |title=Morphological and Biochemical Characterization of Wild Sour Cherry (Prunus cerasus L.) Germplasm |journal=Erwerbs - Obstbau |date=2022 |volume=64 |issue=3 |page=357-363 |doi=10.1007/s10341-022-00656-z|url=https://www.proquest.com/scholarly-journals/morphological-biochemical-characterization-wild/docview/2702345526/se-2|url-access=subscription }} Sour cherries are particularly common in Turkey, especially in the form of ''vişne suyu'' (sour cherry nectar), a widely consumed beverage, and ''vişne reçeli'' (sour cherry jam), often eaten as part of a traditional breakfast or mixed into plain [[yoghurt]].{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} Sour cherries or sour cherry [[syrup]] are used in [[liqueur]]s and [[drinks]], such as the Romanian [[vișinată]] or the Portuguese [[ginjinha]]. In [[Iran]], [[Turkey]], [[Greece]] and [[Cyprus]], sour cherries are prized for making [[spoon sweets]] by slowly boiling pitted sour cherries and sugar; the syrup thereof is used for ''sharbat-e Albalou'', ''vişne şurubu'' or ''vyssináda'', a beverage made by diluting the syrup with ice-cold water. A particular use of sour cherries is in the production of [[kriek lambic]], a cherry-flavored variety of a naturally [[fermented]] [[beer]] made in Belgium.{{Cite book | last = Jackson | first = Michael | title = The Simon Schuster Pocket Guide to Beer | publisher = Simon and Schuster | date = 1997 | page = 80 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=p24Ktw6BDVoC&pg=PA80 | isbn = 978-0-684-84381-0}}{{Cite web|date=28 September 2021|title=Guinda|url=https://frutasdelbosque.org/guinda/|website=Frutasdelbosque.org|language=es}} In Germany and Austria, sour cherries are used for desserts such as the [[donauwelle]]. [[Cherry bounce]] is made by infusing sour cherries in old French brandy. ==Gallery== File:SourcherryYield.png|Worldwide sour cherry production, 2024 File:Ripe sour cherries on a branch.jpg|Ripe sour cherries, Hungary File:Black Che.jpg|Ripe sour cherries and their leaves, Iran File:Owoce Wiśnia.jpg|Sour cherries File:Kriek Beer 1.jpg|[[Kriek lambic]] is infused with sour cherries. ==Cultivars== Some notable cultivars are: * [[Morello cherry|Morello]] * [[Ostheim cherry]] * [[Stevnsbær]] * [[Pándy meggy]] * [[Amarena cherry]] (''Prunus cerasus'' var. U-boot (cocktail):
{{short description|Beer cocktail made by dropping a shot of vodka into a glass of beer}}
{{About|the cocktail|the submarine type also known as a U-boot|U-boat|the boot loader|Das U-Boot}}

[[File:U-Boot_mit_Jägermeister_in_Bierglas.jpg|thumb|U-Boot cocktail, made of beer and a shot of Jägermeister, in a beer glass]]
A '''U-boot''' is a [[beer cocktail]] that is made by placing a shot of [[vodka]] into a glass of [[beer]], typically a [[lager]].<ref>[http://www.football-italia.net/2006/poland.html Info about the Poland national football team, see the "''Perfect Night watching, What to drink…''" section]</ref><ref>[http://kuchnia.o2.pl/przepisy/obiekt_int.php?id_p=834 Recipe for an U-boot/U-boat drink (in Polish)]</ref>  It is popular in [[Germany]], [[Poland]], [[North Macedonia]], and [[Flanders]]. In Germany, the liquor [[korn (liquor)|korn]] is sometimes used instead, while in Flanders and the [[Netherlands]], ''[[jenever#Old and young|jonge jenever]]'' is preferred.

It is called a U-boot (German abbreviation of ''Unterseeboot'', "[[submarine]]") because the [[shot glass]] of vodka sinks to the bottom of the glass of beer.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=U-Boot {{!}} Local Cocktail From Germany|url=https://www.tasteatlas.com/u-boot|access-date=2021-10-08|website=www.tasteatlas.com}}</ref> The shot glass then "surfaces" when the cocktail is drunk.<ref name=":0" />

== Preparation ==
Place a shot glass on upside down glass and fill it with vodka.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=U-Boat|url=https://tipsybartender.com/recipe/u-boat|access-date=2021-10-08|website=tipsybartender.com|language=en}}</ref> Place a pint glass over the two glasses so it sits against the shot glass and flip them over. Fill the pint glass with lager and as the drink is consumed the vodka will leak into drink.<ref name=":1" />

== Other names and variations ==
In Flanders and the Netherlands, it is called a "Duikboot", literally translated "Submarine". It is seen as a variant on the ''kopstoot'' (lit. "headbutt") in the Netherlands. The ''kopstoot'' is a shot of jenever followed by a beer as a chaser.

In North Macedonia it is called "Подморница" - "Podmornica", literally translated "Submarine". It uses tequila which is dropped into a big pint.

In southern Germany, U-boot is usually served as a combination of [[Fanta]] and [[cognac]] instead of beer and vodka.

In Mexico, it is called "Submarino", Spanish for "Submarine". Instead of vodka, it uses tequila, and the shot glass must be left inverted inside the beer glass.

In Russia, it is most often called "Глубинная бомба", Russian for "Depth charge". Usually any cocktail, mixing vodka and beer called in Russia "Ёрш", ([[Yorsh]]) literally meaning a wire brush. It is also rarely called "Водолаз" - "Vodolaz", literally translated as "Diver".

In [[Sorbs|Sorbia]], vodka and orange juice is used.

In Brazil, it is called "Submarino", Portuguese for "Submarine". In the south, where it is more easily found, it is common practice to use [[steinhäger]] instead of vodka.

In Sweden, it is called "Ubåt", Swedish for "Submarine". [[Jägermeister]] is used instead of vodka.

In Greece, it is called "υποβρύχιο", Greek for "Submarine". Served as a [[shot glass]] of Jack Daniels sink into the bottom of a short glass of beer.

The drink's launch in June 1994 proved to be a disaster following reports of the drink fermenting on store shelves, leading to Britvic re-calling over a million bottles of the product.{{cite web|author= |url=http://www.marketingweek.co.uk/still-tango-alive-and-well-in-dorking/2029490.article |title=Still Tango alive and well in Dorking |website=Marketing Week |date=1995-09-08 |access-date=2024-09-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150723125524/http://www.marketingweek.com/1995/09/08/still-tango-alive-and-well-in-dorking/ |archive-date=2015-07-23 |url-status=dead |url-access=registration |language=en}} The drink was relaunched in September 1995, with an advertising campaign focusing on a single newsagent in [[Dorking]], [[Surrey]]. A fellow television advertising campaign in 1996 showcased the failed attempt at the drink's launch.{{Cite web |title=THIS WEEK: Britvic owns up over Still Tango |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/week-britvic-owns-tango/51101 |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}} and in May 1996, Apple, Lemon and Blackcurrant variants were introduced.{{Cite web |title=THIS WEEK: New Tango launched |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/week-new-tango-launched/61416 |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=1997-10-31 |title=Britvic banks on being different |url=https://www.packworld.com/machinery/primary-packaging/article/13329905/britvic-banks-on-being-different |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Packaging World |language=en-us}} ===Tango Strange Soda=== '''Tango Strange Soda''' was a sub-brand that consisted of juice and milk-based drinks, available in "Strange Strawberry" and "Odd Orange" flavours and marketed towards children and teenagers. The drink was put into development in 2000 and was initially announced as '''Freekin' Soda''' in late-2002{{Cite web |title=Britvic to launch Freekin' Soda for teenage market. |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/britvic-launch-freekin-soda-teenage-market/163928 |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}} for a release within the start of 2003, but was pulled following concerns about the brand's name being unsuitable for the brand's target audience, and the word "Freekin" being linked as a milder alternative to a strong [[profanity]], which would have made the drink unsuitable to be marketed on children's television channels at any time or any networks prior to the [[Watershed (broadcasting)|9 pm Watershed]].{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2003-01-16 |title=Britvic forced to pull new brand Freekin' Soda over swearword link |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/britvic-forced-to-pull-new-brand-freekin-soda-over-swearword-link/ |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}} The drink was eventually introduced under the modified name of '''Freekee Soda''' in February 2003;{{Cite web |last= |title=Britvic launches fizzy drink alternative |url=https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2003/01/27/Britvic-launches-fizzy-drink-alternative |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=nutraingredients.com |date=27 January 2003 |language=en-GB}} but suffered from low sales throughout its run.{{Cite web |last= |title=Britvic shoots wide of the mark with Freekee Soda |url=https://www.beveragedaily.com/Article/2003/07/02/Britvic-shoots-wide-of-the-mark-with-Freekee-Soda |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=beveragedaily.com |date=July 2003 |language=en-GB}} Due to a legal complaint over the trademark of the brand name and the initial low sales, it was relaunched under the Tango brand as '''Tango Strange Soda''' in September 2003.{{Cite web |last= |title=Freekee is tango'd |url=https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/freekee-is-tangod/87636.article |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=The Grocer |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=Freekee Soda in rebranding after legal challenge |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/freekee-soda-rebranding-legal-challenge/187740 |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}} Despite this move and a reduction of pricing, the drink continued to suffer from very low sales until Britvic announced the product's discontinuation in January 2004.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2004-01-22 |title=Britvic axes troubled Tango Strange Soda |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/britvic-axes-troubled-tango-strange-soda/ |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}} ===Tango Ice Blast=== '''Tango Ice Blast''' is a [[slushie]] drink originally introduced in 2004. It is currently produced by Frozen Brothers (previously by [[Slush Puppie]]), under license from Britvic and has its own website separate from Tango, at lovetangoiceblast.com.{{Cite web |title=Flavours |url=https://www.lovetangoiceblast.com/flavours |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Tango Ice Blast |language=en-US}} The same company also produces [[Fanta]] Frozen, [[Coca-Cola]] Frozen and Slushy Jack's products.{{Cite web |title=About |url=https://www.frozenfoundation.org/about |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240627114047/https://www.frozenfoundation.org/about |archive-date=2024-06-27 |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Frozen Foundation |language=en-GB}} As of 2024, its core range of flavours are: Blue Raspberry, Strawberry and Kiwi, Lemon, Cherry, Orange, and Bubblegum. Over the years, Tango Ice Blast has released many seasonal limited edition flavours. In 2015 these consisted of Citrus, Tropical, and Strawberry & Kiwi flavours.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2015-05-14 |title=Tango launches summer 'Flavour Festival' |url=https://www.talkingretail.com/products-news/frozen/tango-launches-summer-flavour-festival-14-05-2015/ |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Talking Retail |language=en}} In 2016 they were Lemon Fizz, Pina Coco'lada, Pineapple, and Punchy Peach and Passionfruit.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2016-06-20 |title=Tango Ice Blast gets four summer flavours |url=https://www.talkingretail.com/products-news/frozen/tango-ice-blast-gets-four-summer-flavours-20-06-2016/ |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Talking Retail |language=en}} Other flavours have included Dark Cherry in 2015 (coincided with the release of ''[[Star Wars: The Last Jedi]]''), Sour Watermelon in 2018, Peach & Pomegranate in 2019, and Bubblegum in 2023 (released to promote ''[[Wonka (2023 film)|Wonka]]'').{{Cite web |date=2023-12-09 |title=Bolton cinema offering free treat as Wonka hits the big screen |url=https://www.theboltonnews.co.uk/news/23977146.bolton-vue-offers-bubblegum-tango-ice-blast-wonka-arrives/ |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=The Bolton News |language=en}} ===Tango Clear=== '''Tango Clear''' was a brand of no-calorie clear drinks introduced in April 2005. It was another attempt by Britvic to increase sales of the Tango brand and was aimed at the young female market.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2005-02-17 |title=Britvic aims new Tango variant at older market |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/britvic-aims-new-tango-variant-at-older-market/ |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}}{{Cite web |last= |title=Tango turns on health appeal |url=https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/tango-turns-on-health-appeal/100945.article |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=The Grocer |language=en}} The Drink was initially introduced in Apple and Watermelon and Lemon and Kiwi flavours, and in 2006, the brand was expanded with two more flavours - Raspberry and White Cranberry, and Orange.{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2006-04-06 |title=Tango Clear plans two new flavours |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/tango-clear-plans-two-new-flavours/ |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}} Tango Clear was discontinued in September 2007, after Britvic announced that they would strictly focus the Tango brand on its core flavours.{{Cite web |title=Tango to axe Clear variant |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/tango-axe-clear-variant/735171 |access-date=2024-02-12 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}} === Tango Blast === '''Tango Blast''' is a brand of drinks introduced in initially as a limited edition in April 2024. Inspired by Tango Ice Blast, Tango Blast consists of Raspberry and Cherry flavours in a ready to drink format instead of slushies.{{Cite web |title=Tango unveils iconic Ice Blast flavours in on-the-go format |url=https://www.britvic.com/our-news/performance/tango-unveils-iconic-ice-blast-flavours-in-on-the-go-format/ |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Britvic Limited |language=en-GB}} In April 2025, Britvic announced that the drink will return for another limited run.{{Cite web |title=Tango Blast returns for limited time |url=https://www.betterretailing.com/br/product-news/tango-blast-returns-for-limited-time/ |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Better Retailing |language=en-GB}} ===Other products=== As well as drinks, the brand have also sold chocolate bars, chewy ball sweets and car air fresheners.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} In October 2000, [[Cadbury]] announced they would team up with Britvic to create a limited edition Tango Orange-flavoured [[Crunchie]].{{cite web|author= |url=http://www.marketingweek.co.uk/home/it-takes-two-fun-brands-to-tango/2050427.article |title=It takes two fun brands to Tango |website=Marketing Week |date=2000-10-05 |access-date=2024-09-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121010115321/http://www.marketingweek.co.uk/home/it-takes-two-fun-brands-to-tango/2050427.article |archive-date=2012-10-10 |url-status=dead}} In July 2011, Turbo Tango, when launched, was described as the "first aerosol drink".{{Cite web |last=Brooks |first=Josh |date=2011-06-27 |title=Britvic pumps up Tango in drinks aerosol 'world first' |url=https://www.packagingnews.co.uk/news/britvic-pumps-up-tango-in-drinks-aerosol-world-first-27-06-2011 |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Packaging News |language=en}} During 2011, several flavours of Chew Stick and Chewy Bonbons were introduced. In January 2013, a Tango branded [[shower gel]] was launched.{{Cite web |title=Sector Insight: carbonated soft drinks |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/sector-insight-carbonated-soft-drinks/1145167?utm_source=website&utm_medium=social |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}} A Tango branded [[Antibacterial soap|hand soap]] was also launched around the same time. == Sponsorships == Tango sponsored the television show ''[[The Word (TV series)|The Word]]'' in 1994{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}} and the [[Underage Festival]] in 2010.{{Cite web |last=Fernandez |first=Joe |date=2012-01-01 |title=Tango unveils music-themed £2.5m promotion |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/tango-unveils-music-themed-2-5m-promotion/ |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}} The [[Launch Pad (Pleasure Beach Resort)|Launch Pad]] ride was previously sponsored by Tango and therefore renamed to the "Tango Ice Blast". Tango sponsored the public Christmas Lights in [[London]] in 1998. However there was criticism from the public that the resulting lights display was too commercial.{{Cite web |last=Week |first=Marketing |date=1999-02-11 |title=Public outcry threatens Xmas lights sponsorship |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/public-outcry-threatens-xmas-lights-sponsorship/ |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=BBC News {{!}} Talking Politics {{!}} Have you seen the lights? |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/227237.stm |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=news.bbc.co.uk}} == Marketing and advertisement == Historically, slogans have included "You Taste the Tang in Tango Every Sparkling Sip You Take" in the 1960s and "The Whole Fruit" in the late 1980s.{{Citation needed|date=July 2013}} During August 1999, Tango teamed up with the newspapers ''[[Daily Mail]]'' and ''[[Daily Record (Scotland)|Daily Record]]'' to extend their summer peak sales period in a campaign called "Tango Time". The main thread of the campaign activity was a competition where a time of day is printed on the base of cans of Tango. The winning 'Tango Time' was published in the Daily Mirror and Daily Record and winners invited to call a prize claim line. The newspaper adverts were trailed by branding on the front page, including a free offer for a bottle of Tango. The adverts containing the winning 'Tango Time' ran for twenty six days in August 1999.{{cite web |date=2009-02-23 |title=NMA | Case Studies | Tango team-up with Mirror Group newspapers to extend their peak sales period |url=http://www.nmauk.co.uk/nma/do/live/caseStudy?caseStudyModel=1275 |access-date=2011-08-13 |publisher=Nmauk.co.uk}} Tango Apple has often been subject to experimental advertising including an "Apple Tango Calendar" given free in June 1996 with the ''[[Daily Star (United Kingdom)|Daily Star]]''{{cite web |last=Green |first=Harriet |date=1996-06-07 |title=NEWS: HHCL unveils Tango 'pin-up' |url=http://web3.local.www.brandrepublic.com/news/20209/NEWS-HHCL-unveils-Tango--lsquopin-up-rsquo/?DCMP=ILC-SEARCH |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120328094702/http://web3.local.www.brandrepublic.com/news/20209/NEWS-HHCL-unveils-Tango--lsquopin-up-rsquo/?DCMP=ILC-SEARCH |archive-date=28 March 2012 |access-date=2024-09-18 |website=Brand Republic News}} and, in 2003, the "Big Drench Tour", a roadshow of a thirty foot tall apple shaped installation filled with water. Players must stand underneath and take part in a game of 'drench roulette' to win prizes.{{cite web |date=2003-10-24 |title=Tango pushes apple drink via Big Drench promotion |url=http://www.mad.co.uk/Main/Home/Articles/64879881393140b48248f8aba7c828a1/Tango-pushes-apple-drink-via-Big-Drench-promotion.html |access-date=2011-08-13 |publisher=Mad.co.uk}} In August 2009, a billboard campaign extolled the "weird and wonderful" side effects of drinking too much "Tango with added Tango Orange" (such as "Too much Tango made me suck a bull's udder" and "Too much Tango made me shave my Nan, 'innit.").{{cite web |title=Tango Hub |url=http://www.tango.co.uk/tangowithaddedtango/posters.aspx |access-date=28 August 2009}} The British press pointed out that the initials of "Tango With Added Tango" spelled the insult "[[twat]]" when read vertically, and this was later revealed to be intentional.{{cite web |date=2009-09-30 |title=New Tango launch attracts wrong kind of attention – Marketing News |url=http://www.utalkmarketing.com/pages/Article.aspx?ArticleID=14436&title=New%20Tango%20launch%20attracts%20wrong%20kind%20of%20attention |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717183154/http://www.utalkmarketing.com/pages/Article.aspx?ArticleID=14436&title=New%20Tango%20launch%20attracts%20wrong%20kind%20of%20attention |archive-date=17 July 2011 |access-date=2010-06-26 |publisher=UTalkMarketing}} The British advertising regulator Advertising Standards Authority ruled that the ad was not offensive, following a number of complaints particularly regarding the bull. === Television === Beginning in the late 1980s, [[surrealism]] was becoming a mainstream technique in advertising. Answering Tango's search for a new ad campaign, ad agency [[HHCL]] created the [[catchphrase]] "You know when you've been Tango'd". The campaign began in 1992 with the advert ''[[Orange Man (advertisement)|Orange Man]]''; it featured a man drinking Tango and immediately being slapped around the face by a portly man painted orange (Peter Geeves).{{cite book |last1=Spooner |first1=Catherine |title=Contemporary Gothic |date=February 2007 |publisher=Reaktion Books |isbn=978-1-86189-558-5 |page=122 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YmUyDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT122 |access-date=4 February 2021 |language=en}} The advert received widespread condemnation after a craze for "Tangoing" people swept the nation's playgrounds, and there were reports of children receiving serious injuries, or even being deafened by being slapped on the ears. Tango voluntarily replaced the "slapping" advert with an almost identical new version, where the orange clad person kisses the man instead of hitting him. The original version was ranked third in a list of "[[The 100 Greatest TV Ads]]", in a 2000 poll conducted by ''[[The Sunday Times (UK)|The Sunday Times]]'' and [[Channel 4]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.channel4.com/entertainment/greatest_ads/|title=The 100 Greatest TV Ads|year=2000|publisher=[[Channel 4]]|location=London|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010618095141/http://www.channel4.com/entertainment/greatest_ads/|archive-date=18 June 2001|url-status=dead|access-date=4 August 2019}} Most subsequent Tango advertisements have avoided showing violence, except for the advert from October 2004, "[[Pipes (advertisement)|Pipes]]", which showed a man rolling down a hill with concrete pipes, causing it to be banned,{{Cite news |date=2013-06-20 |title=Cannes Lions: Five controversial TV and internet ads |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2013/jun/20/cannes-lions-five-controversial-tv-internet-ads |access-date=2025-09-13 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} and the advert from March 1997, "Vote Orange Now", where the orange clad man made another appearance, slapping the advert's protagonist several times. This latter advert was featured in the first advert break on [[Channel 5 (UK)|Channel 5]].{{cite web|url=http://www.campaignlive.co.uk/news/63561/Britvic-doubles-Tango-ad-spend/?DCMP=ILC-SEARCH |title=Britvic doubles Tango ad spend | Advertising news | Campaign |publisher=Campaignlive.co.uk |date=1997-03-27 |access-date=2011-08-13}} In May 1994, Tango launched new TV ads for its Apple flavour Tango with seductive themes.{{Cite news |date=7 May 1994 |title=Tango goes hard core |work=[[Daily Mirror]] |pages=47}} In March 2000, an advert originally produced in 1998, which depicted a pre-fame [[James Corden]] being bullied for not drinking Tango, was banned because it was seen as encouraging the bullying of overweight children.{{cite web|url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Tango+advert+ditched+over+bully+fears.-a060845806 |title=Tango advert ditched over bully fears. – Free Online Library |publisher=Thefreelibrary.com |date=2000-03-04 |access-date=2013-09-02}}{{cite web|first=Cordelia |last=Brabbs |url=http://www.marketingmagazine.co.uk/news/66466/Britvic-stands-banned-Tango-ad/|title=Britvic stands by banned Tango ad|website=Marketing Week |date=2000-03-09|access-date=2024-09-18}}{{cite web|author=Belinda Archer |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2000/mar/10/tvandradio.television2 |title=Who are you? What the Tango ad says about you | From |work=The Guardian |date=2000-03-10 |access-date=2013-09-02}} The replacement was a satirically inoffensive advert, ''Drink Tango: It's Nice''.{{Cite web |last=Week |first=Marketing |date=2004-08-12 |title=In a PC world, all ads are being monitored |url=https://www.marketingweek.com/in-a-pc-world-all-ads-are-being-monitored/ |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=Marketing Week |language=en}} Later that year, as Tango Strange Soda launched, three ultimately unsuccessful advertisements for the drink (''Taste Buds'', ''Trainers'' and ''Classroom'') were aired featuring a man's "taste buddies" which are a group of young men behaving as the man's taste buds that vibrate rapidly when the man consumes Strange Soda. The "taste buddy" actors in the advertisements were shot as live action, with the actor standing on a moveable circular frame which was then manoeuvred via a handle to give the "vibrating" trembling effect for each of the "buddies" seen on screen.{{Cite web|url=http://www.4rfv.co.uk/industrynews.asp?id=22845|title = MPC get Tango Strange Soda 'taste buddies' going – UK Broadcast News | 25/11/2003}} In early 2006, Tango spoofed the famous [[Sony Bravia]] LCD TV commercial of bouncing balls recorded in San Francisco.{{Cite web |title=Sony ad gets Tango'd in Britvic campaign |url=https://www.thegrocer.co.uk/news/sony-ad-gets-tangod-in-britvic-campaign/110090.article |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=The Grocer |language=en}} Tango's commercial was set in [[Swansea]] and featured fruit instead of coloured balls, using the same production style and the same music track, and a parody of Sony's slogan turning it into 'Refreshment like no other'. In December 2008, Tango launched the "Save Tango" campaign.{{Cite news |last=Sweney |first=Mark |date=2008-12-03 |title='Save Tango' spoof video launched |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2008/dec/03/advertising-britvic |access-date=2025-09-13 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}} The Save Tango campaign resulted in an 8% increase in sales over 12 weeks. The 'Tanguru' TV campaign was launched in 2019, involving a fictional character called Tanguru solving awkward situations. Tango advertisements have sometimes featured phone numbers for viewers to call, although the phone numbers would typically appear too briefly on the screen for viewers to type in the number or write it down. Many of these advertisements incorporate a send-away prize, including a rubber doll or a clown horn (the Tango Horn). A notable exception was an advert which first premièred in 1993 for Still Tango disguised as a subvert falsely alerting people that the drink is unauthorised, and features a phone number for 'affected' viewers to call. ==== St George commercial ==== {{See also|St George (commercial)}} Blackcurrant Tango is notable for the multiple award-winning television commercial from 1997,{{Cite web|url=http://www.framestore-cfc.com/commercials/blackcurrant_tango/index.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070403042513/http://www.framestore-cfc.com/commercials/blackcurrant_tango/index.html|url-status=dead|title='St. George'|archivedate=3 April 2007}} [[St George (commercial)|St George]], which was used to promote it.{{Cite web |title=How Blackcurrant Tango created an advertising classic - and what creatives can learn 20 years later |url=https://www.campaignlive.co.uk/article/blackcurrant-tango-created-advertising-classic-creatives-learn-20-years-later/1447511?utm_source=website&utm_medium=social |access-date=2025-09-13 |website=www.campaignlive.co.uk |language=en}} For the launch of Blackcurrant Tango in 1996, [[HHCL]] produced the "[[St. George]]" television and cinema advertisement. In the advertisement, a member of Tango's customer service staff, Ray Gardner, provides a response to a letter of complaint about the flavour of Blackcurrant Tango he has received from Sebastien Loyes, a French exchange student. The letter prompts an increasingly [[jingoistic]] tirade during which Ray Gardner removes his suit to reveal bright purple boxing shorts. In one seemingly continuous take, he walks from his office, marches out of Tango's building, and is joined by a flag waving crowd as he enters a boxing ring. As the camera pulls back, the ring is revealed to be perched on the edge of the [[White Cliffs of Dover]]. As the camera circles, Gardner can be heard shouting, "Come on France, Europe, the world. I'll take you all on! I'm Ray Gardner. I drink Blackcurrant Tango. Come and get me!" whilst three [[Harrier jump jet]]s with purple landing lights hover in the background. The advertisement was notable for the use of digital editing to seamlessly merge a number of tracking shots, including the final transition from a sky camera to a helicopter shot. Ray Gardner later won the ITV ''Best Actor in a Commercial'' award for his performance. The commercial was voted the Best Long Commercial (1956–2001), by the United Kingdom's [[Film4]] television channel in June 2007.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} The song that appeared in the advertisement, "[[Don't You Want Me (Felix song)|Don't You Want Me]]" by [[Felix (musician)|Felix]], was rereleased with Tango branding.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} ==Recalls== On 17 June 1994, more than 1 million bottles of Still Tango, the still variant of the drink, was recalled after customers complained that it "tasted off" and caused them to feel ill.{{Cite news |date=18 June 1994 |title=Tango taken off the shelves |work=[[Aberdeen Press and Journal]] |pages=1}} On 25 August 2005, over 100,000 cans of Tango Cherry and Tango Fruit Fling were recalled over fears they could burst due to having higher-than-normal levels of a naturally occurring [[yeast]], which had made its way inside the drinks during the canning process.{{cite web|url=http://www.thefreelibrary.com/TANGO+BANGO%3B+Drinks+recall+after+explosion+warning.-a0135483532 |title=TANGO BANGO; Drinks recall after explosion warning. - Free Online Library |publisher=Thefreelibrary.com |date=2005-08-26 |access-date=2013-09-02}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== * {{cite web |title=Official website |url=https://tango.co.uk/ |website=Tango.co.uk}} {{citrus sodas}} [[Category:1950 establishments in the United Kingdom]] [[Category:Britvic]] [[Category:Fruit sodas]] [[Category:History of advertising]] [[Category:Orange sodas]] [[Category:Products introduced in 1950]] [[Category:Tango (drink)| ]] [[Category:Soft drinks]]
Tom and Jerry (drink):
{{short description|Christmas-time cocktail in the United States}}
{{Infobox drink

A '''Tom and Jerry''' is a traditional [[Christmas and holiday season|Christmas-time]] cocktail in the United States, sometimes attributed to British writer and [[boxing]] journalist [[Pierce Egan]]<ref>https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1014400-tom-and-jerry "It...is frequently (though not definitively) credited to Pierce Egan, the English chronicler of sports and popular culture." Egan was the author of the 1821 novel ''[[Life in London (novel)|Life in London; or, the Day and Night Scenes of Jerry Hawthorn, Esq., and his elegant friend, Corinthian Tom]]'', on which the stage play of the same year ''[[Tom and Jerry, or Life in London]]'' was based</ref> in the 1820s. It is a variant of [[eggnog]] with [[brandy]] and [[rum]] added and served hot, usually in a mug or a bowl.

Another method uses egg whites, beaten stiff, with the yolks and sugar folded back in, and optionally vanilla extract added. A few spoonfuls are added to a mug, then hot milk and rum are added, and it is topped with [[nutmeg]]. Pre-made Tom and Jerry batter, typically produced by manufacturers in Wisconsin, Minnesota, the Dakotas, and Montana, is sold in regional supermarkets during the Christmas season.<ref>Faust, Eric, Tom and Jerry batter is seasonally available in the [[Jamestown, New York]], area, where a strong Swedish influence is prominent. [http://heavytable.com/connollys-tom-and-jerry-batter-from-superior-wi/ "Connolly's Tom and Jerry Batter from Superior, WI]," Heavy Table, 2009; See also [https://web.archive.org/web/20100116125129/http://www.wisconsinmade.com/gift-ideas/Mrs-Bowens-Tom-Jerry-Mix-2662.aspx Mrs. Bowen's Tom and Jerry Mix].</ref><ref>Tom and Jerrys are so popular in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, that Bryant's Cocktail Lounge maintains a [https://www.jsonline.com/story/entertainment/2019/11/19/tom-and-jerry-classic-wisconsin-cocktail-especially-holidays/2567846001/ dedicated Tom and Jerry room in December], in which the only possible order is a Tom and Jerry.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-12-25 |title=Montana Made: City Bar's Tom and Jerrys |url=https://www.kpax.com/community/montana-made/2018/12/25/montana-made-city-bars-tom-and-jerrys/ |access-date=2023-11-26 |website=KPAX News |language=en}}</ref>

==Name==
The drink's name is a reference to Egan's book, ''[[Life in London (novel)|Life in London]], or The Day and Night Scenes of Jerry Hawthorn Esq. and his Elegant Friend Corinthian Tom'' (1821), and the subsequent stage play ''[[Tom and Jerry, or Life in London]]'' (also 1821). To publicize the book and the play, Egan introduced a variation of eggnog by adding {{convert|1/2|USoz}} of brandy,{{dubious|date=May 2016}} calling it a "Tom and Jerry". The additional fortification helped popularize the drink.<ref name="KPHist">{{Cite web |url=http://www.kitchenproject.com/history/eggnoghistory.htm |title=The History of Egg Nog |last=Block |first=Stephen |website=Food History |publisher=The Kitchen Project |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110510040731/http://www.kitchenproject.com/history/eggnoghistory.htm |archive-date=2011-05-10 |access-date=2006-12-16}}</ref>{{Unreliable source?|sure=n|reason=random web page making questionable historical assertions without citing any sources.|date=December 2020}}

==In popular culture==
Tom and Jerry was a favorite of President [[Warren G. Harding]], who served it at an annual Christmas party for his closest friends.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Russell |first=Francis |title=The Shadow of Blooming Grove: Warren G. Harding In His Times |publisher=Easton Press |year=1968 |isbn=0-07-054338-0 |page=141 |author-link=Francis Russell (author)}}</ref>

Two later cartoon duos, a short-lived [[Tom and Jerry (Van Beuren)|Tom and Jerry]] from Van Beuren Studios in the 1930s, and [[MGM]]'s better known [[Tom and Jerry|cat and mouse rivalry]] from the 1940s through the 1960s, also bore the name, possibly as a [[play on words]] with the drink or the literary works that inspired it.<ref>{{cite book|last1=McMahon|first1=Seán|last2=O'Donoghue|first2=Jo|title=Brewer's Dictionary of Irish Phrase & Fable|year=2004|publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson|location=London|isbn=978-0-304-36334-6|page=799}}</ref>

In the story "[[I Yust Go Nuts at Christmas]]" by [[Harry Stewart]], a man drinks a dozen Tom and Jerrys and is [[hangover|hung over]] for the following day's Christmas dinner.

In the movie "Beyond Tomorrow,1940, RKO Radio Pictures, the story takes place at the Christmas season, and every visitor to the house of the three older gentlemen is offered a "Tom And Jerry" Cocktail.

Tarkhuna:
{{Short description|Georgian carbonated soft drink}} {{Infobox drink | title = Tarkhuna
ტარხუნა
Тархуна | image = 龙蒿汽水.jpg | caption = Bottled Tarkhuna by ''Natakhtari'' | type = [[Soft drink]] | origin = [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] | introduced = {{Start date and age|1887}} | color = [[Green]] | flavor = [[Tarragon]] and [[Galium odoratum|woodruff]] }} {{Georgian cuisine}} '''Tarkhuna''' ({{lang-ka|ტარხუნა}}, {{IPA|ka|tʼaɾχuna}}; {{Langx|ru|Тархуна}}) is a [[Georgian cuisine|Georgian]][https://books.google.com/books?id=3PM_FnWgPBAC&q=tarragon+tarkhuna+&pg=PA43 The Georgian Feast by Darra Goldstein p.43, University of California Press, 1999] carbonated [[tarragon]] and/or [[Galium odoratum|woodruff]]-flavored [[soft drink]], first ever created in 1887 in [[Kutaisi]] by Georgian pharmacist Mitrofan Lagidze. Mitrofan Lagidze began to add odorous chukhpuch containing extract of Caucasian tarragon to sparkling water with natural syrups of his own production.{{Cite web |title=This Bright Green Tarragon Soda Was a Soviet Summer Treat |url=https://www.atlasobscura.com/foods/georgian-tarragon-soda-tarkhuna |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=Atlas Obscura |language=en}} Before the First World War, Lagidze repeatedly received gold medals at international exhibitions for his water.{{Cite web |title=Lagidze Water - Manufacturer - Needl by Wabel |url=https://needl.co/company/lagidze/ |access-date=2024-12-27 |website=needl. |language=en-US}} In 1927, the Soviet authorities built a plant for the production of "[[Lagidze water]]" in [[Tbilisi]], and Lagidze himself was appointed director. ==Availability== As of 2019, Tarkhuna is produced in Georgia by multiple brands including Natakhtari, Zedazeni and Lagidze, in Lithuania by Selita Klasika as ''Tarchunas'' and in Russia, where one of the producers is OAO Narzan under the brand Ledyanaya Zhemjushina. The drink became available on the general [[USSR]] market for the first time in 1981. The pilot batch was sold on the territory of the [[Moscow Botanical Garden of Academy of Sciences| Main Botanical Garden of the USSR Academy of Sciences]] in standard 0.33 liter bottles. Subsequently, its recipe was transferred to food industry enterprises, and, since 1983, "Tarhun" began to be sold in many republics of the USSR and administrative regions of the [[RSFSR]] in bottles of 0.33 and 0.5 liters. == Trademark status == In a trademark dispute between OÜ Acerra and AS Tallinna Karastusjoogid, the Estonian [[Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications]] determined that the word ''Tarhun'' is a descriptive term for the drink, and is thus not trademarkable under the laws of the [[Republic of Estonia]].{{cite web |title=ruling 808-o |work=Majandus- ja Kommunikatsiooniministeeriumi Tööstusomandi Apellatsioonikomisjon |publisher=Majandus- ja Kommunikatsiooniministeerium |date=28 April 2006 |url=http://www.mkm.ee/failid/808_o.pdf |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20091229072638/http://www.mkm.ee/failid/808_o.pdf |archivedate=29 December 2009}} In Estonia, it was possible to find both the Estonian-made and Russian-made Tarhun drinks from the same soft drinks aisle, as the soft drink is distilled and bottled in both countries, though by different companies and with slightly different recipes. In 2015, the Estonian soft drinks company AS Tallinna Karastusjoogid, who were the local producer and distributor of "Tarhun", ceased operations, and its owner AS Haljas put the producer on sale to a 'foreign investor', whose name and country of origin has remained unknown.{{cite news |last=Gamzejev |first=Erik |title=Jõhvi joogitehas võib taas tööle hakata |language=Estonian |trans-title=The Jõhvi drinks factory might start working again |publisher=[[Põhjarannik]] |date=2015-03-20 |url=http://pr.pohjarannik.ee/?p=12846 |url-status=dead |archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20170728085710/http://pr.pohjarannik.ee/?p=12846 |archivedate=2017-07-28}} As of 2019, stores in Estonia variously sell tarkhuna lemonades made in Georgia, Lithuania, and Russia; though none of these tarkhuna brands has reached universal distribution across most store chains. == See also == * [[Duchess (drink)]] * [[Lagidze water]] == References == {{reflist}} [[Category:Soft drinks]] [[Category:Georgian drinks]] [[Category:Russian drinks]] [[Category:1887 introductions]]

'''Wests NZ''' is a manufacturer of [[soft drinks]] and [[Squash (drink)|cordials]] based in [[Dunedin]], New Zealand.<ref name=odt>{{citation|title=Cordial 'custodian' moving on|language=en|work=[[Otago Daily Times]]|date=2021-07-19|access-date=2024-02-02|url=https://www.odt.co.nz/business/cordial-%E2%80%98custodian%E2%80%99-moving|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210719213534/https://www.odt.co.nz/business/cordial-%E2%80%98custodian%E2%80%99-moving|archive-date=19 July 2021|url-status=live}}</ref> It is the oldest continuous manufacturer of soft drinks in New Zealand.<ref name=nzherald-sale-2019>{{citation|title=Kiwi beverage maker Wests Cordials seeks new owner|language=en|work=The New Zealand Herald |date=2019-11-29|access-date=2024-02-02|url=https://www.nzherald.co.nz/property/kiwi-beverage-maker-wests-cordials-seeks-new-owner/JTOJ5SXN6XJELJZDTLONQXYE2M/}}</ref>

== History ==
Wests began production in 1876 when Tom West created a range of cordials<ref name=odt/> in the back of his grocery store in Maclaggan Street, Dunedin.<ref name=odt-longevity-2014>{{citation|title=Dunedin company enjoys taste of longevity|language=en|work=[[Otago Daily Times]] |date=2014-03-18|access-date=2024-02-02|url=https://www.odt.co.nz/business/dunedin-company-enjoys-taste-longevity}}</ref> These proved popular with the city's inhabitants and provided growth for the fledgling business. Production expanded to include [[ginger beer]] in 1906, and in 1914 a purpose-built factory was constructed in [[Saint Kilda, New Zealand|Saint Kilda]] in the south of the city.<ref name=odt-longevity-2014/>

The business was owned by Alf and Kaye Loretan from 2007, before they sold it to Angela and Craig McFarlane in 2021.<ref name=odt/>

== Products ==
Wests today produces soft drinks and cordials in a range of flavours, many of them unique to the brand.{{citation needed|date=February 2024}} These include chocolade (chocolate-flavoured lemonade), RedZenergy (energy drink), cola and raspberry, and pineapple and pear. Wests also produce milkshake and slushy syrups, as well as [[Premix and postmix#Postmix|postmix]] concentrates and soda syrup refills in a variety of flavours.{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}}

=== Sugar-free ===
Many of Wests' regular soft-drink flavours are also offered in [[sugar substitute|sugar-free]] varieties, which has led to the company offering New Zealand's largest range of sugar-free soft drinks.<ref name=odt-longevity-2014/> Diet milkshake as well as soda syrup flavours have recently also been added to the company's sugar-free range.{{Citation needed|date=October 2023}}

== Factory shop ==
Located next to the production factory, Wests' factory shop offers the range of Wests' products as well as general convenience store products.

[[Urge (soft drink)|Urge]] |website={{url|drinkvault.com}}}} '''Vault''' was a [[sweetened]] [[energy drink]] and [[Carbonation|carbonated]] beverage that was released by [[The Coca-Cola Company]] in June 2005 and marketed until December 2011. It was touted as an artificially flavored hybrid energy soda. Coca-Cola was marketing Vault as a combination with the slogan "Drinks like a [[Soft drink|soda]], kicks like an [[energy drink]]," as well as "The Taste. The Quench. The Kick." During this time, the drink was only available in certain markets in [[Alabama]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Kansas]], [[Michigan]], [[North Carolina]], [[South Carolina]], [[Tennessee]], [[Virginia]], [[Texas]], and [[West Virginia]]. Vault was released nationally in February 2006 following commercials that were shown during the pregame show for [[Super Bowl XL]]. == Formulation == Coca-Cola representatives and the [[American Beverage Association]] stated that Vault contained 47 mg of [[caffeine]] per 237 ml (8 fl. oz.) serving,{{cite web |url=http://www.energyfiend.com/caffeine-content/vault |title=Caffeine in Vault |publisher=Energyfiend.com |date=2007-02-07 |access-date=2010-06-02 |archive-date=2010-07-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100729170609/http://www.energyfiend.com/caffeine-content/vault |url-status=live }} or 70.5 mg per 355 ml (12 fl. oz.) can, and 117.5 mg per 20 fl. oz. [[Polyethylene terephthalate|PET]] bottle. This caffeine amount was substantially higher than Surge's 52.5 mg per 12 fl. oz., [[Mountain Dew]]'s 54 mg per 12 fl. oz., [[Mello Yello]]'s 51 mg per 12 fl. oz., or [[Sun Drop]]'s 63 mg per 12 fl. oz. [[Polyethylene terephthalate|PET]] bottles, 6-, 12- and 18-, and 24-pack cans, 1- and 2-liter bottles, and 16 oz extended cans. == Variants == In September 2005, The Coca-Cola Company released Vault Zero, a diet version of the citrus soda. Grape Vault and Peach Vault were two variants available only from [[Freestyle (Coca-Cola)|Coca-Cola Freestyle machines]]. == Advertising == Television commercials for Vault featured men performing extraordinary tasks while drinking Vault, in line with the slogan, "Vault. Get to it!" One such commercial featured a man building a [[robotic]] [[scarecrow]] with laser eyes that rids his farm of crows, foxes, rabbits, and [[hippies]]. Other commercials included a man converting his and his neighbors' backyards into a football field using [[explosives]] and a [[chainsaw]]; a man renovating his house into a giant [[birdcage]]; a man who blows up a reef bed to obtain a large amount of pearls in order to win his girlfriend back from a [[Fabio Lanzoni|Fabio]]esque man, and a man excelling at [[paintball]], at one point using a squirrel as an improvised weapon. {{citation needed|date=March 2014}} == Expansion == ''Vault Red Blitz'', a new Vault flavor, was released in late-February 2007 to compete with PepsiCo's Mountain Dew Code Red, along with promotional pricing in select areas. Until its release, Coca-Cola had only released [[Mello Yello]] Cherry in limited markets as a competitor to Code Red, which has been available since 2001. Vault Red Blitz is berry-flavored, red, and also features the herbal supplement [[guarana]].{{cite web |url=http://www.bevnet.com/news/2006/10-11-2006-Coke_innovation.asp |title=The Coca-Cola Company showcases shopper-driven innovation at NACS 2006 |date=11 October 2006 |publisher=BevNET.com |access-date=2010-06-02 |archive-date=2011-06-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613201314/http://www.bevnet.com/news/2006/10-11-2006-Coke_innovation.asp |url-status=live }} [[File:Vault Red Blitz.jpg|thumb|right|Vault Red Blitz]] In 2006, Vault Zero was reformulated in response to a lawsuit over allegations that ingredients in [[Fanta]] Pineapple and Vault Zero had the potential in certain circumstances to combine to form [[benzene]], a [[carcinogenic]] compound.{{cite web |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna18664391 |title=Coca-Cola settles lawsuits over benzene |work=Food Inc. |publisher=NBC News |date=2007-05-14 |access-date=2010-06-02 |archive-date=2021-10-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211025022208/https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna18664391 |url-status=live }} == See also == * [[List of defunct consumer brands]] == References == {{reflist}} ==External links== *{{commons category-inline|Vault (soft drink)}} {{Coca-Cola brands}} {{citrus sodas}} {{energy drinks}} {{DEFAULTSORT:Vault (Soft Drink)}} [[Category:Coca-Cola brands]] [[Category:Energy drinks]] [[Category:Citrus sodas]] [[Category:Food and drink introduced in 2005]] [[Category:Products and services discontinued in 2011]] [[Category:Defunct drink brands]] [[Category:Discontinued soft drinks]]
